knowledge_statements.statement_title: Three-Dimensional Canonical Neighborhood Theorem
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: (cf. Theorem I.12.1) Given \( \epsilon ,\kappa ,\sigma  > 0 \) and a function \( \Phi \) as above, one can find \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) with the following property. Let \( g\left( \cdot \right) \) be a Ricci flow solution on a three-manifold \( M \) , defined for \( 0 \leq  t \leq  T \) with \( T \geq  1 \) . We suppose that for each \( t, g\left( t\right) \) is complete, and the sectional curvature is bounded on compact time intervals. Suppose that the Ricci flow has \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature and is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales less than \( \sigma \) . Then for any point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{0} \geq  1 \) and \( Q = R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , the solution in \( \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  : {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < {\left( \epsilon Q\right) }^{-1},{t}_{0} - {\left( \epsilon Q\right) }^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{0}}\right\} \) is, after scaling by the factor \( Q \) , \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of a \( \kappa \) -solution.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
We give a proof which differs in some points from the proof in [51] but which has the same ingredients. We first outline the argument.

Suppose that the theorem is false. Then for some \( \epsilon ,\kappa ,\sigma  > 0 \) , we have a sequence of such \( \Phi \) -nonnegatively curved 3-dimensional Ricci flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) defined on intervals \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) , and sequences \( {r}_{k} \rightarrow  0,{\widehat{x}}_{k} \in  {M}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k} \geq  1 \) such that \( {M}_{k} \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales \( < \sigma \) and \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{k}^{-2} \) , but the \( {Q}_{k} \) -rescaled solution in \( {B}_{{\left( \epsilon {Q}_{k}\right) }^{-1/2}}\left( {\widehat{x}}_{k}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{\widehat{t}}_{k} - {\left( \epsilon {Q}_{k}\right) }^{-1},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) is not \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of any \( \kappa \) -solution.

We note that if the statement were false for \( \epsilon \) then it would also be false for any smaller \( \epsilon \) . Because of this, somewhat paradoxically, we will begin the argument with a given \( \epsilon \) but will allow ourselves to make \( \epsilon \) small enough later so that the argument works. To be clear, we will eventually get a contradiction using a fixed (small) value of \( \epsilon \) , but as the proof goes along we will impose some upper bounds on this value in order for the proof to work. (If we tried to list all of the constraints at the beginning of the argument then they would look unmotivated.)

The goal is to get a contradiction based on the "bad" points \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) . In a sense, the method of proof of Theorem 52.7 is an induction on the curvature scale. For example, if we were to make the additional assumption in the theorem that \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) for all \( x \in  M \) and \( t \leq  {t}_{0} \) then the theorem would be very easy to prove. We would just take a convergent subsequence of the rescaled solutions, based at \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) , to get a \( \kappa \) -solution; this would give a contradiction. This simple argument can be considered to be the first step in a proof by induction on curvature scale. In the proof of Theorem 52.7 one effectively proves the result at a given curvature scale inductively by assuming that the result is true at higher curvature scales.

The actual proof consists of four steps. Step 1 consists of replacing the sequence \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) by another sequence of "bad" points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) which have the property that points near \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) with distinctly higher scalar curvature are "good" points. It then suffices to get a contradiction based on the existence of the sequence \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

In steps 2-4 one uses the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) to build up a \( \kappa \) -solution, whose existence then contradicts the "badness" of the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . More precisely, let \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be the result of rescaling \( {g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) by \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . We will show that the sequence of pointed flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) accumulates on a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) , thereby obtaining a contradiction.

In step 2 one takes a pointed limit of the manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) in order to construct what will become the final time slice of the \( \kappa \) -solution, \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . In order to take this limit, it is necessary to show that the manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) have uniformly bounded curvature on distance balls of a fixed radius. If this were not true then for some radius, a subsequence of the manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) would have curvatures that asymptotically blowup on the ball of that radius. One shows that geometrically, the curvature blowup is due to the asymptotic formation of a cone-like point at the blowup radius. Doing a further rescaling at this cone-like point, one obtains a Ricci flow solution that ends on a part of a nonflat metric cone. This gives a contradiction as in the case \( 0 < \mathcal{R} < \infty \) of Theorem 41.2.

Thus one can construct the pointed limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . The goal now is to show that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) is the final time slice of a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) . In step 3 one shows that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) extends backward to a Ricci flow solution on some time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - \Delta ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , and that the time slices have bounded nonnegative curvature. In step 4 one shows that the Ricci flow solution can be extended all the way to time \( \left( {-\infty ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , thereby constructing a \( \kappa \) -solution

Step 1: Adjusting the choice of basepoints.

We first modify the points \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) slightly in time to points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) so that in the given Ricci flow solution, there are no other "bad" points with much larger scalar curvature in a earlier time interval whose length is large compared to \( R{\left( {x}_{k},{t}_{k}\right) }^{-1} \) . (The phrase "nearly the smallest curvature \( Q \) " in [51, Proof of Theorem 12.1] should read "nearly the largest curvature \( Q \) ". This is clear from the sentence in parentheses that follows.) The proof of the next lemma is by pointpicking, as in Appendix H.

Lemma 52.9. We can find \( {H}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty ,{x}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) , and \( {t}_{k} \geq  \frac{1}{2} \) such that \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) , and for all \( k \) the conclusion of Theorem 52.7 fails at \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , but holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right)  \in \; {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - {H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for which \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  \geq  {2R}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

Proof. Choose \( {H}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) such that \( {H}_{k}{\left( R\left( {\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}\right) \right) }^{-1} \leq  \frac{1}{10} \) for all \( k \) . For each \( k \) , initially set \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) . Put \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) and look for a point in \( {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - {H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) at which Theorem 52.7 fails, and the scalar curvature is at least \( {2R}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . If such a point exists, replace \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) by this point; otherwise do nothing. Repeat this until the second alternative occurs. This process must terminate with a new choice of \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) satisfying the lemma.

Hereafter we use this modified sequence \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . Let \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be the result of rescaling \( {g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) by \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . We use \( {\bar{R}}_{k} \) to denote its scalar curvature; in particular, \( {\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = 1 \) . Note that the rescaled time interval of Lemma 52.9 has duration \( {H}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) ; this is what we want in order to try to extract an ancient solution.

Step 2: For every \( \rho  < \infty \) , the scalar curvature \( {\bar{R}}_{k} \) is uniformly bounded on the \( \rho \) -balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) (the argument for this is essentially equivalent to [51, Pf. of Claim 2 of Theorem I.12.1]). Before proceeding, we need some bounds which come from our choice of basepoints, and the derivative bounds inherited (by approximation) from \( \kappa \) -solutions.

Lemma 52.10. There is a constant \( C = C\left( \kappa \right) \) so that for any \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in a Ricci flow solution, if \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  > 0 \) and the solution in \( {B}_{t}\left( {x,{\left( \epsilon R\left( x, t\right) \right) }^{-1/2}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {t - {\left( \epsilon R\left( x, t\right) \right) }^{-1}, t}\right\rbrack \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to a corresponding subset of a \( \kappa \) -solution then \( \left| {\nabla {R}^{-1/2}}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C \) and \( \left| {{\partial }_{t}{R}^{-1}}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C \) .

Proof. This follows from the compactness in Theorem 46.1.

Note that the same value of \( C \) in Lemma 52.10 also works for smaller \( \epsilon \) .

Lemma 52.11. (cf. Claim 1 of I.12.1) For each \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{k} - \frac{1}{2}{H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  {t}_{k} \) , we have \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4{\bar{Q}}_{k} \) whenever \( \bar{t} - c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1/2} \) , where \( {\bar{Q}}_{k} = {Q}_{k} + \left| {{R}_{k}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) }\right| \) and \( c = c\left( \kappa \right)  > 0 \) is a small constant.

Proof. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  2{Q}_{k} \) then there is nothing to show. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  > 2{Q}_{k} \) , consider a spacetime curve \( \gamma \) that goes linearly from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) , and then goes from \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) to \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) along a minimizing geodesic. If there is a point on \( \gamma \) with curvature \( 2{Q}_{k} \) , let \( p \) be the nearest such point to \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) . If not, put \( p = \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) . From the conclusion of Lemma 52.9, we can apply Lemma 52.10 along \( \gamma \) from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( p \) . The claim follows from integrating the ensuing derivative bounds along \( \gamma \) .

Lemma 52.12. In terms of the rescaled solution \( {\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) , for each \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{k} - \frac{1}{2}{H}_{k} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  {t}_{k} \) , we have \( {\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4{\widetilde{Q}}_{k} \) whenever \( \bar{t} - c{\widetilde{Q}}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  c{\widetilde{Q}}_{k}^{-1/2} \) , where \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{k} = 1 + \left| {{\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) }\right| . \)

Proof. This is just the rescaled version of Lemma 52.11.

For all \( \rho  \geq  0 \) , put

(52.13)

\[
D\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {{\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {x,{t}_{k}}\right)  \mid  k \geq  1, x \in  B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) }\right\}  ,
\]

and let \( {\rho }_{0} \) be the supremum of the \( \rho \) ’s for which \( D\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \) . Note that \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) , in view of Lemma 52.12 (taking \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  = \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) ). Suppose that \( {\rho }_{0} < \infty \) . After passing to a subsequence if necessary, we can find a sequence \( {y}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) with \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},{y}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} \) and \( \bar{R}\left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) . Let \( {\eta }_{k} \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) be a minimizing geodesic segment from \( {x}_{k} \) to \( {y}_{k} \) . Let \( {z}_{k} \in  {\eta }_{k} \) be the point on \( {\eta }_{k} \) closest to \( {y}_{k} \) at which \( \bar{R}\left( {{z}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = 2 \) , and let \( {\gamma }_{k} \) be the subsegment of \( {\eta }_{k} \) running from \( {y}_{k} \) to \( {z}_{k} \) . By Lemma 52.12 the length of \( {\gamma }_{k} \) is bounded away from zero independent of \( k \) . Due to the \( \Phi \) -pinching (see (52.4)), for all \( \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) , we have a uniform bound on \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| \) on the balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) . The injectivity radius is also controlled in \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right) \) , in view of the curvature bounds and the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing. Therefore after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the pointed sequence \( \left( {B\left( {{x}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the pointed Gromov-Hausdorff topology (i.e. for all \( \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) we have the usual Gromov-Hausdorff convergence) to a pointed \( {C}^{1} \) -Riemannian manifold \( \left( {Z,{\bar{g}}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , the segments \( {\eta }_{k} \) converge to a segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\eta }_{\infty } \subset  Z \) emanating from \( {x}_{\infty } \) , and \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converges to \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {\eta }_{\infty } \) . Let \( \bar{Z} \) denote the completion of \( \left( {Z,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) , and \( {y}_{\infty } \in  \bar{Z} \) the limit point of \( {\eta }_{\infty } \) . Note that by Lemma 52.9 and part 4 of Corollary 42.1, the Riemannian structure near \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) may be chosen to be many times differentiable. (Alternatively, this follows from Lemma 52.12 and the Shi estimates of Appendix D.) In particular the scalar curvature \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty } \) is defined, differentiable, and satisfies the bound in Lemma 52.10 near \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) .

Lemma 52.14. 1. There is a function \( c : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) depending only on \( \kappa \) , with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}c\left( t\right)  = \; \infty \) , such that if \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) then \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) d{\left( {y}_{\infty }, w\right) }^{2} > c\left( \epsilon \right) \) .

2. There is a function \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \cup  \{ \infty \} \) depending only on \( \kappa \) , with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}{\epsilon }^{\prime }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) , such that if \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) and \( d\left( {{y}_{\infty }, w}\right) \) is sufficiently small then the pointed manifold \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( 2{\epsilon }^{\prime }\left( \epsilon \right) \) -close to a round cylinder in the \( {C}^{2} \) topology.

Proof. It follows from Lemma 52.9 that for all \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) , the pointed Riemannian manifold \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to (a time slice of) a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution. From the definition of pointed closeness, there is an embedded region around \( w \) , large on the scale defined by \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) \) , which is close to the corresponding subset of a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution. This gives a lower bound on the distance \( {\rho }_{0} - d\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) to the point of curvature blowup, thereby proving part 1 of the lemma.

We know that \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {N,\star , h\left( t\right) }\right) \) in the pointed \( {C}^{2} \) -topology. By Lemma 52.10, we know \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) \) tends to \( \infty \) as \( d\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} \) , for \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . In particular, \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {d}^{2}\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) . From part 1 above, we can choose \( \epsilon \) small enough in order to make \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {d}^{2}\left( {w,{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) large enough to apply Proposition 49.1. Hence the pointed manifold \( \left( {N,\star , R\left( \star \right) h\left( t\right) }\right) \) is \( {\epsilon }^{\prime \prime }\left( \epsilon \right) \) -close to a round cylinder, where \( {\epsilon }^{\prime \prime } : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) is a function with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}{\epsilon }^{\prime \prime }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) . The lemma follows.

Note that the function \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) in Lemma 52.14 is independent of the particular manifold \( Z \) that arises in our proof.

From part 2 of Lemma 52.14, if \( \epsilon \) is small and \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) is sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) then \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {C}^{2} \) -close to a round cylinder. The cross-section of the cylinder has diameter approximately \( \pi {\left( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) /2\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . If we form the union of the balls \( B\left( {w,{2\pi }{\left( {R}_{\infty }\left( w\right) /2\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) , as \( w \) ranges over such points in \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) , then we obtain a connected Riemannian manifold \( W \) . By adding in the point \( {y}_{\infty } \) , we get a metric space \( \bar{W} \) which is locally complete, and geodesic near \( {y}_{\infty } \) . As the original manifolds \( {M}_{k} \) had \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature, it follows from Lemma 52.5 that \( W \) is nonnegatively curved. Furthermore, \( {y}_{\infty } \) cannot be an interior point of any geodesic segment in \( \bar{W} \) , since such a geodesic would have to pass through a cylindrical region near \( {y}_{\infty } \) twice. The usual proof of the Toponogov triangle comparison inequality now applies near \( {y}_{\infty } \) since minimizers remain in the smooth nonnegatively curved part of \( \bar{W} \) . Then \( \bar{W} \) has nonnegative curvature in the Alexandrov sense.

This implies that blowups of \( \left( {\bar{W},{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) converge to the tangent cone \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) . As \( \bar{W} \) is three-dimensional, so is \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) [12, Corollary 7.11]. It will be \( {C}^{2} \) -smooth away from the vertex and nowhere flat, by part 2 of Lemma 52.14. Pick \( z \in  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) such that \( d\left( {z,{y}_{\infty }}\right)  = 1 \) . Then for any \( \delta  < \frac{1}{2} \) , the ball \( B\left( {z,\delta }\right)  \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) is the Gromov-Hausdorff limit of a sequence of rescaled balls \( B\left( {{\widehat{z}}_{k},{\widehat{r}}_{k}}\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) where \( {\widehat{r}}_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) , whose center points \( \left( {{\widehat{z}}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) satisfy the conclusions of Theorem 52.7. Applying Lemma 52.12 and Appendix B, if \( \delta  = \delta \left( \kappa \right) \) is taken small enough then we get the curvature bounds needed to extract a limiting Ricci flow solution whose time zero slice is isometric to \( B\left( {z,\delta }\right) \) . Now we can apply the reasoning from the \( 0 < \mathcal{R} < \infty \) case of Theorem 41.2 to get a contradiction. This completes step 2.

Step 3: The sequence of pointed flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) ,\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right) \) accumulates on a pointed Ricci flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) ,\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) which is defined on a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) with \( {t}^{\prime } < {t}_{0} \) . By step 2, we know that the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) at \( y \in  {M}_{k} \) is bounded by a function of the distance from \( y \) to \( {x}_{k} \) . Lemma 52.12 extends this curvature control to a backward parabolic neighborhood centered at \( y \) whose radius depends only on \( d\left( {y,{x}_{k}}\right) \) . Thus we can conclude, using \( \Phi \) -pinching (52.4) and Shi’s estimates (Appendix D), that all derivatives of the curvature \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) are controlled as a function of the distance from \( {x}_{k} \) , which means that the sequence of pointed manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) accumulates to a smooth manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) .

From Lemma 52.5, \( {M}_{\infty } \) has nonnegative sectional curvature. We claim that \( {M}_{\infty } \) has bounded curvature. If not then there is a sequence of points \( {q}_{k} \in  {M}_{\infty } \) so that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}\bar{R}\left( {q}_{k}\right)  = \; \infty \) and \( \bar{R}\left( q\right)  \leq  2\bar{R}\left( {q}_{k}\right) \) for \( q \in  B\left( {{y}_{k},{A}_{k}\bar{R}{\left( {q}_{k}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) , where \( {A}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) ; compare [33, Lemma 22.2]. Lemma 52.9 implies that for large \( k \) , a rescaled neighborhood of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{q}_{k}}\right) \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of a time slice of a \( \kappa \) -solution. As in the proof of Theorem 46.1, we obtain a sequence of neck-like regions in \( {M}_{\infty } \) with smaller and smaller cross-sections, which contradicts the existence of the Sharafutdinov retraction.

By Lemma 52.12 again, we now get curvature control on \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) for a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \Delta ,{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for some \( \Delta  > 0 \) , and hence we can extract a subsequence which converges to a pointed Ricci flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - \Delta ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , which has nonnegative curvature and bounded curvature on compact time intervals.

Step 4: Getting an ancient solution. Let \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) be the maximal time interval on which we can extract a limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) with bounded curvature on compact time intervals. Suppose that \( {t}^{\prime } >  - \infty \) . By Lemma 52.12 the maximum of the scalar curvature on the time slice \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) must tend to infinity as \( t \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) . From the trace Harnack inequality, \( {R}_{t} + \frac{R}{t - {t}^{\prime }} \geq  0 \) , and so

(52.15)

\[
{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  Q\frac{{t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }}{t - {t}^{\prime }},
\]

where \( Q \) is the maximum of the scalar curvature on \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . Combining this with Corollary 27.16, we get

(52.16)

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  \text{ const. }\sqrt{Q\frac{{t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }}{t - {t}^{\prime }}}.
\]

Since the right hand side is integrable on \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , and using the fact that distances are nonincreasing in time (since \( \mathrm{{Rm}} \geq  0 \) ), it follows that there is a constant \( C \) such that

(52.17)

\[
\left| {{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  - {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, y}\right) }\right|  < C
\]

for all \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty }, t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) .

If \( {M}_{\infty } \) is compact then by (52.17) the diameter of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is bounded independent of \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . Since the minimum of the scalar curvature is increasing in time, it is also bounded independent of \( t \) . Now the argument in Step 2 shows that the curvature is bounded everywhere independent of \( t \) . (We can apply the argument of Step 2 to the time- \( t \) slice because the main ingredient was Lemma 52.9, which holds for rescaled time \( t \) .)

We may therefore assume \( {M}_{\infty } \) is noncompact. To be consistent with the notation of I.12.1, we now relabel the basepoint \( \left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) \) as \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Since nonnegatively curved manifolds are asymptotically conical (see Appendix G), there is a constant \( D \) such that if \( y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) , and \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right)  > D \) , then there is a point \( x \in  {M}_{\infty } \) such that

(52.18)

\[
{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, y}\right)  = {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right) \;\text{ and }\;{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  \frac{3}{2}{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right) ;
\]

by (52.17) the same conditions hold at all times \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , up to error \( C \) . If for some such \( y \) , and some \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) the scalar curvature were large, then \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {y, t}\right) ,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( {y, t}\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) would be \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {N, h\left( \cdot \right) ,\left( {z,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) . When \( \epsilon \) is small we could use Proposition 49.1 to see that \( y \) lies in a neck region \( U \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) of diameter \( \approx  R{\left( y, t\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \ll  1 \) .

We claim that \( U \) separates \( {x}_{0} \) from \( x \) in the sense that \( {x}_{0} \) and \( x \) belong to disjoint components of \( {M}_{\infty } - U \) , where \( {x}_{0}, y \) , and \( x \) satisfy (52.18). To see this, we recall that if \( {M}_{\infty } \) has more than one end then it splits isometrically, in which case the claim is clear. If \( {M}_{\infty } \) has one end then we consider an exhaustion of \( {M}_{\infty } \) by totally convex compact sets \( {C}_{t} \) as in Section 46. One of the sets \( {C}_{t} \) will have boundary consisting of an approximate 2-sphere cross-section in the neck region \( U \) , giving the separation.

(For another argument, suppose that \( U \) does not separate \( {x}_{0} \) from \( x \) . Since \( {\widetilde{Z}}_{y}\left( {{x}_{0}, x}\right)  > \frac{\pi }{2} \) (from Proposition 49.1), the segments \( \overline{y{x}_{0}} \) and \( \overline{yx} \) must exit \( U \) by different ends. If \( {x}_{0} \) and \( x \) can be joined by a curve avoiding \( U \) then there is a nonzero element of \( {\mathrm{H}}^{1}\left( {{M}_{\infty },\mathbb{Z}}\right) \) . The corresponding infinite cyclic cover of \( {M}_{\infty } \) will then isometrically split off a line and its quotient \( {M}_{\infty } \) will be compact, which is a contradiction. We thank one of the referees for this argument.)

Obviously, at time \( {t}_{0} \) the set \( U \) still separates \( {x}_{0} \) from \( x \) . Since \( {\bar{g}}_{\infty } \) has nonnegative curvature, we have \( {\operatorname{diam}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( U\right)  \leq  {\operatorname{diam}}_{t}\left( U\right)  \ll  1 \) . Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) has bounded geometry, there cannot be topologically separating subsets of arbitrarily small diameter. Thus there must be a uniform upper bound on \( R\left( {y, t}\right) \) and the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is uniformly bounded (in space and time) outside a set of uniformly bounded diameter. Repeating the reasoning from Step 2, we get uniform bounds everywhere. This contradicts our assumption that the curvature blows up as \( t \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) .

It remains to show that the ancient solution is a \( \kappa \) -solution. The only remaining point is to show that it is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed at all scales. This follows from the fact that the original Ricci flow solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) were \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales less than the fixed number \( \sigma \) .

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \( M \) be an \( n \) -dimensional complete noncompact Riemannian manifold. Suppose \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) , x \in  M \) and \( t \in  \left( {-\infty , T}\right) \) with \( T > 0 \) , is a nonflat ancient solution of the Ricci flow with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature. Then the asymptotic volume ratio of the solution metric satisfies

\[
{\nu }_{M}\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{r \rightarrow   + \infty }}\frac{{\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( {{B}_{t}\left( {O, r}\right) }\right) }{{r}^{n}} = 0
\]

for each \( t \in  \left( {-\infty , T}\right) \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
The proof is by induction on the dimension. When the dimension is two, the lemma is valid by Theorem 6.2.2. For dimension \( \geq  3 \) , we argue by contradiction.

Suppose the lemma is valid for dimensions \( \leq  n - 1 \) and suppose \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) for some \( n \) -dimensional nonflat ancient solution with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature at some time \( {t}_{0} \leq  0 \) . Fixing a point \( {x}_{0} \in  M \) , we consider the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio

\[
A = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty }}R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right) .
\]

We divide the proof into three cases.

Case 1: \( A =  + \infty \) .

By Lemma 6.1.3, there exist sequences of points \( {x}_{k} \in  M \) divergent to infinity, of radii \( {r}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) , and of positive constants \( {\delta }_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) such that

(i) \( R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{k}}\right) R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) for all \( x \) in the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) \) of radius \( {r}_{k} \) around \( {x}_{k} \) ,

(ii) \( {r}_{k}^{2}R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) ,

(iii) \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right) /{r}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) .

By scaling the solution around the points \( {x}_{k} \) with factor \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) , and shifting the time \( {t}_{0} \) to the new time zero, we get a sequence of rescaled solutions

\[
{g}_{k}\left( s\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right)
\]

to the Ricci flow. Since the ancient solution has nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature, there holds the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.5). Thus the rescaled solutions satisfy

\[
{R}_{k}\left( {x, s}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{k}}\right)
\]

for all \( s \leq  0 \) and \( x \in  {B}_{{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) \) . Since \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , it follows from the standard volume comparison and Theorem 4.2.2 that the injectivity radii of the rescaled solutions \( {g}_{k} \) at the points \( {x}_{k} \) and the new time zero is uniformly bounded below by a positive number. Then by Hamilton's compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) will converge to a solution \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) , O}\right) \) to the Ricci flow with

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {y, s}\right)  \leq  1\text{ , for all }s \leq  0\text{ and }y \in  \widetilde{M}\text{ , }
\]

and

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {O,0}\right)  = 1\text{ . }
\]

Since the metric is shrinking, by (ii) and (iii), we get

\[
R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) }^{2}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{k}}\right)  \geq  R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }^{2}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{k}}\right)
\]

which tends to \( + \infty \) , as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) , for all \( s \leq  0 \) . Thus by Proposition 6.1.2, for each \( s \leq  0,\left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) }\right) \) splits off a line. We now consider the lifting of the solution \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) }\right) , s \leq  0 \) , to its universal cover and denote it by \( \left( {\widetilde{\widetilde{M}},\widetilde{\widetilde{g}}\left( s\right) }\right) , s \leq  0 \) . Clearly we still have

\[
{\nu }_{\widetilde{M}}\left( 0\right)  > 0\text{ and }{\nu }_{\widetilde{\widetilde{M}}}\left( 0\right)  > 0\text{ . }
\]

By applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle and the de Rham decomposition theorem, the universal cover \( \widetilde{\widetilde{M}} \) splits isometrically as \( X \times  \mathbb{R} \) for some \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) - dimensional nonflat (complete) ancient solution \( X \) with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature. These imply that \( {\nu }_{X}\left( 0\right)  > 0 \) , which contradicts the induction hypothesis.

Case 2: \( 0 < A <  + \infty \) .

Take a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) divergent to infinity such that

\[
R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow  A,\text{ as }k \rightarrow   + \infty .
\]

Consider the rescaled solutions \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) }\right) \) (around the fixed point \( {x}_{0} \) ), where

\[
{g}_{k}\left( s\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) , s \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack .
\]

Then there is a constant \( C > 0 \) such that

(6.3.1)

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} {R}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  C/{d}_{k}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right) , \\  {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right)  = 1, \\  {d}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0},0}\right)  \rightarrow  \sqrt{A} > 0, \end{array}\right.
\]

where \( {d}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,{x}_{0},0}\right) \) is the distance function from the point \( {x}_{0} \) in the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) \) .

Since \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , it is a basic result in Alexandrov space theory (see for example Theorem 7.6 of [20]) that a subsequence of \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) converges in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to an \( n \) -dimensional metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) with vertex \( {x}_{0} \) .

By (6.3.1), the standard volume comparison and Theorem 4.2.2, we know that the injectivity radius of \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) at \( {x}_{k} \) is uniformly bounded from below by a positive number \( {\rho }_{0} \) . After taking a subsequence, we may assume \( {x}_{k} \) converges to a point \( {x}_{\infty } \) in \( M \smallsetminus  \left\{  {x}_{0}\right\} \) . Then by Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), we can take a subsequence such that the metrics \( {g}_{k}\left( s\right) \) on the metric balls \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \left( { \subset  M}\right. \) with respect to the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) ) \) converge in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a solution of the Ricci flow on a ball \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{\infty },\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) . Clearly the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) limit has nonnegative curvature operator and it is a piece of the metric cone at the time \( s = 0 \) . By (6.3.1), we have

(6.3.2)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1
\]

Let \( x \) be any point in the limiting ball \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{\infty },\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) and \( {e}_{1} \) be any radial direction at \( x \) . Clearly \( \widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{1}}\right)  = 0 \) . Recall that the evolution equation of the Ricci tensor in frame coordinates is

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\widetilde{R}}_{ab} = \widetilde{\bigtriangleup }{\widetilde{R}}_{ab} + 2{\widetilde{R}}_{acbd}{\widetilde{R}}_{cd}.
\]

Since the curvature operator is nonnegative, by applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle (Theorem 2.2.1) to the above equation, we deduce that the null space of Ric is invariant under parallel translation. In particular, all radial directions split off locally and isometrically. While by (6.3.2), the piece of the metric cone is nonflat. This gives a contradiction.

Case 3: \( A = 0 \) .

The gap theorem as was initiated by Mok-Siu-Yau [93] and established by Greene-Wu [49, 50], Eschenberg-Shrader-Strake [45], and Drees [44] shows that a complete noncompact \( n \) -dimensional (except \( n = 4 \) or 8) Riemannian manifold with nonnegative sectional curvature and the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( A = 0 \) must be flat. So the present case is ruled out except in dimension \( n = 4 \) or 8 . Since in our situation the asymptotic volume ratio is positive and the manifold is the solution of the Ricci flow, we can give an alternative proof for all dimensions as follows.

We claim the sectional curvature of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is positive everywhere. Indeed, by Theorem 2.2.2, the image of the curvature operator is just the restricted holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) of the manifold. If the sectional curvature vanishes for some two-plane, then the holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) cannot be \( {so}\left( n\right) \) . We observe the manifold is not Einstein since it is noncompact, nonflat and has nonnegative curvature operator. If \( \mathcal{G} \) is irreducible, then by Berger’s Theorem [7], \( \mathcal{G} = u\left( \frac{n}{2}\right) \) . Thus the manifold is Kähler with bounded and nonnegative bisectional curvature and with curvature decay faster than quadratic. Then by the gap theorem obtained by Chen and the second author in [31], this Kähler manifold must be flat. This contradicts the assumption. Hence the holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) is reducible and the universal cover of \( M \) splits isometrically as \( {\widetilde{M}}_{1} \times  {\widetilde{M}}_{2} \) nontrivially. Clearly the universal cover of \( M \) has positive asymptotic volume ratio. So \( {\widetilde{M}}_{1} \) and \( {\widetilde{M}}_{2} \) still have positive asymptotic volume ratio and at least one of them is nonflat. By the induction hypothesis, this is also impossible. Thus our claim is proved.

Now we know that the sectional curvature of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is positive everywhere. Choose a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) divergent to infinity such that

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  = \sup \left\{  {R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \mid  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right) }\right\}  , \\  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  k, \\  R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  = {\varepsilon }_{k} \rightarrow  0. \end{array}\right.
\]

Consider the rescaled metric

\[
{g}_{k}\left( 0\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right)
\]

as before. Then

(6.3.3)

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} {R}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  {\varepsilon }_{k}/{d}_{k}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right) ,\;\text{ for }{d}_{k}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right)  \geq  \sqrt{{\varepsilon }_{k}}, \\  {d}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0},0}\right)  = \sqrt{{\varepsilon }_{k}} \rightarrow  0. \end{array}\right.
\]

As in Case 2, the rescaled marked solutions \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) will converge in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to a metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) . And by the virtue of Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), up to a subsequence, the convergence is in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology in \( \widetilde{M} \smallsetminus  \left\{  {x}_{0}\right\} \) . We next claim the metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) .

Indeed, let us write the metric cone \( \widetilde{M} \) as a warped product \( {\mathbb{R}}_{ + }{ \times  }_{r}{X}^{n - 1} \) for some \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional manifold \( {X}^{n - 1} \) . By (6.3.3), the metric cone must be flat and \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is isometric to a quotient of the round sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{n - 1} \) by fixed point free isometries in the standard metric. To show \( \widetilde{M} \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) , we only need to verify that \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is simply connected.

Let \( \varphi \) be the Busemann function of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) with respect to the point \( {x}_{0} \) . Since \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) has nonnegative sectional curvature, it is easy to see that for any small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there is a \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) such that

\[
\left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \varphi \left( x\right)  \leq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  M \smallsetminus  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) . The strict positivity of the sectional curvature of the manifold \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) implies that the square of the Busemann function is strictly convex (and exhausting). Thus every level set \( {\varphi }^{-1}\left( a\right) \) , with \( a > \inf \{ \varphi \left( x\right)  \mid  x \in  M\} \) , of the Busemann function \( \varphi \) is diffeomorphic to the \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{n - 1} \) . In particular, \( {\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {a,\frac{3}{2}a}\right\rbrack  \right) \) is simply connected for \( a > \inf \{ \varphi \left( x\right)  \mid  x \in  M\} \) since \( n \geq  3 \) .

Consider an annulus portion \( \left\lbrack  {1,2}\right\rbrack   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) of the metric cone \( \widetilde{M} = {\mathbb{R}}_{ + }{ \times  }_{r}{X}^{n - 1} \) . It is the limit of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) , where

\[
{M}_{k} = \left\{  {x \in  M\left| {\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }} \leq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{2}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right. }\right\}  .
\]

It is clear that

\[
{\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }},\frac{2\left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) }{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right\rbrack  \right)  \subset  {M}_{k} \subset  {\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {\frac{1 - \varepsilon }{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }},\frac{2}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right\rbrack  \right)
\]

for \( k \) large enough. Thus any closed loop in \( \left\{  \frac{3}{2}\right\}   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) can be shrunk to a point by a homotopy in \( \left\lbrack  {1,2}\right\rbrack   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) . This shows that \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is simply connected. Hence we have proven that the metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Consequently,

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow   + \infty }}\frac{{\operatorname{Vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right)  \smallsetminus  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{\sigma r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right) }\right) }{{\left( \frac{r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) }^{n}} = {\alpha }_{n}\left( {1 - {\sigma }^{n}}\right)
\]

for any \( r > 0 \) and \( 0 < \sigma  < 1 \) , where \( {\alpha }_{n} \) is the volume of the unit ball in the Euclidean space \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Finally, by combining with the monotonicity of the Bishop-Gromov volume comparison, we conclude that the manifold \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is flat and isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . This contradicts the assumption.

Therefore, we have proved the lemma. Ⓡ

Finally we would like to include an alternative simpler argument, inspired by Ni [98], for the above Case 2 and Case 3 to avoid the use of the gap theorem, holonomy groups, and asymptotic cone structure.

Alternative Proof for Case 2 and Case 3. Let us consider the situation of \( 0 \leq \; A <  + \infty \) in the above proof. Observe that \( {\nu }_{M}\left( t\right) \) is nonincreasing in time \( t \) by using Lemma 3.4.1(ii) and the fact that the metric is shrinking in \( t \) . Suppose \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , then the solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed for \( t \leq  {t}_{0} \) for some uniform \( \kappa  > 0 \) . By combining with Theorem 6.2.1, there exist a sequence of points \( {q}_{k} \) and a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow   - \infty \) such that the scalings of \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) around \( {q}_{k} \) with factor \( {\left| {t}_{k}\right| }^{-1} \) and with the times \( {t}_{k} \) shifting to the new time zero converge to a nonflat gradient shrinking soliton \( \bar{M} \) in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology. This gradient soliton also has maximal volume growth (i.e. \( {\nu }_{\bar{M}}\left( t\right)  > 0 \) ) and satisfies the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.5). If the curvature of the shrinking soliton \( \bar{M} \) at the time -1 is bounded, then we see from the proof of Theorem 6.2.2 that by using the equations (6.2.24)-(6.2.26), the scalar curvature has a positive lower bound everywhere on \( \bar{M} \) at the time -1 . In particular, this implies the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( A = \infty \) for the soliton at the time -1 , which reduces to Case 1 and arrives at a contradiction by the dimension reduction argument. On the other hand, if the scalar curvature is unbounded, then by Lemma 6.1.4, the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.5) and Lemma 6.1.2, we can do the same dimension reduction as in Case 1 to arrive at a contradiction also. 0

The following lemma is a local and space-time version of Lemma 6.1.4 on picking local (almost) maximum curvature points. We formulate it from Perelman's arguments in the section 10 of [103].

(Hamilton [65]). Let \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) ,0 \leq  t <  + \infty \) , be a noncollapsing nonsingular solution of the normalized Ricci flow on a compact three-manifold \( M \) . Then either

(i) there exist a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) and a sequence of diffeomorphisms \( {\varphi }_{k} : M \rightarrow  M \) so that the pull-back of the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {t}_{k}\right) \) by \( {\varphi }_{k} \) converges in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) topology to a metric on \( M \) with constant sectional curvature; or

(ii) we can find a finite collection of complete noncompact hyperbolic three-manifolds \( {\mathcal{H}}_{1},\ldots ,{\mathcal{H}}_{m} \) with finite volume, and for all \( t \) beyond some time \( T <  + \infty \) we can find compact subsets \( {K}_{1},\ldots ,{K}_{m} \) of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{1},\ldots ,{\mathcal{H}}_{m} \) respectively obtained by truncating each cusp of the hyperbolic manifolds along constant mean curvature torus of small area, and diffeomorphisms \( {\varphi }_{l}\left( t\right) ,1 \leq  l \leq  m \) , of \( {K}_{l} \) into \( M \) so that as long as \( t \) sufficiently large, the pull-back of the solution metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) by \( {\varphi }_{l}\left( t\right) \) is as close as to the hyperbolic metric as we like on the compact sets \( {K}_{1},\ldots ,{K}_{m} \) ; and moreover if we call the exceptional part of \( M \) those points where they are not in the image of any \( {\varphi }_{l} \) , we can take the injectivity radii of the exceptional part at everywhere as small as we like and the boundary tori of each \( {K}_{l} \) are incompressible in the sense that each \( {\varphi }_{l} \) injects \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {\partial {K}_{l}}\right) \) into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) .

The rest of this section is devoted to the proof of Theorem 5.3.4. We will divide the proof into three parts.

## Part I: Subsequence Convergence

According to Lemma 5.1.1, the scalar curvature of the normalized flow evolves by the equation

(5.3.3)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}R = {\Delta R} + 2{\left| Ric\right| }^{2} - \frac{2}{3}{rR}
\]

\[
= {\Delta R} + 2\left| \mathop{\operatorname{Ric}}\limits^{ \circ  }\right|  + \frac{2}{3}R\left( {R - r}\right)
\]

where \( \overset{ \circ  }{Ric} \) is the traceless part of the Ricci tensor. As before, we denote by \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  = \; \mathop{\min }\limits_{{x \in  M}}R\left( {x, t}\right) \) . It then follows from the maximum principle that

(5.3.4)

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{R}_{\min } \geq  \frac{2}{3}{R}_{\min }\left( {{R}_{\min } - r}\right) ,
\]

which implies that if \( {R}_{\min } \leq  0 \) it must be nondecreasing, and if \( {R}_{\min } \geq  0 \) it cannot go negative again. We can then divide the noncollapsing solutions of the normalized Ricci flow into three cases.

Case (1): \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  > 0 \) for some \( t > 0 \) ; Case (2): \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \leq  0 \) for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, + \infty ) \) and \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow   + \infty }}{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) ; Case (3): \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \leq  0 \) for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, + \infty ) \) and \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow   + \infty }}{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  < 0 \) .

Let us first consider Case (1). In this case the maximal time interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) of the corresponding solution of the unnormalized flow is finite, since the unnormalized scalar curvature \( \widetilde{R} \) satisfies

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\widetilde{R} = \Delta \widetilde{R} + 2{\left| \widetilde{R}ic\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
\geq  \Delta \widetilde{R} + \frac{2}{3}{\widetilde{R}}^{2}
\]

which implies that the curvature of the unnormalized solution blows up in finite time. Without loss of generality, we may assume that for the initial metric at \( t = 0 \) , the eigenvalues \( \widetilde{\lambda } \geq  \widetilde{\mu } \geq  \widetilde{\nu } \) of the curvature operator are bounded below by \( \widetilde{\nu } \geq   - 1 \) . It follows from Theorem 5.3.2 that the pinching estimate

\[
\widetilde{R} \geq  \left( {-\widetilde{\nu }}\right) \left\lbrack  {\log \left( {-\widetilde{\nu }}\right)  + \log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - 3}\right\rbrack
\]

holds whenever \( \widetilde{\nu } < 0 \) . This shows that when the unnormalized curvature big, the negative ones are not nearly as large as the positive ones. Note that the unnormalized curvature becomes unbounded in finite time. Thus when we rescale the unnormalized flow to the normalized flow, the scaling factor must go to infinity. In the nonsingular case the rescaled positive curvature stay finite, so the rescaled negative curvature (if any) go to zero. Hence we can take a noncollapsing limit for the nonsingular solution of the normalized flow so that it has nonnegative sectional curvature.

Since the volume of the limit is finite, it follows from a result of Calabi and Yau [112] that the limit must be compact and the limiting manifold is the original one. Then by the strong maximum principle as in the proof of Theorem 5.2.3 (i), either the limit is flat, or it is a compact metric quotient of the product of a positively curved surface \( {\sum }^{2} \) with \( \mathbb{R} \) , or it has strictly positive curvature. By the work of Schoen-Yau [110], a flat three-manifold cannot have a metric of positive scalar curvature, but our manifold does in Case (1). This rules out the possibility of a flat limit. Clearly the limit is also a nonsingular solution to the normalized Ricci flow. Note that the curvature of the surface \( {\sum }^{2} \) has a positive lower bound and is compact since it comes from the lifting of the compact limiting manifold. From Theorem 5.1.11, we see the metric of the two-dimensional factor \( {\sum }^{2} \) converges to the round two-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) in the normalized Ricci flow. Note also that the normalized factors in two-dimension and three-dimension are different. This implies that the compact quotient of the product \( {\sum }^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) cannot be nonsingular, which is also ruled out for the limit. Thus the limit must have strictly positive sectional curvature. Since the convergence takes place everywhere for the compact limit, it follows that as \( t \) large enough the original nonsingular solution has strictly positive sectional curvature. This in turn shows that the corresponding unnormalized flow has strictly positive sectional curvature after some finite time. Then in views of the proof of Theorem 5.2.1, in particular the pinching estimate in Proposition 5.2.5, the limit has constant Ricci curvature and then constant sectional curvature for three-manifolds. This finishes the proof in Case (1).

We next consider Case (2). In this case we only need to show that we can take a noncollapsing limit which has nonnegative sectional curvature. Indeed, if this is true, then as in the previous case, the limit is compact and either it is flat, or it splits as a product (or a quotient of a product) of a positively curved \( {S}^{2} \) with a circle \( {S}^{1} \) , or it has strictly positive curvature. But the assumption \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \leq  0 \) for all times \( t \geq  0 \) in this case implies the limit must be flat.

Let us consider the corresponding unnormalized flow \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) associated to the non-collapsing nonsingular solution. The pinching estimate in Theorem 5.3.2 tells us that we may assume the unnormalized flow \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) exists for all times \( 0 \leq  t <  + \infty \) , for otherwise, the scaling factor approaches infinity as in the previous case which implies the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature. The volume \( \widetilde{V}\left( t\right) \) of the unnormalized solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) now changes. We divide the discussion into three subcases.

Subcase (2.1): there is a sequence of times \( {\widetilde{t}}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) such that \( \widetilde{V}\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) ;

Subcase (2.2): there is a sequence of times \( {\widetilde{t}}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) such that \( \widetilde{V}\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) ;

Subcase (2.3): there exist two positive constants \( {C}_{1},{C}_{2} \) such that \( {C}_{1} \leq  \widetilde{V}\left( t\right)  \leq  {C}_{2} \) for all \( 0 \leq  t <  + \infty \) .

For Subcase (2.1), because

\[
\frac{d\widetilde{V}}{dt} =  - r\widetilde{V}
\]

we have

\[
\log \frac{\widetilde{V}\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{k}\right) }{\widetilde{V}\left( 0\right) } =  - {\int }_{0}^{{\widetilde{t}}_{k}}r\left( t\right) {dt} \rightarrow   + \infty ,\text{ as }k \rightarrow   + \infty ,
\]

which implies that there exists another sequence of times, still denoted by \( {\widetilde{t}}_{k} \) , such that \( {\widetilde{t}}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) and \( r\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{k}\right)  \leq  0 \) . Let \( {t}_{k} \) be the corresponding times for the normalized flow. Thus there holds for the normalized flow

\[
r\left( {t}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow  0,\;\text{ as }\;k \rightarrow  \infty ,
\]

since \( 0 \geq  r\left( {t}_{k}\right)  \geq  {R}_{\min }\left( {t}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Then

\[
{\int }_{M}\left( {R - {R}_{\min }}\right) {d\mu }\left( {t}_{k}\right)  = \left( {r\left( {t}_{k}\right)  - {R}_{\min }\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) V \rightarrow  0,\;\text{ as }k \rightarrow  \infty .
\]

As we take a noncollapsing limit along the time sequence \( {t}_{k} \) , we get

\[
{\int }_{{M}^{\infty }}{Rd}{\mu }^{\infty } = 0
\]

for the limit of the normalized solutions at the new time \( t = 0 \) . But \( R \geq  0 \) for the limit because \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow   + \infty }}{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) for the nonsingular solution. So \( R = 0 \) at \( t = 0 \) for the limit. Since the limit flow exists for \( - \infty  < t <  + \infty \) and the scalar curvature of the limit flow evolves by

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}R = {\Delta R} + 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\right| }^{2} - \frac{2}{3}{r}^{\infty }R,\;t \in  \left( {-\infty , + \infty }\right)
\]

where \( {r}^{\infty } \) is the limit of the function \( r\left( t\right) \) by translating the times \( {t}_{k} \) as the new time \( t = 0 \) . It follows from the strong maximum principle that

\[
R \equiv  0,\;\text{ on }\;{M}^{\infty } \times  \left( {-\infty , + \infty }\right) .
\]

This in turn implies, in view of the above evolution equation, that

\[
\operatorname{Ric} \equiv  0,\;\text{ on }\;{M}^{\infty } \times  \left( {-\infty , + \infty }\right) .
\]

Hence this limit must be flat. Since the limit \( {M}^{\infty } \) is complete and has finite volume, the flat manifold \( {M}^{\infty } \) must be compact. Thus the underlying manifold \( {M}^{\infty } \) must agree with the original \( M \) (as a topological manifold). This says that the limit was taken on \( M \) .

For Subcase (2.2), we may assume as before that for the initial metric at \( t = 0 \) of the unnormalized flow \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) , the eigenvalues \( \widetilde{\lambda } \geq  \widetilde{\mu } \geq  \widetilde{\nu } \) of the curvature operator satisfy \( \widetilde{\nu } \geq   - 1 \) . It then follows from Theorem 5.3.2 that

\[
\widetilde{R} \geq  \left( {-\widetilde{\nu }}\right) \left\lbrack  {\log \left( {-\widetilde{\nu }}\right)  + \log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - 3}\right\rbrack  ,\;\text{ for all }t \geq  0
\]

whenever \( \widetilde{\nu } < 0 \) .

Let \( {t}_{k} \) be the sequence of times in the normalized flow which corresponds to the sequence of times \( {\widetilde{t}}_{k} \) . Take a noncollapsing limit for the normalized flow along the times \( {t}_{k} \) . Since \( \widetilde{V}\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) , the normalized curvatures at the times \( {t}_{k} \) are reduced by multiplying the factor \( {\left( \widetilde{V}\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{k}\right) \right) }^{\frac{2}{3}} \) . We claim the noncollapsing limit has nonnegative sectional curvature. Indeed if the maximum value of \( \left( {-\widetilde{\nu }}\right) \) at the time \( {\widetilde{t}}_{k} \) does not go to infinity, the normalized eigenvalue \( - \nu \) at the corresponding time \( {t}_{k} \) must get rescaled to tend to zero; while if the maximum value of \( \left( {-\widetilde{\nu }}\right) \) at the time \( {\widetilde{t}}_{k} \) does go to infinity, the maximum value of \( \widetilde{R} \) at \( {\widetilde{t}}_{k} \) will go to infinity even faster from the pinching estimate, and when we normalize to keep the normalized scalar curvature \( R \) bounded at the time \( {t}_{k} \) so the normalized \( \left( {-\nu }\right) \) at the time \( {t}_{k} \) will go to zero. Thus in either case the noncollapsing limit has nonnegative sectional curvature at the initial time \( t = 0 \) and then has nonnegative sectional curvature for all times \( t \geq  0 \) .

For Subcase (2.3), normalizing the flow only changes quantities in a bounded way. As before we have the pinching estimate

\[
R \geq  \left( {-\nu }\right) \left\lbrack  {\log \left( {-\nu }\right)  + \log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - C}\right\rbrack
\]

for the normalized Ricci flow, where \( C \) is a positive constant depending only on the constants \( {C}_{1},{C}_{2} \) in the assumption of Subcase (2.3). If

\[
\left( {-\nu }\right)  \leq  \frac{A}{1 + t}
\]

for any fixed positive constant \( A \) , then \( \left( {-\nu }\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) and we can take a noncollapsing limit which has nonnegative sectional curvature. On the other hand if we can pick a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) and points \( {x}_{k} \) where \( \left( {-\nu }\right) \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = \; \mathop{\max }\limits_{{x \in  M}}\left( {-\nu }\right) \left( {x,{t}_{k}}\right) \) satisfies

\[
\left( {-\nu }\right) \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \left( {1 + {t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty ,\;\text{ as }k \rightarrow   + \infty ,
\]

then from the pinching estimate, we have

\[
\frac{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }{\left( {-\nu }\right) \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) } \rightarrow   + \infty ,\;\text{ as }\;k \rightarrow   + \infty .
\]

But \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) are uniformly bounded since normalizing the flow only changes quantities in bounded way. This shows \( \sup \left( {-\nu }\right) \left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Thus we can take a noncollapsing limit along \( {t}_{k} \) which has nonnegative sectional curvature. Hence we have completed the proof of Case (2).

We now come to the most interesting Case (3) where \( {R}_{\min } \) increases monotonically to a limit strictly less than zero. By scaling we can assume \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \rightarrow   - 6 \) as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) .

LEMMA 5.3.6. In Case (3) where \( {R}_{\min } \rightarrow   - 6 \) as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) , all noncollapsing limit are hyperbolic with constant sectional curvature -1 .

Proof. By (5.3.4) and the fact \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \leq   - 6 \) , we have

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \geq  4\left( {r\left( t\right)  - {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) }\right)
\]

and

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\left( {r\left( t\right)  - {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) }\right) {dt} <  + \infty .
\]

Since \( r\left( t\right)  - {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \geq  0 \) and \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \rightarrow   - 6 \) as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) , it follows that the function \( r\left( t\right) \) has the limit

\[
r =  - 6,
\]

for any convergent subsequence. And since

\[
{\int }_{M}\left( {R - {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) }\right) {d\mu } = \left( {r\left( t\right)  - {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) }\right)  \cdot  V,
\]

it then follows that

\[
R \equiv   - 6\text{ for the limit. }
\]

The limit still has the following evolution equation for the limiting scalar curvature

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}R = {\Delta R} + 2{\left| \mathop{\operatorname{Ric}}\limits^{ \circ  }\right| }^{2} + \frac{2}{3}R\left( {R - r}\right) .
\]

Since \( R \equiv  r \equiv   - 6 \) in space and time for the limit, it follows directly that \( \left| \mathop{\operatorname{Ric}}\limits^{ \circ  }\right|  \equiv  0 \) for the limit. Thus the limit metric has \( \lambda  = \mu  = \nu  =  - 2 \) , so it has constant sectional curvature -1 as desired. 0

If in the discussion above there exists a compact noncollapsing limit, then we know that the underlying manifold \( M \) is compact and we fall into the conclusion of Theorem 5.3.4(i) for the constant negative sectional curvature limit. Thus it remains to show when every noncollapsing limit is a complete noncompact hyperbolic manifold with finite volume, we have conclusion (ii) in Theorem 5.3.4.

Now we first want to find a finite collection of persistent complete noncompact hyperbolic manifolds as stated in Theorem 5.3.4 (ii).

## Part II: Persistence of Hyperbolic Pieces

We begin with the definition of the topology of \( {C}^{\infty } \) convergence on compact sets for maps \( F : M \rightarrow  N \) of one Riemannian manifold to another. For any compact set \( K \subset   \subset  M \) and any two maps \( F, G : M \rightarrow  N \) , we define

\[
{d}_{K}\left( {F, G}\right)  = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  K}}d\left( {F\left( x\right) , G\left( x\right) }\right)
\]

where \( d\left( {y, z}\right) \) is the geodesic distance from \( y \) to \( z \) on \( N \) . This gives the \( {C}_{loc}^{0} \) topology for maps between \( M \) and \( N \) . To define \( {C}_{loc}^{k} \) topology for any positive integer \( k \geq  1 \) , we consider the \( k \) -jet space \( {J}^{k}M \) of a manifold \( M \) which is the collection of all

\[
\left( {x,{J}^{1},{J}^{2},\ldots ,{J}^{k}}\right)
\]

where \( x \) is a point on \( M \) and \( {J}^{i} \) is a tangent vector for \( 1 \leq  i \leq  k \) defined by the \( {i}^{th} \) covariant derivative \( {J}^{i} = {\nabla }_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}^{i}\gamma \left( 0\right) \) for a path \( \gamma \) passing through the point \( x \) with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = x \) . A smooth map \( F : M \rightarrow  N \) induces a map

\[
{J}^{k}F : \;{J}^{k}M \rightarrow  {J}^{k}N
\]

defined by

\[
{J}^{k}F\left( {x,{J}^{1},\ldots ,{J}^{k}}\right)  = \left( {F\left( x\right) ,{\nabla }_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}\left( {F\left( \gamma \right) }\right) \left( 0\right) ,\ldots ,{\nabla }_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}^{k}\left( {F\left( \gamma \right) }\right) \left( 0\right) }\right)
\]

where \( \gamma \) is a path passing through the point \( x \) with \( {J}^{i} = {\nabla }_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}^{i}\gamma \left( 0\right) ,1 \leq  i \leq  k \) .

Define the k-jet distance between \( F \) and \( G \) on a compact set \( K \subset   \subset  M \) by

\[
{d}_{{C}^{k}\left( K\right) }\left( {F, G}\right)  = {d}_{B{J}^{k}K}\left( {{J}^{k}F,{J}^{k}G}\right)
\]

where \( B{J}^{k}K \) consists of all \( k \) -jets \( \left( {x,{J}^{1},\ldots ,{J}^{k}}\right) \) with \( x \in  K \) and

\[
{\left| {J}^{1}\right| }^{2} + {\left| {J}^{2}\right| }^{2} + \cdots  + {\left| {J}^{k}\right| }^{2} \leq  1
\]

Then the convergence in the metric \( {d}_{{C}^{k}\left( K\right) } \) for all positive integers \( k \) and all compact sets \( K \) defines the topology of \( {C}^{\infty } \) convergence on compact sets for the space of maps.

We will need the following Mostow type rigidity result.

LEMMA 5.3.7. For any complete noncompact hyperbolic three-manifold \( \mathcal{H} \) with finite volume with metric \( h \) , we can find a compact set \( \mathcal{K} \) of \( \mathcal{H} \) such that for every integer \( k \) and every \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there exist an integer \( q \) and a \( \delta  > 0 \) with the following property: if \( F \) is a diffeomorphism of \( \mathcal{K} \) into another complete noncompact hyperbolic three-manifold \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) with no fewer cusps (than \( \mathcal{H} \) ), finite volume with metric \( \widetilde{h} \) such that

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}^{ * }\widetilde{h} - h\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( \mathcal{K}\right) } < \delta
\]

then there exists an isometry I of \( \mathcal{H} \) to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) such that

\[
{d}_{{C}^{k}\left( \mathcal{K}\right) }\left( {F, I}\right)  < \varepsilon .
\]

Proof. First we claim that \( \mathcal{H} \) is isometric to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) for an appropriate choice of compact set \( \mathcal{K} \) , positive integer \( q \) and positive number \( \delta \) . Let \( l : \mathcal{H} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) be a function defined at each point by the length of the shortest non-contractible loop starting and ending at this point. Denote the Margulis constant by \( \mu \) . Then by Margulis lemma (see for example [55] or [76]), for any \( 0 < {\varepsilon }_{0} < \frac{1}{2}\mu \) , the set \( {l}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {0,{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right\rbrack  \right)  \subset  \mathcal{H} \) consists of finitely many components and each of these components is isometric to a cusp or to a tube. Topologically, a tube is just a solid torus. Let \( {\varepsilon }_{0} \) be even smaller than one half of the minimum of the lengths of the all closed geodesics on the tubes. Then \( {l}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {0,{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right\rbrack  \right) \) consists of finite number of cusps. Set \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0} = {l}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {{\varepsilon }_{0},\infty }\right) \right) \) . The boundary of \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0} \) consists of flat tori with constant mean curvatures. Note that each embedded torus in a complete hyperbolic three-manifold with finite volume either bounds a solid torus or is isotopic to a standard torus in a cusp. The diffeomorphism \( F \) implies the boundary \( F\left( {\partial {\mathcal{K}}_{0}}\right) \) are embedded tori. If one of components bounds a solid torus, then as \( \delta \) sufficiently small and \( q \) sufficiently large, \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) would have fewer cusps than \( \mathcal{H} \) , which contradicts with our assumption. Consequently, \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) is diffeomorphic to \( F\left( {\mathcal{K}}_{0}\right) \) . Here \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0} \) is the interior of the set \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0} \) . Since \( \mathcal{H} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0},\mathcal{H} \) is diffeomorphic to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) . Hence by Mostow’s rigidity theorem (see [97] and [107]), \( \mathcal{H} \) is isometric to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) .

So we can assume \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} = \mathcal{H} \) . For \( \mathcal{K} = {\mathcal{K}}_{0} \) , we argue by contradiction. Suppose there is some \( k > 0 \) and \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) so that there exist sequences of integers \( {q}_{j} \rightarrow  \infty ,{\delta }_{j} \rightarrow  {0}^{ + } \) and diffeomorphisms \( {F}_{j} \) mapping \( \mathcal{K} \) into \( \mathcal{H} \) with

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{j}^{ * }h - h\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{{q}_{j}}\left( \mathcal{K}\right) } < {\delta }_{j}
\]

and

\[
{d}_{{C}^{k}\left( \mathcal{K}\right) }\left( {{F}_{j}, I}\right)  \geq  \varepsilon
\]

for all isometries \( I \) of \( \mathcal{H} \) to itself. We can extract a subsequence of \( {F}_{j} \) convergent to a map \( {F}_{\infty } \) with \( {F}_{\infty }^{ * }h = h \) on \( \mathcal{K} \) .

We need to check that \( {F}_{\infty } \) is still a diffeomorphism on \( \mathcal{K} \) . Since \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a local diffeomorphism and is the limit of diffeomorphisms, we can find an inverse of \( {F}_{\infty } \) on \( {F}_{\infty }\left( \mathcal{K}\right) \) . So \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a diffeomorphism on \( \mathcal{K} \) . We claim the image of the boundary can not touch the image of the interior. Indeed, if \( {F}_{\infty }\left( {x}_{1}\right)  = {F}_{\infty }\left( {x}_{2}\right) \) with \( {x}_{1} \in  \partial \mathcal{K} \) and \( {x}_{2} \in  \overset{o}{\mathcal{K}} \) , then we can find \( {x}_{3} \in  \overset{o}{\mathcal{K}} \) near \( {x}_{1} \) and \( {x}_{4} \in  \overset{o}{\mathcal{K}} \) near \( {x}_{2} \) with \( {F}_{\infty }\left( {x}_{3}\right)  = {F}_{\infty }\left( {x}_{4}\right) \) , since \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a local diffeomorphism. This contradicts with the fact that \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a diffeomorphism on \( \mathcal{K} \) . This proves our claim. Hence, the only possible overlap is at the boundary. But the image \( {F}_{\infty }\left( {\partial \mathcal{K}}\right) \) is strictly concave, this prevents the boundary from touching itself. We conclude that the mapping \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a diffeomorphism on \( \mathcal{K} \) , hence an isometry.

To extend \( {F}_{\infty } \) to a global isometry, we argue as follows. For each truncated cusp end of \( \mathcal{K} \) , the area of constant mean curvature flat torus is strictly decreasing. Since \( {F}_{\infty } \) takes each such torus to another of the same area, we see that \( {F}_{\infty } \) takes the foliation of an end by constant mean curvature flat tori to another such foliation. So \( {F}_{\infty } \) takes cusps to cusps and preserves their foliations. Note that the isometric type of a cusp is just the isometric type of the torus, more precisely, let \( \left( {N, d{r}^{2} + {e}^{-{2r}}{g}_{\mathcal{V}}}\right) \) be a cusp (where \( {g}_{\mathcal{V}} \) is the flat metric on the torus \( \mathcal{V} \) ), \( 0 < a < b \) are two constants, any isometry of \( N \cap  {l}^{-1}\left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack \) to itself is just an isometry of \( \mathcal{V} \) . Hence the isometry \( {F}_{\infty } \) can be extended to the whole cusps. This gives a global isometry \( I \) contradicting our assumption when \( j \) large enough.

The proof of the Lemma 5.3.7 is completed. [

\[

F\right| }_{s = 0} = {Id} \) and \( {\left. \frac{dF}{ds}\right| }_{s = 0} = V \) , a smooth vector field on \( X \) tangent to the boundary (with respect to \( g \) ). \[
{\left. \frac{d}{ds}\right| }_{s = 0}{\left( \Delta F\right) }^{\alpha } = \Delta \left( {V}^{\alpha }\right)  + {g}^{ij}\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{k}}{\Gamma }_{ij}^{\alpha }}\right) {V}^{k}.

\[

\[

Thus we obtain

(5.3.5)

\[
\frac{d}{ds}{ \mid  }_{s = 0}{\left( \Delta F\right) }^{\alpha } = {\left( \Delta V\right) }^{\alpha } + {g}^{ij}\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{k}}{\Gamma }_{ij}^{\alpha } - \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}{\Gamma }_{jk}^{\alpha }}\right) {V}^{k}

\[

- {\left. \left\langle  {\nabla }_{N}F,{\nabla }_{V}N\right\rangle  N\right| }_{s = 0} - {\left. \left\langle  {\nabla }_{N}F, N\right\rangle  {\nabla }_{V}N\right| }_{s = 0}

where \( {II} \) is the second fundamental form of the boundary (as an automorphism of \( T\left( {\partial X}\right) ) \) . \[
\left\{  \begin{array}{ll} {\Delta V} + \operatorname{Ric}\left( V\right)  = 0 & \text{ on }X \\  {V}_{ \bot  } = 0, & \text{ at }\partial X, \\  {\left( {\nabla }_{N}V\right) }_{//} - {2II}\left( V\right)  = 0, & \text{ at }\partial X, \end{array}\right.

Since \( {Rc} < 0 \) and \( {II} < 0 \) we conclude that the kernel is trivial. Clearly this elliptic boundary value is self-adjoint because of the free boundary condition. Thus the cokernel is trivial also. This proves the lemma.
