Thus \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) is a diffeomorphism. A limit of harmonic maps is harmonic, so \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) is a harmonic diffeomorphism from \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) into \( M \) with the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right) \) . Moreover \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) takes \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) to the constant mean curvature hypersurface \( \partial \left( {{F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) }\right) \) of the area \( a \) in \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right) }\right) \) and continue to satisfy the free boundary condition. As a consequence of the standard regularity result of elliptic partial differential equations (see for example [48]), the map \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right)  \in  {C}^{\infty }\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) \) and then from (5.3.10) we have

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }\left( \omega \right) {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } \leq  \delta .
\]

If \( {\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }\left( \omega \right) {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } = \delta \) , we then finish the proof of the claim. So we may assume that \( {\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }\left( \omega \right) {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } < \delta \) . We want to show that \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) can be extended forward in time a little.

We argue by contradiction. Suppose not, then we consider the new sequence of the manifolds \( M \) with metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right) \) and the origins \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( P\right) \) . Since \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) are close to isometries, the injectivity radii of the metrics \( {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right) \) at \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( P\right) \) do not go to zero, and we can extract a subsequence which converges to a hyperbolic limit \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) with the metric \( {\widetilde{h}}_{ij} \) and the origin \( \widetilde{P} \) and with finite volume. The new limit \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) has at least as many cusps as the old limit \( \mathcal{H} \) , since we choose \( \mathcal{H} \) with cusps as few as possible. By the definition of convergence, we can find a sequence of compact sets \( {\widetilde{B}}_{k} \) exhausting \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) and containing \( \widetilde{P} \) , and a sequence of diffeomorphisms \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k} \) of neighborhoods of \( {\widetilde{B}}_{k} \) into \( M \) with \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k}\left( \widetilde{P}\right)  = {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( P\right) \) such that for each compact set \( \widetilde{B} \) in \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) and each integer \( m \)

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{\widetilde{F}}_{k}^{ * }\left( {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right) \right)  - {\widetilde{h}}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{m}\left( \widetilde{B}\right) } \rightarrow  0
\]

as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) . For large enough \( k \) the set \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k}\left( {\widetilde{B}}_{k}\right) \) will contain all points out to any fixed distance we need from the point \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( P\right) \) , and then

\[
{\widetilde{F}}_{k}\left( {\widetilde{B}}_{k}\right)  \supset  {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right)
\]

since the points of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) have a bounded distance from \( P \) and \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) are reasonably close to preserving the metrics. Hence we can form the composition

\[
{G}_{k} = {\widetilde{F}}_{k}^{-1} \circ  {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right)  : {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \rightarrow  \widetilde{\mathcal{H}}.
\]

Arbitrarily fix \( {\delta }^{\prime } \in  \left( {\delta ,{\delta }_{0}}\right) \) . Since the \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k} \) are as close to preserving the metric as we like, we have

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{G}_{k}^{ * }{\widetilde{h}}_{ij} - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } < {\delta }^{\prime }
\]

for all sufficiently large \( k \) . By Lemma 5.3.7, we deduce that there exists an isometry \( I \) of \( \mathcal{H} \) to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) , and then \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right) ,{F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( P\right) }\right) \) (on compact subsets) is very close to \( \left( {\mathcal{H},{h}_{ij}, P}\right) \) as long as \( \delta \) small enough and \( k \) large enough. Since \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( {\partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \) is strictly concave and the foliation of a neighborhood of \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( {\partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \) by constant mean curvature hypersurfaces has the area as a function with nonzero gradient, by the implicit function theorem, there exists a unique constant mean curvature hypersurface with the same area \( a \) near \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( {\partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \) in \( M \) with the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) for \( t \) close to \( \omega \) . Hence, when \( k \) sufficiently large, \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) can be extended forward in time a little. This is a contradiction and we have proved claim (5.3.9).

We further claim that there must be some \( k \) such that \( {\omega }_{k} =  + \infty \) (i.e., we can smoothly continue the family of harmonic diffeomorphisms \( {F}_{k}\left( t\right) \) for all \( {t}_{k} \leq  t <  + \infty \) , in other words, there must be at least one hyperbolic piece persisting). We argue by contradiction. Suppose for each \( k \) large enough, we can continue the family \( {F}_{k}\left( t\right) \) for \( {t}_{k} \leq  t \leq  {\omega }_{k} <  + \infty \) with

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) {g}_{ij}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } = \delta .
\]

Then as before, we consider the new sequence of the manifolds \( M \) with metrics \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) \) and origins \( {F}_{k}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) \left( P\right) \) . For sufficiently large \( k \) , we can obtain diffeomorphisms \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k} \) of neighborhoods of \( {\widetilde{B}}_{k} \) into \( M \) with \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k}\left( \widetilde{P}\right)  = {F}_{k}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) \left( P\right) \) which are as close to preserving the metric as we like, where \( {\widetilde{B}}_{k} \) is a sequence of compact sets, exhausting some hyperbolic three-manifold \( \mathcal{H} \) , of finite volume and with no fewer cusps (than \( \mathcal{H} \) ), and containing \( \widetilde{P} \) ; moreover, the set \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k}\left( {\widetilde{B}}_{k}\right) \) will contain all the points out to any fixed distance we need from the point \( {F}_{k}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) \left( P\right) \) ; and hence

\[
{\widetilde{F}}_{k}\left( {\widetilde{B}}_{k}\right)  \supseteq  {F}_{k}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) \left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right)
\]

since \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) is at bounded distance from \( P \) and \( {F}_{k}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) \) is reasonably close to preserving the metrics. Then we can form the composition

\[
{G}_{k} = {\widetilde{F}}_{k}^{-1} \circ  {F}_{k}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right)  : \;{\mathcal{H}}_{a} \rightarrow  \widetilde{\mathcal{H}}.
\]

Since the \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k} \) are as close to preserving the metric as we like, for any \( \widetilde{\delta } > \delta \) we have

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{G}_{k}^{ * }{\widetilde{h}}_{ij} - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } < \widetilde{\delta }
\]

for large enough \( k \) . Then a subsequence of \( {G}_{k} \) converges at least in \( {C}^{q - 1}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) \) topology to a map \( {G}_{\infty } \) of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) into \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) . By the same reason as in the argument of previous two paragraphs, the limit map \( {G}_{\infty } \) is a smooth harmonic diffeomorphism from \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) into \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) with the metric \( {\widetilde{h}}_{ij} \) , and takes \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) to a constant mean curvature hypersurface \( {G}_{\infty }\left( {\partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \) of \( \left( {\widetilde{\mathcal{H}},{\widetilde{h}}_{ij}}\right) \) with the area \( a \) , and also satisfies the free boundary condition. Moreover we still have

(5.3.11)

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{G}_{\infty }^{ * }{\widetilde{h}}_{ij} - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } = \delta .
\]

Now by Lemma 5.3.7 we deduce that there exists an isometry \( I \) of \( \mathcal{H} \) to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) with

\[
{d}_{{C}^{{l}_{0}}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) }\left( {{G}_{\infty }, I}\right)  < {\varepsilon }_{0}.
\]

By using \( I \) to identify \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}}_{a} \) and \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) , we see that the map \( {I}^{-1} \circ  {G}_{\infty } \) is a harmonic diffeomorphism of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) to itself which satisfies the free boundary condition and

\[
{d}_{{C}^{{l}_{0}}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) }\left( {{I}^{-1} \circ  {G}_{\infty },{Id}}\right)  < {\varepsilon }_{0}.
\]

From the uniqueness in Lemma 5.3.8 we conclude that \( {I}^{-1} \circ  {G}_{\infty } = {Id} \) which contradicts with (5.3.11). This shows at least one hyperbolic piece persists. Moreover the pull-back of the solution metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) by \( {F}_{k}\left( t\right) \) , for \( {t}_{k} \leq  t <  + \infty \) , is as close to the hyperbolic metric \( {h}_{ij} \) as we like.

We can continue to form other persistent hyperbolic pieces in the same way as long as there are any points \( {P}_{k} \) outside of the chosen pieces where the injectivity radius at times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) are all at least some fixed positive number \( \rho  > 0 \) . The only modification in the proof is to take the new limit \( \mathcal{H} \) to have the least possible number of cusps out of all remaining possible limits.

Note that the volume of the normalized Ricci flow is constant in time. Therefore by combining with Margulis lemma (see for example [55] [76]), we have proved that there exists a finite collection of complete noncompact hyperbolic three-manifolds \( {\mathcal{H}}_{1},\ldots ,{\mathcal{H}}_{m} \) with finite volume, a small number \( a > 0 \) and a time \( T <  + \infty \) such that for all \( t \) beyond \( T \) we can find diffeomorphisms \( {\varphi }_{l}\left( t\right) \) of \( {\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{l}\right) }_{a} \) into \( M,1 \leq  l \leq  m \) , so that the pull-back of the solution metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) by \( {\varphi }_{l}\left( t\right) \) is as close to the hyperbolic metrics as we like and the exceptional part of \( M \) where the points are not in the image of any \( {\varphi }_{l} \) has the injectivity radii everywhere as small as we like.

## Part III: Incompressibility

We remain to show that the boundary tori of any persistent hyperbolic piece are incompressible, in the sense that the fundamental group of the torus injects into that of the whole manifold. The argument of this part is a parabolic version of Schoen and Yau's minimal surface argument in [109, 110, 111].

Let \( B \) be a small positive number and assume the above positive number \( a \) is much smaller than \( B \) . Denote by \( {M}_{a} \) a persistent hyperbolic piece of the manifold \( M \) truncated by boundary tori of area \( a \) with constant mean curvature and denote by \( {M}_{a}^{c} = M \smallsetminus  {\overset{ \circ  }{M}}_{a} \) the part of \( M \) exterior to \( {M}_{a} \) . Thus there is a persistent hyperbolic piece \( {M}_{B} \subset  {M}_{a} \) of the manifold \( M \) truncated by boundary tori of area \( B \) with constant mean curvature. We also denote by \( {M}_{B}^{c} = M \smallsetminus  {M}_{B} \) . By Van Kampen’s Theorem, if \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {\partial {M}_{B}}\right) \) injects into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {M}_{B}^{c}\right) \) then it injects into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) also. Thus we only need to show \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {\partial {M}_{B}}\right) \) injects into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {M}_{B}^{c}\right) \) .

We will argue by contradiction. Let \( T \) be a torus in \( \partial {M}_{B} \) . Suppose \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) does not inject into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {M}_{B}^{c}\right) \) , then by Dehn’s Lemma the kernel is a cyclic subgroup of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) generated by a primitive element. The work of Meeks-Yau [86] or Meeks-Simon-Yau [87] shows that among all disks in \( {M}_{B}^{c} \) whose boundary curve lies in \( T \) and generates the kernel, there is a smooth embedded disk normal to the boundary which has the least possible area. Let \( A = A\left( t\right) \) be the area of this disk. This is defined for all \( t \) sufficiently large. We will show that \( A\left( t\right) \) decreases at a rate bounded away from zero which will be a contradiction.

Let us compute the rate at which \( A\left( t\right) \) changes under the Ricci flow. We need to show \( A\left( t\right) \) decrease at least at a certain rate, and since \( A\left( t\right) \) is the minimum area to bound any disk in the given homotopy class, it suffices to find some such disk whose area decreases at least that fast. We choose this disk as follows. Pick the minimal disk at time \( {t}_{0} \) , and extend it smoothly a little past the boundary torus since the minimal disk is normal to the boundary. For times \( t \) a little bigger than \( {t}_{0} \) , the boundary torus may need to move a little to stay constant mean curvature with area \( B \) as the metrics change, but we leave the surface alone and take the bounding disk to be the one cut off from it by the new torus. The change of the area \( \widetilde{A}\left( t\right) \) of such disk comes from the change in the metric and the change in the boundary.

For the change in the metric, we choose an orthonormal frame \( X, Y, Z \) at a point \( x \) in the disk so that \( X \) and \( Y \) are tangent to the disk while \( Z \) is normal and compute the rate of change of the area element \( {d\sigma } \) on the disk as

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{d\sigma } = \frac{1}{2}{\left( {g}^{ij}\right) }^{T}\left( {\frac{2}{3}r{\left( {g}_{ij}\right) }^{T} - 2{\left( {R}_{ij}\right) }^{T}}\right) {d\sigma }
\]

\[
= \left\lbrack  {\frac{2}{3}r - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right) }\right\rbrack  {d\sigma },
\]

since the metric evolves by the normalized Ricci flow. Here \( {\left( \cdot \right) }^{T} \) denotes the tangential projections on the disk. Notice the torus \( T \) may move in time to preserve constant mean curvature and constant area \( B \) . Suppose the boundary of the disk evolves with a normal velocity \( N \) . The change of the area at boundary along a piece of length \( {ds} \) is given by \( {Nds} \) . Thus the total change of the area \( \widetilde{A}\left( t\right) \) is given by

\[
\frac{d\widetilde{A}}{dt} = \iint \left( {\frac{2}{3}r - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right) }\right) {d\sigma } + {\int }_{\partial }{Nds}.
\]

Note that

\[
\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right)  = R\left( {X, Y, X, Y}\right)  + R\left( {X, Z, X, Z}\right)
\]

\[
+ R\left( {Y, X, Y, X}\right)  + R\left( {Y, Z, Y, Z}\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}R + R\left( {X, Y, X, Y}\right) .
\]

By the Gauss equation, the Gauss curvature \( K \) of the disk is given by

\[
K = R\left( {X, Y, X, Y}\right)  + \det {II}
\]

where \( {II} \) is the second fundamental form of the disk in \( {M}_{B}^{c} \) . This gives at \( t = {t}_{0} \) ,

\[
\frac{dA}{dt} \leq  \iint \left( {\frac{2}{3}r - \frac{1}{2}R}\right) {d\sigma } - \iint \left( {K - \det {II}}\right) {d\sigma } + {\int }_{\partial }{Nds}
\]

Since the bounding disk is a minimal surface, we have

\[
\det {II} \leq  0\text{ . }
\]

The Gauss-Bonnet Theorem tells us that for a disk

\[
\int \int {Kd\sigma } + {\int }_{\partial }{kds} = {2\pi }
\]

where \( k \) is the geodesic curvature of the boundary. Thus we obtain

(5.3.12)

\[
\frac{dA}{dt} \leq  \iint \left( {\frac{2}{3}r - \frac{1}{2}R}\right) {d\sigma } + {\int }_{\partial }{kds} + {\int }_{\partial }{Nds} - {2\pi }.
\]

Recall that we are assuming \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) \) increases monotonically to -6 as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) . By the evolution equation of the scalar curvature,

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \geq  4\left( {r\left( t\right)  - {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) }\right)
\]

and then

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\left( {r\left( t\right)  - {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) }\right) {dt} <  + \infty .
\]

This implies that \( r\left( t\right)  \rightarrow   - 6 \) as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) by using the derivatives estimate for the curvatures. Thus for every \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) we have

\[
\frac{2}{3}r - \frac{1}{2}R \leq   - \left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right)
\]

for \( t \) sufficiently large. And then the first term on RHS of (5.3.12) is bounded above by

\[
\iint \left( {\frac{2}{3}r - \frac{1}{2}R}\right) {d\sigma } \leq   - \left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) A.
\]

The geodesic curvature \( k \) of the boundary of the minimal disk is the acceleration of a curve moving with unit speed along the intersection of the disk with the torus; since the disk and torus are normal, this is the same as the second fundamental form of the torus in the direction of the curve of intersection. Now if the metric were actually hyperbolic, the second fundamental form of the torus would be exactly 1 in all directions. Note that the persistent hyperbolic pieces are as close to the standard hyperbolic as we like. This makes that the second term of RHS of (5.3.12) is bounded above by

\[
{\int }_{\partial }{kds} \leq  \left( {1 + {\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) L
\]

for some sufficiently small positive number \( {\varepsilon }_{0} > 0 \) , where \( L \) is the length of the boundary curve. Also since the metric on the persistent hyperbolic pieces are close to the standard hyperbolic as we like, its change under the normalized Ricci flow is as small as we like; So the motion of the constant mean curvature torus of fixed area \( B \) will have a normal velocity \( N \) as small as we like. This again makes the third term of RHS of (5.3.12) bounded above by

\[
{\int }_{\partial }{Nds} \leq  {\varepsilon }_{0}L
\]

Combining these estimates, we obtain

(5.3.13)

\[
\frac{dA}{dt} \leq  \left( {1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) L - \left( {1 - {\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) A - {2\pi }
\]

on the persistent hyperbolic piece, where \( {\varepsilon }_{0} \) is some sufficiently small positive number.

We next need to bound the length \( L \) in terms of the area \( A \) . Since \( a \) is much smaller than \( B \) , for large \( t \) the metric is as close as we like to the standard hyperbolic one; not just on the persistent hyperbolic piece \( {M}_{B} \) but as far beyond as we like. Thus for a long distance into \( {M}_{B}^{c} \) the metric will look nearly like a standard hyperbolic cusplike collar.

Let us first recall a special coordinate system on the standard hyperbolic cusp projecting beyond torus \( {T}_{1} \) in \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{1} \) as follows. The universal cover of the flat torus \( {T}_{1} \) can be mapped conformally to the \( x - y \) plane so that the deck transformation of \( {T}_{1} \) become translations in \( x \) and \( y \) , and so that the Euclidean area of the quotient is 1 ; then these coordinates are unique up to a translation. The hyperbolic cusp projecting beyond the torus \( {T}_{1} \) in \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{1} \) can be parametrized by \( \left\{  {\left( {x, y, z}\right)  \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \mid  z > 0}\right\} \) with the hyperbolic metric

(5.3.14)

\[
d{s}^{2} = \frac{d{x}^{2} + d{y}^{2} + d{z}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}.
\]

Note that we can make the solution metric, in an arbitrarily large neighborhood of the torus \( T \) (of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) ), as close to hyperbolic as we wish (in the sense that there exists a diffeomorphism from a large neighborhood of the torus \( {T}_{B} \) (of \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{B} \) ) on the standard hyperbolic cusp to the above neighborhood of the torus \( T \) (of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) ) such that the pull-back of the solution metric by the diffeomorphism is as close to the hyperbolic metric as we wish). Then by using this diffeomorphism (up to a slight modification) we can parametrize the cusplike tube of \( {M}_{B}^{c} \) projecting beyond the torus \( T \) in \( \partial {M}_{B} \) by \( \{ \left( {x, y, z}\right)  \mid  z \geq  \zeta \} \) where the height \( \zeta \) is chosen so that the torus in the hyperbolic cusp at height \( \zeta \) has the area \( B \) .

Now consider our minimal disk, and let \( L\left( z\right) \) be the length of the curve of the intersection of the disk with the torus at height \( z \) in the above coordinate system, and also let \( A\left( z\right) \) be the area of the part of the disk between \( \zeta \) and \( z \) . We now want to derive a monotonicity formula on the area \( A\left( z\right) \) for the minimal surface.

For almost every \( z \) the intersection of the disk with the torus at height \( z \) is a smooth embedded curve or a finite union of them by the standard transversality theorem. If there is more than one curve, at least one of them is not homotopic to a point in \( T \) and represents the primitive generator in the kernel of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) such that a part of the original disk beyond height \( z \) continues to a disk that bounds it. We extend this disk back to the initial height \( \zeta \) by dropping the curve straight down. Let \( \widetilde{L}\left( z\right) \) be the length of the curve we picked at height \( z \) ; of course \( \widetilde{L}\left( z\right)  \leq  L\left( z\right) \) with equality if it is the only piece. Let \( \widetilde{L}\left( w\right) \) denote the length of the same curve in the \( x - y \) plane dropped down to height \( w \) for \( \zeta  \leq  w \leq  z \) . In the hyperbolic space we would have

\[
\widetilde{L}\left( w\right)  = \frac{z}{w}\widetilde{L}\left( z\right)
\]

exactly. In our case there is a small error proportional to \( \widetilde{L}\left( z\right) \) and we can also take it proportional to the distance \( z - w \) by which it drops since \( {\left. \widetilde{L}\left( w\right) \right| }_{w = z} = \widetilde{L}\left( z\right) \) and the solution metric is close to the hyperbolic in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology. Thus, for arbitrarily given \( \delta  > 0 \) and \( {\zeta }^{ * } > \zeta \) , as the solution metric is sufficiently close to hyperbolic, we have

\[
\left| {\widetilde{L}\left( w\right)  - \frac{z}{w}\widetilde{L}\left( z\right) }\right|  \leq  \delta \left( {z - w}\right) \widetilde{L}\left( z\right)
\]

for all \( z \) and \( w \) in \( \zeta  \leq  w \leq  z \leq  {\zeta }^{ * } \) . Now given \( \varepsilon \) and \( {\zeta }^{ * } \) pick \( \delta  = {2\varepsilon }/{\zeta }^{ * } \) . Then

(5.3.15)

\[
\widetilde{L}\left( w\right)  \leq  \frac{z}{w}\widetilde{L}\left( z\right) \left\lbrack  {1 + \frac{{2\varepsilon }\left( {z - w}\right) }{w}}\right\rbrack  .
\]

When we drop the curve vertically for the construction of the new disk we get an area \( \widetilde{A}\left( z\right) \) between \( \zeta \) and \( z \) given by

\[
\widetilde{A}\left( z\right)  = \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) {\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{\widetilde{L}\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}.
\]

Here and in the following \( o\left( 1\right) \) denotes various small error quantities as the solution metric close to hyperbolic. On the other hand if we do not drop vertically we pick up even more area, so the area \( A\left( z\right) \) of the original disk between \( \zeta \) and \( z \) has

(5.3.16)

\[
A\left( z\right)  \geq  \left( {1 - o\left( 1\right) }\right) {\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}.
\]

Since the original disk minimized among all disks bounded a curve in the primitive generator of the kernel of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) , and the new disk beyond the height \( z \) is part of the original disk, we have

\[
A\left( z\right)  \leq  \widetilde{A}\left( z\right)
\]

and then by combining with (5.3.15),

\[
{\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw} \leq  \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) z\widetilde{L}\left( z\right) {\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\left\lbrack  {\frac{1 - {2\varepsilon }}{{w}^{2}} + \frac{2\varepsilon z}{{w}^{3}}}\right\rbrack  {dw}
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) L\left( z\right) \frac{\left( z - \zeta \right) }{\zeta }\left\lbrack  {1 + \varepsilon \left( \frac{z - \zeta }{\zeta }\right) }\right\rbrack  .
\]

Here we used the fact that \( \widetilde{L}\left( z\right)  \leq  L\left( z\right) \) . Since the solution metric is sufficiently close to hyperbolic, we have

\[
\frac{d}{dz}\left( {{\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}}\right)  = \frac{L\left( z\right) }{z}
\]

\[
\geq  \left( {1 - o\left( 1\right) }\right) \frac{\zeta }{z\left( {z - \zeta }\right) }\left\lbrack  {1 - \varepsilon \left( \frac{z - \zeta }{\zeta }\right) }\right\rbrack  {\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}
\]

\[
\geq  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{z - \zeta } - \frac{1 + {2\varepsilon }}{z}}\right\rbrack  {\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}
\]

or equivalently

(5.3.17)

\[
\frac{d}{dz}\log \left\{  {\frac{{z}^{1 + {2\varepsilon }}}{\left( z - \zeta \right) }{\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}}\right\}   \geq  0.
\]

This is the desired monotonicity formula for the area \( A\left( z\right) \) .

It follows directly from (5.3.16) and (5.3.17) that

\[
\frac{{z}^{1 + {2\varepsilon }}}{\left( z - \zeta \right) }A\left( z\right)  \geq  \left( {1 - o\left( 1\right) }\right) {\zeta }^{2\varepsilon }L\left( \zeta \right)
\]

or equivalently

\[
L\left( \zeta \right)  \leq  \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) {\left( \frac{z}{\zeta }\right) }^{2\varepsilon }\frac{z}{z - \zeta }A\left( z\right)
\]

for all \( z \in  \left\lbrack  {\zeta ,{\zeta }^{ * }}\right\rbrack \) . Since the solution metric, in an arbitrarily large neighborhood of the torus \( T \) (of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) ), as close to hyperbolic as we wish, we may assume that \( {\zeta }^{ * } \) is so large that \( \sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }} > \zeta \) and \( \frac{\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }}}{\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }} - \zeta } \) is close to 1, and also \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) is so small that \( {\left( \frac{\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }}}{\zeta }\right) }^{2\varepsilon } \) is close to 1 . Thus for arbitrarily small \( {\delta }_{0} > 0 \) , we have

(5.3.18)

\[
L\left( \zeta \right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{0}}\right) A\left( \sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }}\right) .
\]

Now recall that (5.3.13) states

\[
\frac{dA}{dt} \leq  \left( {1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) L - \left( {1 - {\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) A - {2\pi }.
\]

We now claim that if

\[
\left( {1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) L - \left( {1 - {\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) A \geq  0
\]

then \( L = L\left( \zeta \right) \) is uniformly bounded from above.

Indeed by the assumption we have

\[
A\left( {\zeta }^{ * }\right)  \leq  \frac{\left( 1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}\right) }{\left( 1 - {\varepsilon }_{0}\right) }L\left( \zeta \right)
\]

since \( A\left( {\zeta }^{ * }\right)  \leq  A \) . By combining with (5.3.16) we have some \( {z}_{0} \in  \left( {\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }},{\zeta }^{ * }}\right) \) satisfying

\[
\frac{L\left( {z}_{0}\right) }{{z}_{0}}\left( {{\zeta }^{ * } - \sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }}}\right)  \leq  {\int }_{\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }}}^{{\zeta }^{ * }}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) A\left( {\zeta }^{ * }\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) \left( \frac{1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}}{1 - {\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) L\left( \zeta \right) .
\]

Thus for \( {\zeta }^{ * } \) suitably large, by noting that the solution metric on a large neighborhood of \( T \) (of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) ) is sufficiently close to hyperbolic, we have

(5.3.19)

\[
L\left( {z}_{0}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + 4{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) \frac{{z}_{0}}{{\zeta }^{ * }}L\left( \zeta \right)
\]

for some \( {z}_{0} \in  \left( {\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }},{\zeta }^{ * }}\right) \) . It is clear that we may assume the intersection curve between the minimal disk with the torus at this height \( {z}_{0} \) is smooth and embedded. If the intersection curve at the height \( {z}_{0} \) has more than one piece, as before one of them will represent the primitive generator in the kernel of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) , and we can ignore the others. Let us move (the piece of) the intersection curve on the torus at height \( {z}_{0} \) through as small as possible area in the same homotopy class of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) to a curve which is a geodesic circle in the flat torus coming from our special coordinates, and then drop this geodesic circle vertically in the special coordinates to obtain another new disk. We will compare the area of this new disk with the original minimal disk as follows.

Denote by \( G \) the length of the geodesic circle in the standard hyperbolic cusp at height 1 . Then the length of the geodesic circle at height \( {z}_{0} \) will be \( G/{z}_{0} \) . Observe that given an embedded curve of length \( l \) circling the cylinder \( {S}^{1} \times  \mathbb{R} \) of circumference \( w \) once, it is possible to deform the curve through an area not bigger than \( {lw} \) into a meridian circle. Note that (the piece of) the intersection curve represents the primitive generator in the kernel of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) . Note also that the solution metric is sufficiently close to the hyperbolic metric. Then the area of the deformation from (the piece of) the intersection curve on the torus at height \( {z}_{0} \) to the geodesic circle at height \( {z}_{0} \) is bounded by

\[
\left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) \left( \frac{G}{{z}_{0}}\right)  \cdot  L\left( {z}_{0}\right) .
\]

The area to drop the geodesic circle from height \( {z}_{0} \) to height \( \zeta \) is bounded by

\[
\left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) {\int }_{\zeta }^{{z}_{0}}\frac{G}{{w}^{2}}{dw}.
\]

Hence comparing the area of the original minimal disk to that of this new disk gives

\[
A\left( {z}_{0}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) G\left\lbrack  {\frac{L\left( {z}_{0}\right) }{{z}_{0}} + \left( {\frac{1}{\zeta } - \frac{1}{{z}_{0}}}\right) }\right\rbrack  .
\]

By (5.3.18),(5.3.19) and the fact that \( {z}_{0} \in  \left( {\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }},{\zeta }^{ * }}\right) \) , this in turn gives

\[
L\left( \zeta \right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{0}}\right) A\left( {z}_{0}\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{0}}\right) G\left\lbrack  {\left( {1 + 4{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) \frac{L\left( \zeta \right) }{{\zeta }^{ * }} + \frac{1}{\zeta }}\right\rbrack  .
\]

Since \( {\zeta }^{ * } \) is suitably large, we obtain

\[
L\left( \zeta \right)  \leq  {2G}/\zeta
\]

This gives the desired assertion since \( G \) is fixed from the geometry of the limit hyperbolic manifold \( \mathcal{H} \) and \( \zeta \) is very large as long as the area \( B \) of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) small enough.

Thus the combination of (5.3.13), (5.3.18) and the assertion implies that either

\[
\frac{d}{dt}A \leq   - {2\pi }
\]

\[
\frac{d}{dt}A \leq  \left( {1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) L - \left( {1 - {\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) A - {2\pi }
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) \frac{2G}{\zeta } - {2\pi }
\]

\[
\leq   - \pi
\]

since the solution metric on a very large neighborhood of the torus \( T \) (of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) ) is sufficiently close to hyperbolic and \( \zeta \) is very large as the area \( B \) of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) small enough. This is impossible because \( A \geq  0 \) and the persistent hyperbolic pieces go on forever. The contradiction shows that \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) in fact injects into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {M}_{B}^{c}\right) \) . This proves that \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {\partial {M}_{B}}\right) \) injects into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) .

Therefore we have completed the proof of Theorem 5.3.4. [

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: (Singularity structure theorem). Given \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) and \( {T}_{0} > 1 \) , one can find \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) with the following property. If \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) , x \in  M \) and \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( 1 < T \leq  {T}_{0} \) , is a solution to the Ricci flow on a compact orientable three-manifold \( M \) with normalized initial metric, then for any point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{0} \geq  1 \) and \( Q = \; R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , the solution in \( \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < {\varepsilon }^{-2}{Q}^{-1},\;{t}_{0} - {\varepsilon }^{-2}{Q}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{0}}\right\} \) is, after scaling by the factor \( Q,\varepsilon \) -close (in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  {\varepsilon }^{-1}\right\rbrack  } \) -topology) to the corresponding subset of some orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution (for some \( \kappa  > 0 \) ).

Since the initial metric is normalized, it follows from the no local collapsing theorem I or I' (and their proofs) that there is a positive constant \( \kappa \) , depending only on \( {T}_{0} \) , such that the solution in Theorem 7.1.1 is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on all scales less than \( \sqrt{{T}_{0}} \) . Let \( C\left( \varepsilon \right) \) be a positive constant larger than or equal to \( {\varepsilon }^{-2} \) . It suffices to prove that there exists \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) such that for any point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{0} \geq  1 \) and \( Q = \; R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , the solution in the parabolic region \( \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  M\times \lbrack 0, T) \mid  {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < }\right. \; \left. {C\left( \varepsilon \right) {Q}^{-1},{t}_{0} - C\left( \varepsilon \right) {Q}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{0}}\right\} \) is, after scaling by the factor \( Q,\varepsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of some orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. The constant \( C\left( \varepsilon \right) \) will be determined later.

We argue by contradiction. Suppose for some \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there exist a sequence of solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) to the Ricci flow on compact orientable three-manifolds with normalized initial metrics, defined on the time intervals \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{k}}\right) \) with \( 1 < {T}_{k} \leq  {T}_{0} \) , a sequence of positive numbers \( {r}_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) , and a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) and times \( {t}_{k} \geq  1 \) with \( {Q}_{k} = {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{k}^{-2} \) such that each solution \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) in the parabolic region \( \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{k}}\right)  \mid  {d}_{{t}_{k}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{k}}\right)  < C\left( \varepsilon \right) {Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k} - C\left( \varepsilon \right) {Q}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{k}}\right\} \) is not, after scaling by the factor \( {Q}_{k},\varepsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of any orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, where \( {R}_{k} \) denotes the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}}\right) \) .

For each solution \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) , we may adjust the point \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{k} \geq  \frac{1}{2} \) and with \( {Q}_{k} = {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) to be as large as possible so that the conclusion of the theorem fails at \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , but holds for any \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - {H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) satisfying \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  2{Q}_{k} \) , where \( {H}_{k} = \frac{1}{4}{r}_{k}^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Indeed, suppose not, by setting \( \left( {{x}_{{k}_{1}},{t}_{{k}_{1}}}\right)  = \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , we can choose a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{{k}_{l}},{t}_{{k}_{l}}}\right)  \in  {M}_{k} \times \; \left\lbrack  {{t}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }} - {H}_{k}{R}_{k}{\left( {x}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }},{t}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }}\right) }^{-1},{t}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }}}\right\rbrack \) such that \( {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{l}},{t}_{{k}_{l}}}\right)  \geq  2{R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }},{t}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }}}\right) \) and the conclusion of the theorem fails at \( \left( {{x}_{{k}_{l}},{t}_{{k}_{l}}}\right) \) for each \( l = 2,3,\ldots \) . Since the solution is smooth, but

\[
{R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{l}},{t}_{{k}_{l}}}\right)  \geq  2{R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }},{t}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }}}\right)  \geq  \cdots  \geq  {2}^{l - 1}{R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,
\]

and

\[
{t}_{{k}_{l}} \geq  {t}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }} - {H}_{k}{R}_{k}{\left( {x}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }},{t}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }}\right) }^{-1}
\]

\[
\geq  {t}_{k} - {H}_{k}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{{l - 1}}\frac{1}{{2}^{i - 1}}{R}_{k}{\left( {x}_{k},{t}_{k}\right) }^{-1}
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{1}{2}
\]

this process must terminate after a finite number of steps and the last element fits.

Let \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) be the rescaled solutions obtained by rescaling \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) around \( {x}_{k} \) with the factors \( {Q}_{k} = {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) and shifting the time \( {t}_{k} \) to the new time zero. Denote by \( {\widetilde{R}}_{k} \) the rescaled scalar curvature. We will show that a subsequence of the orientable rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, which is a contradiction. In the following we divide the argument into four steps.

Step 1. First of all, we need a local bound on curvatures.

Lemma 7.1.2. For each \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{k} - \frac{1}{2}{H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  {t}_{k} \) , we have \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4{\bar{Q}}_{k} \) whenever \( \bar{t} - c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {d}_{\bar{t}}^{2}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1} \) , where \( {\bar{Q}}_{k} = {Q}_{k} + {R}_{k}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) and \( c > 0 \) is a small universal constant.

Proof. Consider any point \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {B}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{\left( c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} - c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) with \( c > 0 \) to be determined. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  2{Q}_{k} \) , there is nothing to show. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  > 2{Q}_{k} \) , consider a space-time curve \( \gamma \) from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) that goes straight from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) and goes from \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) to \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) along a minimizing geodesic (with respect to the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,\bar{t}}\right) \) ). If there is a point on \( \gamma \) with the scalar curvature \( 2{Q}_{k} \) , let \( {y}_{0} \) be the nearest such point to \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) . If not, put \( {y}_{0} = \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) . On the segment of \( \gamma \) from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( {y}_{0} \) , the scalar curvature is at least \( 2{Q}_{k} \) . According to the choice of the point \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , the solution along the segment is \( \varepsilon \) -close to that of some ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. It follows from Theorem 6.4.3 (ii) that

\[
\left| {\nabla \left( {R}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) }\right|  \leq  {2\eta }\text{ and }\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {R}_{k}^{-1}\right) }\right|  \leq  {2\eta }
\]

on the segment. (Here, without loss of generality, we may assume \( \varepsilon \) is suitably small). Then by choosing \( c > 0 \) (depending only on \( \eta \) ) small enough we get the desired curvature bound by integrating the above derivative estimates along the segment. This proves the lemma.

Step 2. Next we want to show that for each \( A <  + \infty \) , there exist a positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) (independent of \( k \) ) such that the curvatures of the rescaled solutions

\( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at the new time \( t = 0 \) (corresponding to the original times \( {t}_{k} \) ) satisfy the estimate

\[
\left| \widetilde{R{m}_{k}}\right| \left( {y,0}\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)
\]

whenever \( {d}_{{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) }\left( {y,{x}_{k}}\right)  \leq  A \) and \( k \geq  1 \) .

For each \( \rho  \geq  0 \) , set

\[
M\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {{\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \mid  k \geq  1, x \in  {M}_{k}\text{ with }{d}_{0}\left( {x,{x}_{k}}\right)  \leq  \rho }\right\}
\]

and

\[
{\rho }_{0} = \sup \{ \rho  \geq  0 \mid  M\left( \rho \right)  <  + \infty \} .
\]

By the pinching estimate (7.1.1), it suffices to show \( {\rho }_{0} =  + \infty \) .

Note that \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) by applying Lemma 7.1.2 with \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  = \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . We now argue by contradiction to show \( {\rho }_{0} =  + \infty \) . Suppose not, we may find (after passing to a subsequence if necessary) a sequence of points \( {y}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) with \( {d}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},{y}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) and \( {\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {{y}_{k},0}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Let \( {\gamma }_{k}\left( { \subset  {M}_{k}}\right) \) be a minimizing geodesic segment from \( {x}_{k} \) to \( {y}_{k} \) . Let \( {z}_{k} \in  {\gamma }_{k} \) be the point on \( {\gamma }_{k} \) closest to \( {y}_{k} \) with \( {\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {{z}_{k},0}\right)  = 2 \) , and let \( {\beta }_{k} \) be the subsegment of \( {\gamma }_{k} \) running from \( {z}_{k} \) to \( {y}_{k} \) . By Lemma 7.1.2 the length of \( {\beta }_{k} \) is bounded away from zero independent of \( k \) . By the pinching estimate (7.1.1), for each \( \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) , we have a uniform bound on the curvatures on the open balls \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}}\right) \) . The injectivity radii of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k} \) at the points \( {x}_{k} \) and the time \( t = 0 \) are also uniformly bounded from below by the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property. Therefore by Lemma 7.1.2 and Hamilton's compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the marked sequence \( \left( {{B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , the segments \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( {x}_{\infty } \) , and \( {\beta }_{k} \) converges to a subsegment \( {\beta }_{\infty } \) of \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . Let \( {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) denote the completion of \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) , and \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) the limit point of \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) .

Denote by \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty } \) the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) . Since the rescaled scalar curvatures \( {\widetilde{R}}_{k} \) along \( {\beta }_{k} \) are at least 2, it follows from the choice of the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) that for any \( {q}_{0} \in  {\beta }_{\infty } \) , the manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) in \( \left\{  {q \in  {B}_{\infty } \mid  {\operatorname{dist}}_{{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }}^{2}\left( {q,{q}_{0}}\right)  < C\left( \varepsilon \right) {\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-1}}\right\} \) is \( {2\varepsilon } \) -close to the corresponding subset of (a time slice of) some orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. Then by Theorem 6.4.6, we know that the orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution at each point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) has a radius \( r,0 < r < {C}_{1}\left( {2\varepsilon }\right) R{\left( x, t\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , such that its canonical neighborhood \( B \) , with \( {B}_{t}\left( {x, r}\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{t}\left( {x,{2r}}\right) \) , is either an evolving \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, or an evolving \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap, or a compact manifold (without boundary) diffeomorphic to a metric quotient of the round three-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) , and moreover the scalar curvature is between \( {\left( {C}_{2}\left( 2\varepsilon \right) \right) }^{-1}R\left( {x, t}\right) \) and \( {C}_{2}\left( {2\varepsilon }\right) R\left( {x, t}\right) \) , where \( {C}_{1}\left( {2\varepsilon }\right) \) and \( {C}_{2}\left( {2\varepsilon }\right) \) are the positive constants in Theorem 6.4.6.

We now choose \( C\left( \varepsilon \right)  = \max \left\{  {2{C}_{1}^{2}\left( {2\varepsilon }\right) ,{\varepsilon }^{-2}}\right\} \) . By the local curvature estimate in Lemma 7.1.2, we see that the scalar curvature \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty } \) becomes unbounded when approaching \( {y}_{\infty } \) along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . This implies that the canonical neighborhood around \( {q}_{0} \) cannot be a compact manifold (without boundary) diffeomorphic to a metric quotient of the round three-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) . Note that \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) is shortest since it is the limit of a sequence of shortest geodesics. Without loss of generality, we may assume \( \varepsilon \) is suitably small (say, \( \varepsilon  \leq  \frac{1}{100} \) ). These imply that as \( {q}_{0} \) gets sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) , the canonical neighborhood around \( {q}_{0} \) cannot be an evolving \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap. Thus we conclude that each \( {q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) is the center of an evolving \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck.

Let

\[
U = \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{{q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty }}}B\left( {{q}_{0},{4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \;\left( { \subset  \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }}\right) }\right) ,
\]

where \( B\left( {{q}_{0},{4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) is the ball centered at \( {q}_{0} \in  {B}_{\infty } \) with the radius \( {4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . Clearly \( U \) has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching estimate (7.1.1). Since the metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{\infty } \) is cylindrical at any point \( {q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) which is sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) , we see that the metric space \( \bar{U} = U \cup  \left\{  {y}_{\infty }\right\} \) by adding in the point \( {y}_{\infty } \) , is locally complete and intrinsic near \( {y}_{\infty } \) . Furthermore \( {y}_{\infty } \) cannot be an interior point of any geodesic segment in \( \bar{U} \) . This implies the curvature of \( \bar{U} \) at \( {y}_{\infty } \) is nonnegative in the Alexandrov sense. It is a basic result in Alexandrov space theory (see for example Theorem 10.9.3 and Corollary 10.9.5 of [9]) that there exists a three-dimensional tangent cone \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{U} \) at \( {y}_{\infty } \) which is a metric cone. It is clear that its aperture is \( \leq  {10\varepsilon } \) , thus the tangent cone is nonflat.

Pick a point \( p \in  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{U} \) such that the distance from the vertex \( {y}_{\infty } \) to \( p \) is one and it is nonflat around \( p \) . Then the ball \( B\left( {p,\frac{1}{2}}\right)  \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{U} \) is the Gromov-Hausdorff limit of the scalings of a sequence of balls \( {B}_{0}\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{k}}\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) }\right) \) by some factors \( {a}_{k} \) , where \( {s}_{k} \rightarrow  {0}^{ + } \) . Since the tangent cone is three-dimensional and nonflat around \( p \) , the factors \( {a}_{k} \) must be comparable with \( {\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right) \) . By using the local curvature estimate in Lemma 7.1.2, we actually have the convergence in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology for the solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) on the balls \( {B}_{0}\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{k}}\right) \) and over some time interval \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-\delta ,0}\right\rbrack \) for some sufficiently small \( \delta  > 0 \) . The limiting ball \( B\left( {p,\frac{1}{2}}\right)  \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{U} \) is a piece of the nonnegative curved and nonflat metric cone whose radial directions are all Ricci flat. On the other hand, by applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle to the evolution equation of the Ricci curvature tensor as in the proof of Lemma 6.3.1, the limiting ball \( B\left( {p,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \) would split off all radial directions isometrically (and locally). Since the limit is nonflat around \( p \) , this is impossible. Therefore we have proved that the curvatures of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at the new times \( t = 0 \) (corresponding to the original times \( {t}_{k} \) ) stay uniformly bounded at bounded distances from \( {x}_{k} \) for all \( k \) .

We have proved that for each \( A <  + \infty \) , the curvature of the marked manifold \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) at each point \( y \in  {M}_{k} \) with distance from \( {x}_{k} \) at most \( A \) is bounded by \( C\left( A\right) \) . Lemma 7.1.2 extends this curvature control to a backward parabolic neighborhood centered at \( y \) whose radius depends only on the distance from \( y \) to \( {x}_{k} \) . Thus by Shi's local derivative estimates (Theorem 1.4.2) we can control all derivatives of the curvature in such backward parabolic neighborhoods. Then by using the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing and Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), we can take a \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) subsequent limit to obtain \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , which is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on all scales and is defined on a space-time open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing the time slice \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \{ 0\} \) . Clearly it follows from the pinching estimate (7.1.1) that the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) has nonnegative curvature operator (and hence nonnegative sectional curvature).

Step 3. We further claim that the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) at the time slice \( \{ t = 0\} \) has bounded curvature.

We know that the sectional curvature of the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) is nonnegative everywhere. Argue by contradiction. Suppose the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) is not bounded, then by Lemma 6.1.4, there exists a sequence of points \( {q}_{j} \in  {M}_{\infty } \) diverging to infinity such that their scalar curvatures \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{j},0}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) as \( j \rightarrow   + \infty \)

and

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  4{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{j},0}\right)
\]

for \( x \in  B\left( {{q}_{j}, j/\sqrt{{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{j},0}\right) }}\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) }\right) \) . By combining with Lemma 7.1.2 and the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing, a subsequence of the rescaled and marked manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{j},0}\right) {\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{q}_{j}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a smooth nonflat limit \( Y \) . By Proposition 6.1.2, the new limit \( Y \) is isometric to a metric product \( N \times  \mathbb{R} \) for some two-dimensional manifold \( N \) . On the other hand, in view of the choice of the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , the original limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) at the point \( {q}_{j} \) has a canonical neighborhood which is either a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap, or a compact manifold (without boundary) diffeomorphic to a metric quotient of the round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) . It follows that for \( j \) large enough, \( {q}_{j} \) is the center of a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck of radius \( {\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{j},0\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . Without loss of generality, we may further assume that \( {2\varepsilon } < {\varepsilon }_{0} \) , where \( {\varepsilon }_{0} \) is the positive constant given in Proposition 6.1.1. Since \( {\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{j},0\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \rightarrow  0 \) as \( j \rightarrow   + \infty \) , this contradicts Proposition 6.1.1. So the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) }\right) \) is bounded.

Step 4. Finally we want to extend the limit backwards in time to \( - \infty \) .

By Lemma 7.1.2 again, we now know that the limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) is defined on a backward time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-a,0}\right\rbrack \) for some \( a > 0 \) .

Denote by

\( {t}^{\prime } = \inf \{ \widetilde{t} \mid \) we can take a smooth limit on \( (\widetilde{t},0\rbrack \) (with bounded curvature at each time slice) from a subsequence of the convergent rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k} \) \}.

We first claim that there is a subsequence of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k} \) which converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a smooth limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) on the maximal time interval \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Indeed, let \( {t}_{k}^{\prime } \) be a sequence of negative numbers such that \( {t}_{k}^{\prime } \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) and there exist smooth limits \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }^{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) defined on \( \left( {{t}_{k}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . For each \( k \) , the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature and has bounded curvature at each time slice. Moreover by Lemma 7.1.2, the limit has bounded curvature on each subinterval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \subset  \left( {{t}_{k}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . Denote by \( \widetilde{Q} \) the scalar curvature upper bound of the limit at time zero (where \( \widetilde{Q} \) is the same for all \( k \) ). Then we can apply the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.7) to get

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }^{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{Q}\left( \frac{-{t}_{k}^{\prime }}{t - {t}_{k}^{\prime }}\right) ,
\]

where \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }^{k}\left( {x, t}\right) \) are the scalar curvatures of the limits \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }^{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) . Hence by the definition of convergence and the above curvature estimates, we can find a subsequence of the above convergent rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k} \) which converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a smooth limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) on the maximal time interval \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) .

We next claim that \( {t}^{\prime } =  - \infty \) .

Suppose not, then by Lemma 7.1.2, the curvature of the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) becomes unbounded as \( t \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } >  - \infty \) . By applying the maximum principle to the evolution equation of the scalar curvature, we see that the infimum of the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time. Note that \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1 \) . Thus there exists some point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty } \) such that

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{10}}\right)  < \frac{3}{2}
\]

where \( c > 0 \) is the universal constant in Lemma 7.1.2. By using Lemma 7.1.2 again we see that the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) in a small neighborhood of the point \( \left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{10}}\right) \) extends backwards to the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{10},{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{10}}\right\rbrack \) . We remark that the distances at time \( t \) and time 0 are roughly equivalent in the following sense

(7.1.3)

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  {d}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  {d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  - \text{ const. }
\]

for any \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . Indeed from the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.7) we have the estimate

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{Q}\left( \frac{-{t}^{\prime }}{t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) ,\;\text{ on }{M}_{\infty } \times  \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack  .
\]

By applying Lemma 3.4.1 (ii), we have

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {d}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  + {30}\left( {-{t}^{\prime }}\right) \sqrt{\widetilde{Q}}
\]

for any \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . On the other hand, since the curvature of the limit metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) is nonnegative, we have

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  {d}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)
\]

for any \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . Thus we obtain the estimate (7.1.3).

Let us still denote by \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) the subsequence which converges on the maximal time interval \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . Consider the rescaled sequence \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) with the marked points \( {x}_{k} \) replaced by the associated sequence of points \( {y}_{k} \rightarrow  {y}_{\infty } \) and the (original unshifted) times \( {t}_{k} \) replaced by any \( {s}_{k} \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} + \left( {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{20}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k} + \left( {{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{20}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) . It follows from Lemma 7.1.2 that for \( k \) large enough, the rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) at \( {y}_{k} \) satisfy

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {{y}_{k}, t}\right)  \leq  {10}
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{10},{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{10}}\right\rbrack \) . By applying the same arguments as in the above Step 2, we conclude that for any \( A > 0 \) , there is a positive constant \( C\left( A\right)  <  + \infty \) such that

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( {d}_{t}\left( {x,{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  A \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{20},{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{20}}\right\rbrack \) . The estimate (7.1.3) implies that there is a positive constant \( {A}_{0} \) such that for arbitrarily given small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \in  \left( {0,\frac{c}{100}}\right) \) , for \( k \) large enough, there hold

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{k},{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  {A}_{0}
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . By combining with Lemma 7.1.2, we then conclude that for any \( A > 0 \) , there is a positive constant \( \widetilde{C}\left( A\right) \) such that for \( k \) large enough, the rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) satisfy

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{C}\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{100}{\left( C\left( A\right) \right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) .

Now, by taking convergent subsequences from the (original) rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) , we see that the limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) is defined on a spacetime open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . By repeating the argument of Step 3 and using Lemma 7.1.2, we further conclude the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) has uniformly bounded curvature on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . This is a contradiction.

Therefore we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) converges to an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, which gives the desired contradiction. This completes the proof of the theorem. 0

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
(Long-time behavior of the Ricci flow with surgery). Let \( w > \) 0 and \( 0 < \varepsilon  \leq  \frac{1}{2}w \) be any small positive constants and let \( \left( {{M}_{t},{g}_{ij}\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 < t < \; + \infty \) , be a solution to the Ricci flow with surgery, constructed by Theorem 7.4.3 with the nonincreasing (continuous) positive functions \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) and \( \widetilde{r}\left( t\right) \) and with a compact, orientable, irreducible and normalized three-manifold \( M \) as initial data, where each \( \delta \) -cutoff at a time \( t \) has \( \delta  = \delta \left( t\right)  \leq  \min \{ \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) ,\widetilde{r}\left( {2t}\right) \} \) . Then one of the following holds: either

(i) for all sufficiently large \( t \) , we have \( {M}_{t} = {M}_{\text{ thin }}\left( {w, t}\right) \) ; or

(ii) there exists a sequence of times \( {t}^{\alpha } \rightarrow   + \infty \) such that the scalings of \( {g}_{ij}\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) \) on the essential component \( {M}_{{t}^{\alpha }}^{\left( 1\right) } \) , with factor \( {\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-1} \) , converge in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) topology to a hyperbolic metric on the initial compact manifold \( M \) with constant sectional curvature \( - \frac{1}{4} \) ; or

(iii) we can find a finite collection of complete noncompact hyperbolic three-manifolds \( {\mathcal{H}}_{1},\ldots ,{\mathcal{H}}_{m} \) , with finite volume, and compact subsets \( {K}_{1},\ldots ,{K}_{m} \) of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{1},\ldots ,{\mathcal{H}}_{m} \) respectively obtained by truncating each cusp of the hyperbolic manifolds along constant mean curvature torus of small area, and for all t beyond some time \( T <  + \infty \) we can find diffeomorphisms \( {\varphi }_{l},1 \leq  l \leq  m \) , of \( {K}_{l} \) into \( {M}_{t} \) so that as long as \( t \) is sufficiently large, the metric \( {t}^{-1}{\varphi }_{l}^{ * }\left( t\right) {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) is as close to the hyperbolic metric as we like on the compact sets \( {K}_{1},\ldots ,{K}_{m} \) ; moreover, the complement \( {M}_{t} \smallsetminus  \left( {{\varphi }_{1}\left( {K}_{1}\right)  \cup  \cdots  \cup  {\varphi }_{m}\left( {K}_{m}\right) }\right) \) is contained in the thin part \( {M}_{\text{ thin }}\left( {w, t}\right) \) , and the boundary tori of each \( {K}_{l} \) are incompressible in the sense that each \( {\varphi }_{l} \) injects \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {\partial {K}_{l}}\right) \) into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {M}_{t}\right) \) .
