knowledge_statements.statement_latex: (cf. Theorem I.12.1) Given \( \epsilon ,\kappa ,\sigma  > 0 \) and a function \( \Phi \) as above, one can find \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) with the following property. Let \( g\left( \cdot \right) \) be a Ricci flow solution on a three-manifold \( M \) , defined for \( 0 \leq  t \leq  T \) with \( T \geq  1 \) . We suppose that for each \( t, g\left( t\right) \) is complete, and the sectional curvature is bounded on compact time intervals. Suppose that the Ricci flow has \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature and is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales less than \( \sigma \) . Then for any point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{0} \geq  1 \) and \( Q = R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , the solution in \( \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  : {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < {\left( \epsilon Q\right) }^{-1},{t}_{0} - {\left( \epsilon Q\right) }^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{0}}\right\} \) is, after scaling by the factor \( Q \) , \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of a \( \kappa \) -solution.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
We give a proof which differs in some points from the proof in [51] but which has the same ingredients. We first outline the argument.

Suppose that the theorem is false. Then for some \( \epsilon ,\kappa ,\sigma  > 0 \) , we have a sequence of such \( \Phi \) -nonnegatively curved 3-dimensional Ricci flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) defined on intervals \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) , and sequences \( {r}_{k} \rightarrow  0,{\widehat{x}}_{k} \in  {M}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k} \geq  1 \) such that \( {M}_{k} \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales \( < \sigma \) and \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{k}^{-2} \) , but the \( {Q}_{k} \) -rescaled solution in \( {B}_{{\left( \epsilon {Q}_{k}\right) }^{-1/2}}\left( {\widehat{x}}_{k}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{\widehat{t}}_{k} - {\left( \epsilon {Q}_{k}\right) }^{-1},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) is not \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of any \( \kappa \) -solution.

We note that if the statement were false for \( \epsilon \) then it would also be false for any smaller \( \epsilon \) . Because of this, somewhat paradoxically, we will begin the argument with a given \( \epsilon \) but will allow ourselves to make \( \epsilon \) small enough later so that the argument works. To be clear, we will eventually get a contradiction using a fixed (small) value of \( \epsilon \) , but as the proof goes along we will impose some upper bounds on this value in order for the proof to work. (If we tried to list all of the constraints at the beginning of the argument then they would look unmotivated.)

The goal is to get a contradiction based on the "bad" points \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) . In a sense, the method of proof of Theorem 52.7 is an induction on the curvature scale. For example, if we were to make the additional assumption in the theorem that \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) for all \( x \in  M \) and \( t \leq  {t}_{0} \) then the theorem would be very easy to prove. We would just take a convergent subsequence of the rescaled solutions, based at \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) , to get a \( \kappa \) -solution; this would give a contradiction. This simple argument can be considered to be the first step in a proof by induction on curvature scale. In the proof of Theorem 52.7 one effectively proves the result at a given curvature scale inductively by assuming that the result is true at higher curvature scales.

The actual proof consists of four steps. Step 1 consists of replacing the sequence \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) by another sequence of "bad" points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) which have the property that points near \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) with distinctly higher scalar curvature are "good" points. It then suffices to get a contradiction based on the existence of the sequence \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

In steps 2-4 one uses the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) to build up a \( \kappa \) -solution, whose existence then contradicts the "badness" of the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . More precisely, let \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be the result of rescaling \( {g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) by \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . We will show that the sequence of pointed flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) accumulates on a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) , thereby obtaining a contradiction.

In step 2 one takes a pointed limit of the manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) in order to construct what will become the final time slice of the \( \kappa \) -solution, \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . In order to take this limit, it is necessary to show that the manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) have uniformly bounded curvature on distance balls of a fixed radius. If this were not true then for some radius, a subsequence of the manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) would have curvatures that asymptotically blowup on the ball of that radius. One shows that geometrically, the curvature blowup is due to the asymptotic formation of a cone-like point at the blowup radius. Doing a further rescaling at this cone-like point, one obtains a Ricci flow solution that ends on a part of a nonflat metric cone. This gives a contradiction as in the case \( 0 < \mathcal{R} < \infty \) of Theorem 41.2.

Thus one can construct the pointed limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . The goal now is to show that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) is the final time slice of a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) . In step 3 one shows that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) extends backward to a Ricci flow solution on some time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - \Delta ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , and that the time slices have bounded nonnegative curvature. In step 4 one shows that the Ricci flow solution can be extended all the way to time \( \left( {-\infty ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , thereby constructing a \( \kappa \) -solution

Step 1: Adjusting the choice of basepoints.

We first modify the points \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) slightly in time to points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) so that in the given Ricci flow solution, there are no other "bad" points with much larger scalar curvature in a earlier time interval whose length is large compared to \( R{\left( {x}_{k},{t}_{k}\right) }^{-1} \) . (The phrase "nearly the smallest curvature \( Q \) " in [51, Proof of Theorem 12.1] should read "nearly the largest curvature \( Q \) ". This is clear from the sentence in parentheses that follows.) The proof of the next lemma is by pointpicking, as in Appendix H.

Lemma 52.9. We can find \( {H}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty ,{x}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) , and \( {t}_{k} \geq  \frac{1}{2} \) such that \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) , and for all \( k \) the conclusion of Theorem 52.7 fails at \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , but holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right)  \in \; {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - {H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for which \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  \geq  {2R}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

Proof. Choose \( {H}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) such that \( {H}_{k}{\left( R\left( {\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}\right) \right) }^{-1} \leq  \frac{1}{10} \) for all \( k \) . For each \( k \) , initially set \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) . Put \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) and look for a point in \( {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - {H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) at which Theorem 52.7 fails, and the scalar curvature is at least \( {2R}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . If such a point exists, replace \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) by this point; otherwise do nothing. Repeat this until the second alternative occurs. This process must terminate with a new choice of \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) satisfying the lemma.

Hereafter we use this modified sequence \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . Let \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be the result of rescaling \( {g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) by \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . We use \( {\bar{R}}_{k} \) to denote its scalar curvature; in particular, \( {\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = 1 \) . Note that the rescaled time interval of Lemma 52.9 has duration \( {H}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) ; this is what we want in order to try to extract an ancient solution.

Step 2: For every \( \rho  < \infty \) , the scalar curvature \( {\bar{R}}_{k} \) is uniformly bounded on the \( \rho \) -balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) (the argument for this is essentially equivalent to [51, Pf. of Claim 2 of Theorem I.12.1]). Before proceeding, we need some bounds which come from our choice of basepoints, and the derivative bounds inherited (by approximation) from \( \kappa \) -solutions.

Lemma 52.10. There is a constant \( C = C\left( \kappa \right) \) so that for any \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in a Ricci flow solution, if \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  > 0 \) and the solution in \( {B}_{t}\left( {x,{\left( \epsilon R\left( x, t\right) \right) }^{-1/2}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {t - {\left( \epsilon R\left( x, t\right) \right) }^{-1}, t}\right\rbrack \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to a corresponding subset of a \( \kappa \) -solution then \( \left| {\nabla {R}^{-1/2}}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C \) and \( \left| {{\partial }_{t}{R}^{-1}}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C \) .

Proof. This follows from the compactness in Theorem 46.1.

Note that the same value of \( C \) in Lemma 52.10 also works for smaller \( \epsilon \) .

Lemma 52.11. (cf. Claim 1 of I.12.1) For each \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{k} - \frac{1}{2}{H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  {t}_{k} \) , we have \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4{\bar{Q}}_{k} \) whenever \( \bar{t} - c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1/2} \) , where \( {\bar{Q}}_{k} = {Q}_{k} + \left| {{R}_{k}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) }\right| \) and \( c = c\left( \kappa \right)  > 0 \) is a small constant.

Proof. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  2{Q}_{k} \) then there is nothing to show. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  > 2{Q}_{k} \) , consider a spacetime curve \( \gamma \) that goes linearly from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) , and then goes from \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) to \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) along a minimizing geodesic. If there is a point on \( \gamma \) with curvature \( 2{Q}_{k} \) , let \( p \) be the nearest such point to \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) . If not, put \( p = \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) . From the conclusion of Lemma 52.9, we can apply Lemma 52.10 along \( \gamma \) from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( p \) . The claim follows from integrating the ensuing derivative bounds along \( \gamma \) .

Lemma 52.12. In terms of the rescaled solution \( {\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) , for each \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{k} - \frac{1}{2}{H}_{k} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  {t}_{k} \) , we have \( {\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4{\widetilde{Q}}_{k} \) whenever \( \bar{t} - c{\widetilde{Q}}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  c{\widetilde{Q}}_{k}^{-1/2} \) , where \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{k} = 1 + \left| {{\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) }\right| . \)

Proof. This is just the rescaled version of Lemma 52.11.

For all \( \rho  \geq  0 \) , put

(52.13)

\[
D\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {{\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {x,{t}_{k}}\right)  \mid  k \geq  1, x \in  B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) }\right\}  ,
\]

and let \( {\rho }_{0} \) be the supremum of the \( \rho \) ’s for which \( D\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \) . Note that \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) , in view of Lemma 52.12 (taking \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  = \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) ). Suppose that \( {\rho }_{0} < \infty \) . After passing to a subsequence if necessary, we can find a sequence \( {y}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) with \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},{y}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} \) and \( \bar{R}\left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) . Let \( {\eta }_{k} \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) be a minimizing geodesic segment from \( {x}_{k} \) to \( {y}_{k} \) . Let \( {z}_{k} \in  {\eta }_{k} \) be the point on \( {\eta }_{k} \) closest to \( {y}_{k} \) at which \( \bar{R}\left( {{z}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = 2 \) , and let \( {\gamma }_{k} \) be the subsegment of \( {\eta }_{k} \) running from \( {y}_{k} \) to \( {z}_{k} \) . By Lemma 52.12 the length of \( {\gamma }_{k} \) is bounded away from zero independent of \( k \) . Due to the \( \Phi \) -pinching (see (52.4)), for all \( \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) , we have a uniform bound on \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| \) on the balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) . The injectivity radius is also controlled in \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right) \) , in view of the curvature bounds and the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing. Therefore after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the pointed sequence \( \left( {B\left( {{x}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the pointed Gromov-Hausdorff topology (i.e. for all \( \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) we have the usual Gromov-Hausdorff convergence) to a pointed \( {C}^{1} \) -Riemannian manifold \( \left( {Z,{\bar{g}}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , the segments \( {\eta }_{k} \) converge to a segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\eta }_{\infty } \subset  Z \) emanating from \( {x}_{\infty } \) , and \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converges to \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {\eta }_{\infty } \) . Let \( \bar{Z} \) denote the completion of \( \left( {Z,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) , and \( {y}_{\infty } \in  \bar{Z} \) the limit point of \( {\eta }_{\infty } \) . Note that by Lemma 52.9 and part 4 of Corollary 42.1, the Riemannian structure near \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) may be chosen to be many times differentiable. (Alternatively, this follows from Lemma 52.12 and the Shi estimates of Appendix D.) In particular the scalar curvature \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty } \) is defined, differentiable, and satisfies the bound in Lemma 52.10 near \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) .

Lemma 52.14. 1. There is a function \( c : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) depending only on \( \kappa \) , with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}c\left( t\right)  = \; \infty \) , such that if \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) then \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) d{\left( {y}_{\infty }, w\right) }^{2} > c\left( \epsilon \right) \) .

2. There is a function \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \cup  \{ \infty \} \) depending only on \( \kappa \) , with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}{\epsilon }^{\prime }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) , such that if \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) and \( d\left( {{y}_{\infty }, w}\right) \) is sufficiently small then the pointed manifold \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( 2{\epsilon }^{\prime }\left( \epsilon \right) \) -close to a round cylinder in the \( {C}^{2} \) topology.

Proof. It follows from Lemma 52.9 that for all \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) , the pointed Riemannian manifold \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to (a time slice of) a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution. From the definition of pointed closeness, there is an embedded region around \( w \) , large on the scale defined by \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) \) , which is close to the corresponding subset of a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution. This gives a lower bound on the distance \( {\rho }_{0} - d\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) to the point of curvature blowup, thereby proving part 1 of the lemma.

We know that \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {N,\star , h\left( t\right) }\right) \) in the pointed \( {C}^{2} \) -topology. By Lemma 52.10, we know \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) \) tends to \( \infty \) as \( d\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} \) , for \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . In particular, \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {d}^{2}\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) . From part 1 above, we can choose \( \epsilon \) small enough in order to make \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {d}^{2}\left( {w,{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) large enough to apply Proposition 49.1. Hence the pointed manifold \( \left( {N,\star , R\left( \star \right) h\left( t\right) }\right) \) is \( {\epsilon }^{\prime \prime }\left( \epsilon \right) \) -close to a round cylinder, where \( {\epsilon }^{\prime \prime } : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) is a function with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}{\epsilon }^{\prime \prime }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) . The lemma follows.

Note that the function \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) in Lemma 52.14 is independent of the particular manifold \( Z \) that arises in our proof.

From part 2 of Lemma 52.14, if \( \epsilon \) is small and \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) is sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) then \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {C}^{2} \) -close to a round cylinder. The cross-section of the cylinder has diameter approximately \( \pi {\left( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) /2\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . If we form the union of the balls \( B\left( {w,{2\pi }{\left( {R}_{\infty }\left( w\right) /2\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) , as \( w \) ranges over such points in \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) , then we obtain a connected Riemannian manifold \( W \) . By adding in the point \( {y}_{\infty } \) , we get a metric space \( \bar{W} \) which is locally complete, and geodesic near \( {y}_{\infty } \) . As the original manifolds \( {M}_{k} \) had \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature, it follows from Lemma 52.5 that \( W \) is nonnegatively curved. Furthermore, \( {y}_{\infty } \) cannot be an interior point of any geodesic segment in \( \bar{W} \) , since such a geodesic would have to pass through a cylindrical region near \( {y}_{\infty } \) twice. The usual proof of the Toponogov triangle comparison inequality now applies near \( {y}_{\infty } \) since minimizers remain in the smooth nonnegatively curved part of \( \bar{W} \) . Then \( \bar{W} \) has nonnegative curvature in the Alexandrov sense.

This implies that blowups of \( \left( {\bar{W},{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) converge to the tangent cone \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) . As \( \bar{W} \) is three-dimensional, so is \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) [12, Corollary 7.11]. It will be \( {C}^{2} \) -smooth away from the vertex and nowhere flat, by part 2 of Lemma 52.14. Pick \( z \in  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) such that \( d\left( {z,{y}_{\infty }}\right)  = 1 \) . Then for any \( \delta  < \frac{1}{2} \) , the ball \( B\left( {z,\delta }\right)  \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) is the Gromov-Hausdorff limit of a sequence of rescaled balls \( B\left( {{\widehat{z}}_{k},{\widehat{r}}_{k}}\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) where \( {\widehat{r}}_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) , whose center points \( \left( {{\widehat{z}}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) satisfy the conclusions of Theorem 52.7. Applying Lemma 52.12 and Appendix B, if \( \delta  = \delta \left( \kappa \right) \) is taken small enough then we get the curvature bounds needed to extract a limiting Ricci flow solution whose time zero slice is isometric to \( B\left( {z,\delta }\right) \) . Now we can apply the reasoning from the \( 0 < \mathcal{R} < \infty \) case of Theorem 41.2 to get a contradiction. This completes step 2.

Step 3: The sequence of pointed flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) ,\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right) \) accumulates on a pointed Ricci flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) ,\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) which is defined on a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) with \( {t}^{\prime } < {t}_{0} \) . By step 2, we know that the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) at \( y \in  {M}_{k} \) is bounded by a function of the distance from \( y \) to \( {x}_{k} \) . Lemma 52.12 extends this curvature control to a backward parabolic neighborhood centered at \( y \) whose radius depends only on \( d\left( {y,{x}_{k}}\right) \) . Thus we can conclude, using \( \Phi \) -pinching (52.4) and Shi’s estimates (Appendix D), that all derivatives of the curvature \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) are controlled as a function of the distance from \( {x}_{k} \) , which means that the sequence of pointed manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) accumulates to a smooth manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) .

From Lemma 52.5, \( {M}_{\infty } \) has nonnegative sectional curvature. We claim that \( {M}_{\infty } \) has bounded curvature. If not then there is a sequence of points \( {q}_{k} \in  {M}_{\infty } \) so that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}\bar{R}\left( {q}_{k}\right)  = \; \infty \) and \( \bar{R}\left( q\right)  \leq  2\bar{R}\left( {q}_{k}\right) \) for \( q \in  B\left( {{y}_{k},{A}_{k}\bar{R}{\left( {q}_{k}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) , where \( {A}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) ; compare [33, Lemma 22.2]. Lemma 52.9 implies that for large \( k \) , a rescaled neighborhood of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{q}_{k}}\right) \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of a time slice of a \( \kappa \) -solution. As in the proof of Theorem 46.1, we obtain a sequence of neck-like regions in \( {M}_{\infty } \) with smaller and smaller cross-sections, which contradicts the existence of the Sharafutdinov retraction.

By Lemma 52.12 again, we now get curvature control on \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) for a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \Delta ,{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for some \( \Delta  > 0 \) , and hence we can extract a subsequence which converges to a pointed Ricci flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - \Delta ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , which has nonnegative curvature and bounded curvature on compact time intervals.

Step 4: Getting an ancient solution. Let \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) be the maximal time interval on which we can extract a limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) with bounded curvature on compact time intervals. Suppose that \( {t}^{\prime } >  - \infty \) . By Lemma 52.12 the maximum of the scalar curvature on the time slice \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) must tend to infinity as \( t \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) . From the trace Harnack inequality, \( {R}_{t} + \frac{R}{t - {t}^{\prime }} \geq  0 \) , and so

(52.15)

\[
{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  Q\frac{{t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }}{t - {t}^{\prime }},
\]

where \( Q \) is the maximum of the scalar curvature on \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . Combining this with Corollary 27.16, we get

(52.16)

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  \text{ const. }\sqrt{Q\frac{{t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }}{t - {t}^{\prime }}}.
\]

Since the right hand side is integrable on \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , and using the fact that distances are nonincreasing in time (since \( \mathrm{{Rm}} \geq  0 \) ), it follows that there is a constant \( C \) such that

(52.17)

\[
\left| {{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  - {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, y}\right) }\right|  < C
\]

for all \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty }, t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) .

If \( {M}_{\infty } \) is compact then by (52.17) the diameter of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is bounded independent of \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . Since the minimum of the scalar curvature is increasing in time, it is also bounded independent of \( t \) . Now the argument in Step 2 shows that the curvature is bounded everywhere independent of \( t \) . (We can apply the argument of Step 2 to the time- \( t \) slice because the main ingredient was Lemma 52.9, which holds for rescaled time \( t \) .)

We may therefore assume \( {M}_{\infty } \) is noncompact. To be consistent with the notation of I.12.1, we now relabel the basepoint \( \left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) \) as \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Since nonnegatively curved manifolds are asymptotically conical (see Appendix G), there is a constant \( D \) such that if \( y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) , and \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right)  > D \) , then there is a point \( x \in  {M}_{\infty } \) such that

(52.18)

\[
{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, y}\right)  = {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right) \;\text{ and }\;{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  \frac{3}{2}{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right) ;
\]

by (52.17) the same conditions hold at all times \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , up to error \( C \) . If for some such \( y \) , and some \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) the scalar curvature were large, then \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {y, t}\right) ,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( {y, t}\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) would be \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {N, h\left( \cdot \right) ,\left( {z,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) . When \( \epsilon \) is small we could use Proposition 49.1 to see that \( y \) lies in a neck region \( U \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) of diameter \( \approx  R{\left( y, t\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \ll  1 \) .

We claim that \( U \) separates \( {x}_{0} \) from \( x \) in the sense that \( {x}_{0} \) and \( x \) belong to disjoint components of \( {M}_{\infty } - U \) , where \( {x}_{0}, y \) , and \( x \) satisfy (52.18). To see this, we recall that if \( {M}_{\infty } \) has more than one end then it splits isometrically, in which case the claim is clear. If \( {M}_{\infty } \) has one end then we consider an exhaustion of \( {M}_{\infty } \) by totally convex compact sets \( {C}_{t} \) as in Section 46. One of the sets \( {C}_{t} \) will have boundary consisting of an approximate 2-sphere cross-section in the neck region \( U \) , giving the separation.

(For another argument, suppose that \( U \) does not separate \( {x}_{0} \) from \( x \) . Since \( {\widetilde{Z}}_{y}\left( {{x}_{0}, x}\right)  > \frac{\pi }{2} \) (from Proposition 49.1), the segments \( \overline{y{x}_{0}} \) and \( \overline{yx} \) must exit \( U \) by different ends. If \( {x}_{0} \) and \( x \) can be joined by a curve avoiding \( U \) then there is a nonzero element of \( {\mathrm{H}}^{1}\left( {{M}_{\infty },\mathbb{Z}}\right) \) . The corresponding infinite cyclic cover of \( {M}_{\infty } \) will then isometrically split off a line and its quotient \( {M}_{\infty } \) will be compact, which is a contradiction. We thank one of the referees for this argument.)

Obviously, at time \( {t}_{0} \) the set \( U \) still separates \( {x}_{0} \) from \( x \) . Since \( {\bar{g}}_{\infty } \) has nonnegative curvature, we have \( {\operatorname{diam}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( U\right)  \leq  {\operatorname{diam}}_{t}\left( U\right)  \ll  1 \) . Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) has bounded geometry, there cannot be topologically separating subsets of arbitrarily small diameter. Thus there must be a uniform upper bound on \( R\left( {y, t}\right) \) and the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is uniformly bounded (in space and time) outside a set of uniformly bounded diameter. Repeating the reasoning from Step 2, we get uniform bounds everywhere. This contradicts our assumption that the curvature blows up as \( t \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) .

It remains to show that the ancient solution is a \( \kappa \) -solution. The only remaining point is to show that it is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed at all scales. This follows from the fact that the original Ricci flow solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) were \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales less than the fixed number \( \sigma \) .

(Perelman [104]). For any \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) and \( 1 \leq  A <  + \infty \) , one can find \( \kappa  = \kappa \left( {A,\varepsilon }\right)  > 0,{K}_{1} = {K}_{1}\left( {A,\varepsilon }\right)  <  + \infty ,{K}_{2} = {K}_{2}\left( {A,\varepsilon }\right)  <  + \infty \) and \( \bar{r} = \; \bar{r}\left( {A,\varepsilon }\right)  > 0 \) such that for any \( {t}_{0} <  + \infty \) there exists \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A} = {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) (depending also on \( \varepsilon \) ), nonincreasing in \( {t}_{0} \) , with the following property. Suppose we have a solution, constructed by Theorem 7.4.3 with the nonincreasing (continuous) positive functions \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) and \( \widetilde{r}\left( t\right) \) , to the Ricci flow with \( \delta \) -cutoff surgeries on time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) and with a compact orientable normalized three-manifold as initial data, where each \( \delta \) -cutoff at a time \( t \) satisfies \( \delta  = \delta \left( t\right)  \leq  \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) on \( \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) and \( \delta  = \delta \left( t\right)  \leq  {\bar{\delta }}_{A} \) on \( \left\lbrack  {\frac{{t}_{0}}{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) ; assume that the solution is defined on the whole parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}, - {r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  \triangleq \; \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  x \in  {B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\}  ,2{r}_{0}^{2} < {t}_{0} \) , and satisfies

\[
\left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2}\;\text{ on }\;P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}, - {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) ,
\]

\[
\text{ and }\;{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  {A}^{-1}{r}_{0}^{3}\text{ . }
\]

Then

(i) the solution is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on all scales less than \( {r}_{0} \) in the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, A{r}_{0}}\right) \)

(ii) every point \( x \in  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, A{r}_{0}}\right) \) with \( R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {K}_{1}{r}_{0}^{-2} \) has a canonical neighborhood \( B \) , with \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,\sigma }\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{2\sigma }}\right) \) for some \( 0 < \sigma  < {C}_{1}\left( \varepsilon \right) {R}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \) , which is either a strong \( \varepsilon \) -neck or an \( \varepsilon \) -cap;

\]

When \( m \) is large enough, we observe again that Lemma 3.4.1 (ii) is applicable for \( {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},\bar{x}}\right) \) with \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . Then by repeating the argument as in the derivation of (7.2.1),(7.2.2) and (7.2.3), we deduce that for all sufficiently large \( m \) , the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) . \)

Let \( \left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) be a sequence of associated points and times in the (unrescaled) solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) so that after rescaling, the sequence converges to \( \left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty } + \theta }\right) \) in the limit. Clearly \( \frac{\theta }{2} \leq  {\theta }_{m} \leq  {2\theta } \) for all sufficiently large \( m \) . Then by the argument as in the derivation of (7.5.13), we know that for all sufficiently large \( m \) , the solution \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at \( {y}_{m} \) is defined on the whole time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m} - }\right. }\right. \; \left. {\left. {\frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies the curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {{y}_{m}, t}\right)  \leq  8\bar{Q}
\]

there; moreover the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) with \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  \geq  4\bar{Q} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) .

We now consider the rescaled sequence \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) with the marked points replaced by \( {y}_{m} \) and the times replaced by \( {s}_{m} \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{4}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{c}{4}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) . As before the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality implies the rescaling limit around \( \left( {{y}_{m},{s}_{m}}\right) \) agrees with the original one. Then the arguments in previous paragraphs imply the limit is well-defined and smooth on a space-time open neighborhood of the maximal time slice \( \left\{  {t = {t}_{\infty }}\right\} \) . Particularly this excludes the possibility of existing surgeries in finite distance around the time \( {t}_{\infty } \) . Moreover, the limit at \( t = {t}_{\infty } \) also has bounded curvature. By using the gradient estimates in the canonical neighborhood assumption on the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) , we see that the second possibility is also impossible. Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Therefore we have proved the canonical neighborhood statement (ii).

(iii) This is analogous to Theorem 7.2.1. We also argue by contradiction. Suppose for some \( A <  + \infty \) and sequences of positive numbers \( {K}_{2}^{\alpha } \rightarrow   + \infty ,{\bar{r}}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) there exists a sequence of times \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \) such that for any sequences \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } > 0 \) with \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \rightarrow  0 \) for fixed \( \alpha \) , we have sequences of solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) to the Ricci flow with surgery and sequences of points \( {x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) , of positive constants \( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  {\bar{r}}^{\alpha }\sqrt{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }} \) which satisfy the assumptions, but for all \( \alpha ,\beta \) there hold

(7.5.16)

\[
R\left( {{x}^{\alpha \beta },{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\right)  > {K}_{2}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2}\text{ , for some }{x}^{\alpha \beta } \in  {B}_{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\left( {{x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }, A{r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }}\right) .
\]

We may assume that \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  {\bar{\delta }}_{4A}\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) \) for all \( \alpha ,\beta \) , where \( {\bar{\delta }}_{4A}\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) \) is chosen so that the statements (i) and (ii) hold on \( {B}_{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\left( {{x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta },{4A}{r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }}\right) \) . Let \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) be the rescaled solutions of \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) around the origins \( {x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) with factor \( {\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2} \) and shift the times \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \) to zero. Then by applying the statement (ii), we know that the regions, where the scalar curvature of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) is at least \( {K}_{1}\left( { = {K}_{1}\left( {4A}\right) }\right) \) , are canonical neighborhood regions. Note that canonical \( \varepsilon \) -neck neighborhoods are strong. Also note that the pinching assumption and the assertion

\[
{t}_{0}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2} \geq  {\left( {\bar{r}}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty ,\text{ as }\alpha  \rightarrow   + \infty ,
\]

imply that any subsequent limit of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) must have nonnegative sectional curvature. Thus by the above argument in the proof of the statement (ii) (or the argument in Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 7.1.1), we conclude that there exist subsequences \( \alpha  = {\alpha }_{m},\beta  = {\beta }_{m} \) such that the curvatures of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) stay uniformly bounded at distances from the origins \( {x}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) not exceeding \( {2A} \) . This contradicts (7.5.16) for \( m \) sufficiently large. This proves the statements (iii).

Clearly for fixed \( A \) , after defining the \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) for each \( {t}_{0} \) , one can adjust the \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) so that it is nonincreasing in \( {t}_{0} \) .

Therefore we have completed the proof of the theorem.

From now on we redefine the function \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) so that it is also less than \( {\bar{\delta }}_{2\left( {t + 1}\right) }\left( {2t}\right) \) and then the above theorem always holds for \( A \in  \left\lbrack  {1,2\left( {{t}_{0} + 1}\right) }\right\rbrack \) . Particularly, we still

have

\[
\widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right)  \leq  \bar{\delta }\left( t\right)  = \min \left\{  {\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}\log \left( {1 + t}\right) },{\delta }_{0}}\right\}  ,
\]

which tends to zero as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) . We may also require that \( \widetilde{r}\left( t\right) \) tends to zero as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) .

Let \( \left( {W, h\left( t\right) }\right) ,{t}_{0} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{1} \) , be a Ricci flow and fix \( \Theta  < \infty \) . Then there exist constants \( \delta  > 0 \) and \( 0 < {r}_{0} \leq  1 \) depending only on the curvature bound for the ambient Ricci flow and \( \Theta \) such that the following holds. Let \( c\left( {x, t}\right) ,{t}_{0} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{1} \) , be a curve-shrinking flow with \( c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) immersed for each \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack \) and with the total curvature of \( c\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) \) being at most \( \Theta \) . Suppose that there is \( 0 < r \leq  {r}_{0} \) and at a time \( {t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1} - \delta {r}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) such that the length of \( c\left( {\cdot ,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) is at least \( r \) and the total curvature of \( c\left( {\cdot ,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) on any sub-arc of length \( r \) is at most \( \delta \) . Then for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) the curvature \( k \) satisfies

\[
{k}^{2} \leq  \frac{2}{\left( t - {t}^{\prime }\right) }.
\]
