The proof is by induction on the dimension. When the dimension is two, the lemma is valid by Theorem 6.2.2. For dimension \( \geq  3 \) , we argue by contradiction.

Suppose the lemma is valid for dimensions \( \leq  n - 1 \) and suppose \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) for some \( n \) -dimensional nonflat ancient solution with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature at some time \( {t}_{0} \leq  0 \) . Fixing a point \( {x}_{0} \in  M \) , we consider the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio

\[
A = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty }}R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right) .
\]

We divide the proof into three cases.

Case 1: \( A =  + \infty \) .

By Lemma 6.1.3, there exist sequences of points \( {x}_{k} \in  M \) divergent to infinity, of radii \( {r}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) , and of positive constants \( {\delta }_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) such that

(i) \( R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{k}}\right) R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) for all \( x \) in the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) \) of radius \( {r}_{k} \) around \( {x}_{k} \) ,

(ii) \( {r}_{k}^{2}R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) ,

(iii) \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right) /{r}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) .

By scaling the solution around the points \( {x}_{k} \) with factor \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) , and shifting the time \( {t}_{0} \) to the new time zero, we get a sequence of rescaled solutions

\[
{g}_{k}\left( s\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right)
\]

to the Ricci flow. Since the ancient solution has nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature, there holds the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.5). Thus the rescaled solutions satisfy

\[
{R}_{k}\left( {x, s}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{k}}\right)
\]

for all \( s \leq  0 \) and \( x \in  {B}_{{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) \) . Since \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , it follows from the standard volume comparison and Theorem 4.2.2 that the injectivity radii of the rescaled solutions \( {g}_{k} \) at the points \( {x}_{k} \) and the new time zero is uniformly bounded below by a positive number. Then by Hamilton's compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) will converge to a solution \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) , O}\right) \) to the Ricci flow with

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {y, s}\right)  \leq  1\text{ , for all }s \leq  0\text{ and }y \in  \widetilde{M}\text{ , }
\]

and

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {O,0}\right)  = 1\text{ . }
\]

Since the metric is shrinking, by (ii) and (iii), we get

\[
R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) }^{2}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{k}}\right)  \geq  R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }^{2}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{k}}\right)
\]

which tends to \( + \infty \) , as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) , for all \( s \leq  0 \) . Thus by Proposition 6.1.2, for each \( s \leq  0,\left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) }\right) \) splits off a line. We now consider the lifting of the solution \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) }\right) , s \leq  0 \) , to its universal cover and denote it by \( \left( {\widetilde{\widetilde{M}},\widetilde{\widetilde{g}}\left( s\right) }\right) , s \leq  0 \) . Clearly we still have

\[
{\nu }_{\widetilde{M}}\left( 0\right)  > 0\text{ and }{\nu }_{\widetilde{\widetilde{M}}}\left( 0\right)  > 0\text{ . }
\]

By applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle and the de Rham decomposition theorem, the universal cover \( \widetilde{\widetilde{M}} \) splits isometrically as \( X \times  \mathbb{R} \) for some \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) - dimensional nonflat (complete) ancient solution \( X \) with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature. These imply that \( {\nu }_{X}\left( 0\right)  > 0 \) , which contradicts the induction hypothesis.

Case 2: \( 0 < A <  + \infty \) .

Take a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) divergent to infinity such that

\[
R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow  A,\text{ as }k \rightarrow   + \infty .
\]

Consider the rescaled solutions \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) }\right) \) (around the fixed point \( {x}_{0} \) ), where

\[
{g}_{k}\left( s\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) , s \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack .
\]

Then there is a constant \( C > 0 \) such that

(6.3.1)

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} {R}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  C/{d}_{k}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right) , \\  {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right)  = 1, \\  {d}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0},0}\right)  \rightarrow  \sqrt{A} > 0, \end{array}\right.
\]

where \( {d}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,{x}_{0},0}\right) \) is the distance function from the point \( {x}_{0} \) in the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) \) .

Since \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , it is a basic result in Alexandrov space theory (see for example Theorem 7.6 of [20]) that a subsequence of \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) converges in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to an \( n \) -dimensional metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) with vertex \( {x}_{0} \) .

By (6.3.1), the standard volume comparison and Theorem 4.2.2, we know that the injectivity radius of \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) at \( {x}_{k} \) is uniformly bounded from below by a positive number \( {\rho }_{0} \) . After taking a subsequence, we may assume \( {x}_{k} \) converges to a point \( {x}_{\infty } \) in \( M \smallsetminus  \left\{  {x}_{0}\right\} \) . Then by Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), we can take a subsequence such that the metrics \( {g}_{k}\left( s\right) \) on the metric balls \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \left( { \subset  M}\right. \) with respect to the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) ) \) converge in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a solution of the Ricci flow on a ball \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{\infty },\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) . Clearly the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) limit has nonnegative curvature operator and it is a piece of the metric cone at the time \( s = 0 \) . By (6.3.1), we have

(6.3.2)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1
\]

Let \( x \) be any point in the limiting ball \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{\infty },\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) and \( {e}_{1} \) be any radial direction at \( x \) . Clearly \( \widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{1}}\right)  = 0 \) . Recall that the evolution equation of the Ricci tensor in frame coordinates is

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\widetilde{R}}_{ab} = \widetilde{\bigtriangleup }{\widetilde{R}}_{ab} + 2{\widetilde{R}}_{acbd}{\widetilde{R}}_{cd}.
\]

Since the curvature operator is nonnegative, by applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle (Theorem 2.2.1) to the above equation, we deduce that the null space of Ric is invariant under parallel translation. In particular, all radial directions split off locally and isometrically. While by (6.3.2), the piece of the metric cone is nonflat. This gives a contradiction.

Case 3: \( A = 0 \) .

The gap theorem as was initiated by Mok-Siu-Yau [93] and established by Greene-Wu [49, 50], Eschenberg-Shrader-Strake [45], and Drees [44] shows that a complete noncompact \( n \) -dimensional (except \( n = 4 \) or 8) Riemannian manifold with nonnegative sectional curvature and the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( A = 0 \) must be flat. So the present case is ruled out except in dimension \( n = 4 \) or 8 . Since in our situation the asymptotic volume ratio is positive and the manifold is the solution of the Ricci flow, we can give an alternative proof for all dimensions as follows.

We claim the sectional curvature of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is positive everywhere. Indeed, by Theorem 2.2.2, the image of the curvature operator is just the restricted holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) of the manifold. If the sectional curvature vanishes for some two-plane, then the holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) cannot be \( {so}\left( n\right) \) . We observe the manifold is not Einstein since it is noncompact, nonflat and has nonnegative curvature operator. If \( \mathcal{G} \) is irreducible, then by Berger’s Theorem [7], \( \mathcal{G} = u\left( \frac{n}{2}\right) \) . Thus the manifold is Kähler with bounded and nonnegative bisectional curvature and with curvature decay faster than quadratic. Then by the gap theorem obtained by Chen and the second author in [31], this Kähler manifold must be flat. This contradicts the assumption. Hence the holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) is reducible and the universal cover of \( M \) splits isometrically as \( {\widetilde{M}}_{1} \times  {\widetilde{M}}_{2} \) nontrivially. Clearly the universal cover of \( M \) has positive asymptotic volume ratio. So \( {\widetilde{M}}_{1} \) and \( {\widetilde{M}}_{2} \) still have positive asymptotic volume ratio and at least one of them is nonflat. By the induction hypothesis, this is also impossible. Thus our claim is proved.

Now we know that the sectional curvature of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is positive everywhere. Choose a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) divergent to infinity such that

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  = \sup \left\{  {R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \mid  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right) }\right\}  , \\  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  k, \\  R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  = {\varepsilon }_{k} \rightarrow  0. \end{array}\right.
\]

Consider the rescaled metric

\[
{g}_{k}\left( 0\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right)
\]

as before. Then

(6.3.3)

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} {R}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  {\varepsilon }_{k}/{d}_{k}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right) ,\;\text{ for }{d}_{k}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right)  \geq  \sqrt{{\varepsilon }_{k}}, \\  {d}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0},0}\right)  = \sqrt{{\varepsilon }_{k}} \rightarrow  0. \end{array}\right.
\]

As in Case 2, the rescaled marked solutions \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) will converge in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to a metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) . And by the virtue of Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), up to a subsequence, the convergence is in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology in \( \widetilde{M} \smallsetminus  \left\{  {x}_{0}\right\} \) . We next claim the metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) .

Indeed, let us write the metric cone \( \widetilde{M} \) as a warped product \( {\mathbb{R}}_{ + }{ \times  }_{r}{X}^{n - 1} \) for some \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional manifold \( {X}^{n - 1} \) . By (6.3.3), the metric cone must be flat and \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is isometric to a quotient of the round sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{n - 1} \) by fixed point free isometries in the standard metric. To show \( \widetilde{M} \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) , we only need to verify that \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is simply connected.

Let \( \varphi \) be the Busemann function of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) with respect to the point \( {x}_{0} \) . Since \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) has nonnegative sectional curvature, it is easy to see that for any small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there is a \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) such that

\[
\left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \varphi \left( x\right)  \leq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  M \smallsetminus  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) . The strict positivity of the sectional curvature of the manifold \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) implies that the square of the Busemann function is strictly convex (and exhausting). Thus every level set \( {\varphi }^{-1}\left( a\right) \) , with \( a > \inf \{ \varphi \left( x\right)  \mid  x \in  M\} \) , of the Busemann function \( \varphi \) is diffeomorphic to the \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{n - 1} \) . In particular, \( {\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {a,\frac{3}{2}a}\right\rbrack  \right) \) is simply connected for \( a > \inf \{ \varphi \left( x\right)  \mid  x \in  M\} \) since \( n \geq  3 \) .

Consider an annulus portion \( \left\lbrack  {1,2}\right\rbrack   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) of the metric cone \( \widetilde{M} = {\mathbb{R}}_{ + }{ \times  }_{r}{X}^{n - 1} \) . It is the limit of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) , where

\[
{M}_{k} = \left\{  {x \in  M\left| {\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }} \leq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{2}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right. }\right\}  .
\]

It is clear that

\[
{\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }},\frac{2\left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) }{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right\rbrack  \right)  \subset  {M}_{k} \subset  {\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {\frac{1 - \varepsilon }{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }},\frac{2}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right\rbrack  \right)
\]

for \( k \) large enough. Thus any closed loop in \( \left\{  \frac{3}{2}\right\}   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) can be shrunk to a point by a homotopy in \( \left\lbrack  {1,2}\right\rbrack   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) . This shows that \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is simply connected. Hence we have proven that the metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Consequently,

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow   + \infty }}\frac{{\operatorname{Vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right)  \smallsetminus  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{\sigma r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right) }\right) }{{\left( \frac{r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) }^{n}} = {\alpha }_{n}\left( {1 - {\sigma }^{n}}\right)
\]

for any \( r > 0 \) and \( 0 < \sigma  < 1 \) , where \( {\alpha }_{n} \) is the volume of the unit ball in the Euclidean space \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Finally, by combining with the monotonicity of the Bishop-Gromov volume comparison, we conclude that the manifold \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is flat and isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . This contradicts the assumption.

Therefore, we have proved the lemma. Ⓡ

Finally we would like to include an alternative simpler argument, inspired by Ni [98], for the above Case 2 and Case 3 to avoid the use of the gap theorem, holonomy groups, and asymptotic cone structure.

Alternative Proof for Case 2 and Case 3. Let us consider the situation of \( 0 \leq \; A <  + \infty \) in the above proof. Observe that \( {\nu }_{M}\left( t\right) \) is nonincreasing in time \( t \) by using Lemma 3.4.1(ii) and the fact that the metric is shrinking in \( t \) . Suppose \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , then the solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed for \( t \leq  {t}_{0} \) for some uniform \( \kappa  > 0 \) . By combining with Theorem 6.2.1, there exist a sequence of points \( {q}_{k} \) and a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow   - \infty \) such that the scalings of \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) around \( {q}_{k} \) with factor \( {\left| {t}_{k}\right| }^{-1} \) and with the times \( {t}_{k} \) shifting to the new time zero converge to a nonflat gradient shrinking soliton \( \bar{M} \) in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology. This gradient soliton also has maximal volume growth (i.e. \( {\nu }_{\bar{M}}\left( t\right)  > 0 \) ) and satisfies the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.5). If the curvature of the shrinking soliton \( \bar{M} \) at the time -1 is bounded, then we see from the proof of Theorem 6.2.2 that by using the equations (6.2.24)-(6.2.26), the scalar curvature has a positive lower bound everywhere on \( \bar{M} \) at the time -1 . In particular, this implies the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( A = \infty \) for the soliton at the time -1 , which reduces to Case 1 and arrives at a contradiction by the dimension reduction argument. On the other hand, if the scalar curvature is unbounded, then by Lemma 6.1.4, the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.5) and Lemma 6.1.2, we can do the same dimension reduction as in Case 1 to arrive at a contradiction also. 0

The set of nonflat three-dimensional ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solutions is compact modulo scaling in the sense that for any sequence of such solutions and marking points \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) with \( R\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right)  = 1 \) , we can extract a \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) converging subsequence whose limit is also an ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Consider any sequence of three-dimensional ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solutions and marking points \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) with \( R\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right)  = 1 \) . By Theorem 6.4.3(i), the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality and Hamilton's compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), we can extract a \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) converging subsequence such that the limit \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) , with \( - \infty  < t \leq  0 \) , is an ancient solution to the Ricci flow with nonnegative curvature operator and \( {\kappa }_{{0}^{ - }} \) noncollapsed on all scales. Since any ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution satisfies the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality, it implies that the scalar curvature \( \bar{R}\left( {x, t}\right) \) of the limit \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) is pointwise nondecreasing in time. Thus it remains to show that the limit solution has bounded curvature at \( t = 0 \) .

Obviously we may assume the limiting manifold \( \bar{M} \) is noncompact. By pulling back the limiting solution to its orientable cover, we can assume that the limiting manifold \( \bar{M} \) is orientable. We now argue by contradiction. Suppose the scalar curvature \( \bar{R} \) of the limit at \( t = 0 \) is unbounded.

By applying Lemma 6.1.4, we can choose a sequence of points \( {x}_{j} \in  \bar{M}, j = \; 1,2,\ldots \) , divergent to infinity such that the scalar curvature \( \bar{R} \) of the limit satisfies

\[
\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)  \geq  j\text{ and }\bar{R}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  4\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)
\]

for all \( j = 1,2,\ldots \) , and \( x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{j}, j/\sqrt{\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }}\right) \) . Then from the fact that the limiting scalar curvature \( \bar{R}\left( {x, t}\right) \) is pointwise nondecreasing in time, we have

(6.4.20)

\[
\bar{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)
\]

for all \( j = 1,2,\ldots , x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{j}, j/\sqrt{\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }}\right) \) and \( t \leq  0 \) . By combining with Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5) and the \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -noncollapsing, we know that a subsequence of the rescaled solutions

\[
\left( {\bar{M},\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) {\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t/\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }\right) ,{x}_{j}}\right) ,\;j = 1,2,\ldots ,
\]

converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a nonflat smooth solution of the Ricci flow. Then Proposition 6.1.2 implies that the new limit at the new time \( \{ t = 0\} \) must split off a line. By pulling back the new limit to its universal cover and applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle, we deduce that the pull-back of the new limit on the universal cover splits off a line for all time \( t \leq  0 \) . Thus by combining with Theorem 6.2.2 and the argument in the proof of Lemma 6.4.1, we further deduce that the new limit is either the round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or the round \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Since \( \bar{M} \) is orientable, the new limit must be \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Moreover, since \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right) }\right) \) has nonnegative curvature operator and the points \( \left\{  {x}_{j}\right\} \) are going to infinity and \( \bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) , this gives a contradiction to Proposition 6.1.1. So we have proved that the limit \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) has uniformly bounded curvature. \( \square \)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: (Singularity structure theorem). Given \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) and \( {T}_{0} > 1 \) , one can find \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) with the following property. If \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) , x \in  M \) and \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( 1 < T \leq  {T}_{0} \) , is a solution to the Ricci flow on a compact orientable three-manifold \( M \) with normalized initial metric, then for any point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{0} \geq  1 \) and \( Q = \; R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , the solution in \( \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < {\varepsilon }^{-2}{Q}^{-1},\;{t}_{0} - {\varepsilon }^{-2}{Q}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{0}}\right\} \) is, after scaling by the factor \( Q,\varepsilon \) -close (in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  {\varepsilon }^{-1}\right\rbrack  } \) -topology) to the corresponding subset of some orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution (for some \( \kappa  > 0 \) ).

\[
U = \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{{q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty }}}B\left( {{q}_{0},{4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \;\left( { \subset  \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }}\right) }\right) ,
\]

where \( B\left( {{q}_{0},{4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) is the ball centered at \( {q}_{0} \in  {B}_{\infty } \) with the radius \( {4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . Furthermore \( {y}_{\infty } \) cannot be an interior point of any geodesic segment in \( \bar{U} \) . This implies the curvature of \( \bar{U} \) at \( {y}_{\infty } \) is nonnegative in the Alexandrov sense. It is a basic result in Alexandrov space theory (see for example Theorem 10.9.3 and Corollary 10.9.5 of [9]) that there exists a three-dimensional tangent cone \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{U} \) at \( {y}_{\infty } \) which is a metric cone. It is clear that its aperture is \( \leq  {10\varepsilon } \) , thus the tangent cone is nonflat.

Pick a point \( p \in  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{U} \) such that the distance from the vertex \( {y}_{\infty } \) to \( p \) is one and it is nonflat around \( p \) . Thus by Shi's local derivative estimates (Theorem 1.4.2) we can control all derivatives of the curvature in such backward parabolic neighborhoods. Then by using the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing and Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), we can take a \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) subsequent limit to obtain \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , which is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on all scales and is defined on a space-time open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing the time slice \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \{ 0\} \) . Clearly it follows from the pinching estimate (7.1.1) that the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) has nonnegative curvature operator (and hence nonnegative sectional curvature).

Step 3. We further claim that the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) at the time slice \( \{ t = 0\} \) has bounded curvature.

We know that the sectional curvature of the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) is nonnegative everywhere. Argue by contradiction. Suppose the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) is not bounded, then by Lemma 6.1.4, there exists a sequence of points \( {q}_{j} \in  {M}_{\infty } \) diverging to infinity such that their scalar curvatures \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{j},0}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) as \( j \rightarrow   + \infty \)

and

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  4{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{j},0}\right)
\]

for \( x \in  B\left( {{q}_{j}, j/\sqrt{{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{j},0}\right) }}\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) }\right) \) . By combining with Lemma 7.1.2 and the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing, a subsequence of the rescaled and marked manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{j},0}\right) {\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{q}_{j}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a smooth nonflat limit \( Y \) . By Proposition 6.1.2, the new limit \( Y \) is isometric to a metric product \( N \times  \mathbb{R} \) for some two-dimensional manifold \( N \) . On the other hand, in view of the choice of the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , the original limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) at the point \( {q}_{j} \) has a canonical neighborhood which is either a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap, or a compact manifold (without boundary) diffeomorphic to a metric quotient of the round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) . It follows that for \( j \) large enough, \( {q}_{j} \) is the center of a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck of radius \( {\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{j},0\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . Without loss of generality, we may further assume that \( {2\varepsilon } < {\varepsilon }_{0} \) , where \( {\varepsilon }_{0} \) is the positive constant given in Proposition 6.1.1. Since \( {\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{j},0\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \rightarrow  0 \) as \( j \rightarrow   + \infty \) , this contradicts Proposition 6.1.1. So the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) }\right) \) is bounded.

Step 4. Finally we want to extend the limit backwards in time to \( - \infty \) .

By Lemma 7.1.2 again, we now know that the limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) is defined on a backward time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-a,0}\right\rbrack \) for some \( a > 0 \) .

Denote by

\( {t}^{\prime } = \inf \{ \widetilde{t} \mid \) we can take a smooth limit on \( (\widetilde{t},0\rbrack \) (with bounded curvature at each time slice) from a subsequence of the convergent rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k} \) \}.

We first claim that there is a subsequence of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k} \) which converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a smooth limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) on the maximal time interval \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Indeed, let \( {t}_{k}^{\prime } \) be a sequence of negative numbers such that \( {t}_{k}^{\prime } \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) and there exist smooth limits \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }^{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) defined on \( \left( {{t}_{k}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . For each \( k \) , the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature and has bounded curvature at each time slice. Moreover by Lemma 7.1.2, the limit has bounded curvature on each subinterval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \subset  \left( {{t}_{k}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . Denote by \( \widetilde{Q} \) the scalar curvature upper bound of the limit at time zero (where \( \widetilde{Q} \) is the same for all \( k \) ). Then we can apply the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.7) to get

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }^{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{Q}\left( \frac{-{t}_{k}^{\prime }}{t - {t}_{k}^{\prime }}\right) ,
\]

where \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }^{k}\left( {x, t}\right) \) are the scalar curvatures of the limits \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }^{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) . Hence by the definition of convergence and the above curvature estimates, we can find a subsequence of the above convergent rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k} \) which converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a smooth limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) on the maximal time interval \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) .

We next claim that \( {t}^{\prime } =  - \infty \) .

Suppose not, then by Lemma 7.1.2, the curvature of the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) becomes unbounded as \( t \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } >  - \infty \) . By applying the maximum principle to the evolution equation of the scalar curvature, we see that the infimum of the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time. Note that \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1 \) . Thus there exists some point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty } \) such that

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{10}}\right)  < \frac{3}{2}
\]

where \( c > 0 \) is the universal constant in Lemma 7.1.2. By using Lemma 7.1.2 again we see that the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) in a small neighborhood of the point \( \left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{10}}\right) \) extends backwards to the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{10},{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{10}}\right\rbrack \) . We remark that the distances at time \( t \) and time 0 are roughly equivalent in the following sense

(7.1.3)

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  {d}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  {d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  - \text{ const. }
\]

for any \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . Indeed from the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.7) we have the estimate

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{Q}\left( \frac{-{t}^{\prime }}{t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) ,\;\text{ on }{M}_{\infty } \times  \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack  .
\]

By applying Lemma 3.4.1 (ii), we have

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {d}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  + {30}\left( {-{t}^{\prime }}\right) \sqrt{\widetilde{Q}}
\]

for any \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . On the other hand, since the curvature of the limit metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) is nonnegative, we have

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  {d}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)
\]

for any \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . Thus we obtain the estimate (7.1.3).

Let us still denote by \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) the subsequence which converges on the maximal time interval \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . Consider the rescaled sequence \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) with the marked points \( {x}_{k} \) replaced by the associated sequence of points \( {y}_{k} \rightarrow  {y}_{\infty } \) and the (original unshifted) times \( {t}_{k} \) replaced by any \( {s}_{k} \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} + \left( {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{20}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k} + \left( {{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{20}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) . It follows from Lemma 7.1.2 that for \( k \) large enough, the rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) at \( {y}_{k} \) satisfy

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {{y}_{k}, t}\right)  \leq  {10}
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{10},{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{10}}\right\rbrack \) . By applying the same arguments as in the above Step 2, we conclude that for any \( A > 0 \) , there is a positive constant \( C\left( A\right)  <  + \infty \) such that

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( {d}_{t}\left( {x,{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  A \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{20},{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{20}}\right\rbrack \) . The estimate (7.1.3) implies that there is a positive constant \( {A}_{0} \) such that for arbitrarily given small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \in  \left( {0,\frac{c}{100}}\right) \) , for \( k \) large enough, there hold

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{k},{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  {A}_{0}
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . By combining with Lemma 7.1.2, we then conclude that for any \( A > 0 \) , there is a positive constant \( \widetilde{C}\left( A\right) \) such that for \( k \) large enough, the rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) satisfy

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{C}\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{100}{\left( C\left( A\right) \right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) .

Now, by taking convergent subsequences from the (original) rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) , we see that the limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) is defined on a spacetime open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . By repeating the argument of Step 3 and using Lemma 7.1.2, we further conclude the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) has uniformly bounded curvature on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . This is a contradiction.

Therefore we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) converges to an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, which gives the desired contradiction. This completes the proof of the theorem. 0

Fix a compact interval \( \left\lbrack  {\alpha ,\beta }\right\rbrack   \subset  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) . Then there exists a real number \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , depending only on \( \alpha ,\beta \) , and \( n \) , with the following property.

If \( F \subset  {\mathcal{C}}_{B}\left( {\mathbb{R}}^{n}\right) \) is a closed set which is invariant under the Hamilton ODE and satisfies

\[
F \subset  \left\{  {R \in  {\mathcal{C}}_{B}\left( {\mathbb{R}}^{n}\right)  : R + {hI} \in  \widehat{C}\left( s\right) }\right\}
\]

for some \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {\alpha ,\beta }\right\rbrack \) and some \( h > 0 \) , then the set

\[
\widehat{F} = \{ R \in  F : R + {2hI} \in  \widehat{C}\left( {s + \varepsilon }\right) \}
\]

is also invariant under the Hamilton ODE. Moreover, we have

\[
\{ R \in  F : \operatorname{scal}\left( R\right)  \leq  h\}  \subset  \widehat{F}.
\]

The proof is similar to the proof of Theorem 4.1 in [14] (see also [20], Proposition 16). If \( R \in  \widehat{C}\left( s\right)  \smallsetminus  \{ 0\} \) for some \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {\alpha ,\beta  + 1}\right\rbrack \) , then \( Q\left( R\right) \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone \( {T}_{R}\widehat{C}\left( s\right) \) by Proposition 8.8. Hence, there exists a constant \( N \geq  1 \) , depending only on \( \alpha ,\beta \) , and \( n \) , with the following property: if \( \operatorname{scal}\left( R\right)  \geq  N \) and \( R \in  \widehat{C}\left( s\right) \) for some \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {\alpha ,\beta  + 1}\right\rbrack \) , then \( Q\left( {R - {2I}}\right) \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone \( {T}_{R}\widehat{C}\left( s\right) \) .

Since the cones \( \widehat{C}\left( s\right) \) vary continuously in \( s \) , we can find a real number \( \varepsilon  \in  (0,1\rbrack \) , depending only on \( \alpha ,\beta \) , and \( n \) , such that

\[
\left\{  {R \in  {\mathcal{C}}_{B}\left( {\mathbb{R}}^{n}\right)  : R + I \in  \widehat{C}\left( s\right) \text{ and }\operatorname{scal}\left( R\right)  \leq  N}\right\}
\]

(69)

\[
\subset  \left\{  {R \in  {\mathcal{C}}_{B}\left( {\mathbb{R}}^{n}\right)  : R + {2I} \in  \widehat{C}\left( {s + \varepsilon }\right) }\right\}
\]

for each \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {\alpha ,\beta }\right\rbrack \) .

We claim that \( \varepsilon \) has the desired property. It suffices to verify this in the special case when \( h = 1 \) . (The general case follows by scaling.) Therefore, let us assume that \( F \subset  {\mathcal{C}}_{B}\left( {\mathbb{R}}^{n}\right) \) is a closed set which is invariant under the Hamilton ODE and satisfies

(70)

\[
F \subset  \left\{  {R \in  {\mathcal{C}}_{B}\left( {\mathbb{R}}^{n}\right)  : R + I \in  \widehat{C}\left( s\right) }\right\}
\]

for some \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {\alpha ,\beta }\right\rbrack \) . Moreover, we define a set \( \widehat{F} \subset  {\mathcal{C}}_{B}\left( {\mathbb{R}}^{n}\right) \) by

\[
\widehat{F} = \{ R \in  F : R + {2I} \in  \widehat{C}\left( {s + \varepsilon }\right) \} .
\]

Using (69) and (70), we obtain

(71)

\[
\{ R \in  F : \operatorname{scal}\left( R\right)  \leq  N\}  \subset  \widehat{F}.
\]

It remains to show that the set \( \widehat{F} \) is invariant under the Hamilton ODE. Suppose that \( R\left( t\right) , t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , is a solution of the ODE \( \frac{d}{dt}R\left( t\right)  = Q\left( {R\left( t\right) }\right) \) such that \( R\left( 0\right)  \in  \widehat{F} \) . Since \( F \) is invariant under the Hamilton ODE, we have \( R\left( t\right)  \in  F \) for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) . Hence, it suffices to prove that \( R\left( t\right)  + {2I} \in  \widehat{C}\left( {s + \varepsilon }\right) \) for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) . Suppose this is false. We define

\[
{t}_{0} = \inf \{ t \in  \lbrack 0, T) : R\left( t\right)  + {2I} \notin  \widehat{C}\left( {s + \varepsilon }\right) \} .
\]

Clearly, \( R\left( {t}_{0}\right)  + {2I} \in  \widehat{C}\left( {s + \varepsilon }\right) \) . There are two possibilities now:

Case 1. Suppose that \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {R\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right)  \geq  N \) . It follows from our choice of \( N \) that \( Q\left( {R\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone \( {T}_{R\left( {t}_{0}\right)  + {2I}}\widehat{C}\left( {s + \varepsilon }\right) \) . By Proposition 5.4, there exists a real number \( {t}_{1} \in  \left( {{t}_{0}, T}\right) \) such that \( R\left( t\right)  + {2I} \in \; \widehat{C}\left( {s + \varepsilon }\right) \) for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack \) . This contradicts the definition of \( {t}_{0} \) .

Case 2. Suppose that \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {R\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right)  < N \) . By continuity, there exists a real number \( {t}_{1} \in  \left( {{t}_{0}, T}\right) \) such that \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {R\left( t\right) }\right)  \leq  N \) for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack \) . Using (71), we conclude that \( R\left( t\right)  + {2I} \in  \widehat{C}\left( {s + \varepsilon }\right) \) for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack \) . Again, this contradicts the definition of \( {t}_{0} \) .

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
(Justification of the canonical neighborhood assumption). Given any small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there exist decreasing sequences \( 0 < {\widetilde{r}}_{j} < \varepsilon ,{\kappa }_{j} > 0 \) , and \( 0 < {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} < {\varepsilon }^{2}, j = 1,2,\cdots \) , with the following property. Define the positive function \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) on \( \lbrack 0, + \infty ) \) by \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right)  = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) . Suppose there is a surgically modified solution, defined on \( \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( T <  + \infty \) , to the Ricci flow which satisfies the following:

(1) it starts on a compact orientable three-manifold with normalized initial metric, and

(2) it has only a finite number of surgeries such that each surgery at a time \( t \in  \left( {0, T}\right) \) is a \( \delta \left( t\right) \) -cutoff surgery with

\[
0 < \delta \left( t\right)  \leq  \min \{ \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) ,\bar{\delta }\left( t\right) \} .
\]

Then on each time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack  \bigcap \lbrack 0, T), j = 1,2,\cdots \) , the solution satisfies the \( {\kappa }_{j} \) -noncollapsing condition on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) and the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {\widetilde{r}}_{j} \) .

Here and in the following, we call a (three-dimensional) surgically modified solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) ,0 \leq  t < T,\kappa \) -noncollapsed at \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) on the scales less than \( \rho \) (for some \( \kappa  > 0,\rho  > 0 \) ) if it satisfies the following property: whenever \( r < \rho \) and

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {r}^{-2}
\]

for all those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}, r, - {r}^{2}}\right)  = \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {B}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the solution is defined, we have

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}^{3}.
\]

The proof of the proposition is by induction: having constructed our sequences for \( 1 \leq  j \leq  m \) , we make one more step, defining \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) , \( {\kappa }_{m + 1},{\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) , and redefining \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) . In view of the previous lemma, we only need to define \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .

In Theorem 7.1.1 we have obtained the canonical neighborhood structure for smooth solutions. When adapting the arguments in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1 to the present surgical solutions, we will encounter the new difficulty of how to take a limit for the surgically modified solutions. The idea to overcome the difficulty consists of two parts. The first part, due to Perelman [104], is to choose \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) small enough to push the surgical regions to infinity in space. (This is the reason why we need to redefine \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .) The second part is to show that solutions are smooth on some small, but uniform, time intervals (on compact subsets) so that we can apply Hamilton's compactness theorem, since we only have curvature bounds; otherwise Shi's interior derivative estimate may not be applicable. In fact, the second part is more crucial. That is just concerned with the question of whether the surgery times accumulate or not. Our argument will use the canonical neighborhood characterization of the standard solution in Lemma 7.3.5.

We now start to prove the proposition by contradiction. Suppose for sequence of positive numbers \( {r}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) , satisfying \( {r}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) as \( \alpha  \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  \frac{1}{\alpha  \cdot  \beta }\left( { \rightarrow  0}\right) \) , there exist sequences of solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) to the Ricci flow with surgery, where each of them has only a finite number of cutoff surgeries and has a compact orientable normalized three-manifold as initial data, so that the following two assertions hold:

(i) each \( \delta \) -cutoff at a time \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) satisfies \( \delta  \leq  {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) ; and

(ii) the solutions satisfy the statement of the proposition on \( \left\lbrack  {0, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) , but violate the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) on \( \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) .

For each solution \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) , we choose \( \bar{t} \) (depending on \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) ) to be the nearly first time for which the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) is violated. More precisely, we choose \( \bar{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) so that the canonical neighborhood assumption with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) and with accuracy parameter \( \varepsilon \) is violated at some \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , however the canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) holds on \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . After passing to subsequences, we may assume each \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) is less than the \( \widetilde{\delta } \) in Lemma 7.4.2 with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) when \( \alpha \) is fixed. Then by Lemma 7.4.2 we have uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) on \( \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) with some \( \kappa  > 0 \) independent of \( \alpha ,\beta \) .

Slightly abusing notation, we will often drop the indices \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) .

Let \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) be the rescaled solutions around \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with factors \( R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \left( { \geq  {r}^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty }\right) \) and shift the times \( \bar{t} \) to zero. We hope to take a limit of the rescaled solutions for subsequences of \( \alpha ,\beta  \rightarrow  \infty \) and show the limit is an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, which will give the desired contradiction. We divide our arguments into the following six steps.

Step 1. Let \( \left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right) \) be a point on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( \widetilde{R}\left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right)  \leq  A \) (for some \( A \geq  1 \) ) and \( \widehat{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {-\left( {\bar{t} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) ,0}\right\rbrack \) . Then we have estimate

(7.4.14)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10A}
\]

for those \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {y,\widehat{t},\frac{1}{2}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-1}}\right)  \triangleq \; \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {y,\frac{1}{2}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {\widehat{t} - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-1},\widehat{t}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the rescaled solution is defined.

Indeed, as in the first step of the proof of Theorem 7.1.1, this follows directly from the gradient estimates (7.3.4) in the canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) .

Step 2. In this step, we will prove three time extension results.

Assertion 1. For arbitrarily fixed \( \alpha ,0 < A <  + \infty ,1 \leq  C <  + \infty \) and \( 0 \leq  B < \frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon }^{2}{\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{C}^{-1} \) , there is a \( {\beta }_{0} = {\beta }_{0}\left( {\varepsilon , A, B, C}\right) \) (independent of \( \alpha \) ) such that if \( \beta  \geq  {\beta }_{0} \) and the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) is defined on a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack \) with \( 0 \leq  b \leq  B \) and the scalar curvature satisfies

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C,\;\text{ on }{\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack  ,
\]

(7.4.18)

\[

for all \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) . and the completion \( {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) of \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) \) with \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) the limit point of \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . As before, by the choice of the points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , we know that the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty } \) is cylindrical at any point \( {q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) which is sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) . Then by the same reason as before the metric space \( \bar{V} = V \cup  \left\{  {y}_{\infty }\right\} \) has nonnegative curvature in Alexandrov sense, and we have a three-dimensional nonflat tangent cone \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V} \) at \( {y}_{\infty } \) . Pick \( z \in  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V} \) with distance one from the vertex and it is nonflat around \( z \) . By definition \( B\left( {z,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \left( { \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V}}\right) \) is the Gromov-Hausdoff convergent limit of the scalings of a sequence of balls \( {B}_{\infty }\left( {{z}_{k},{\sigma }_{k}}\right) \left( { \subset  \left( {V,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) }\right) \) with \( {\sigma }_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) . Since the estimate (7.5.14) survives on \( \left( {V,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) \) for all \( \widetilde{K} <  + \infty \) , we know that this convergence is actually in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology and over some time interval. Since the limit \( B\left( {z,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \left( { \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V}}\right) \) is a piece of a nonnegatively curved nonflat metric cone, we get a contradiction with Hamilton's strong maximum Principle (Theorem 2.2.1) as before. Hence we have proved that a subsequence of the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) has uniformly bounded curvatures at bounded distance from \( \bar{x} \) at the new times zero.

Further, by the uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing at the points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) and the estimate (7.5.14) again, we can take a \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , defined on a space-time subset which contains the time slice \( \{ t = 0\} \) and is relatively open in \( {M}_{\infty } \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , for the subsequence of the rescaled solutions. The limit is a smooth solution to the Ricci flow, and is complete at \( t = 0 \) , as well as has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching assumption and the estimate (7.5.15). Thus by repeating the same argument as in the Step 4 of the proof Proposition 7.4.1, we conclude that the curvature of the limit at \( t = 0 \) is bounded.

Finally we try to extend the limit backwards in time to get an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. Since the curvature of the limit is bounded at \( t = 0 \) , it follows from the estimate (7.5.14) that the limit is a smooth solution to the Ricci flow defined at least on a backward time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-a,0}\right\rbrack \) for some positive constant \( a \) . Let \( \left( {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) be the maximal time interval over which we can extract a smooth limiting solution. It suffices to show \( {t}_{\infty } =  - \infty \) . If \( {t}_{\infty } >  - \infty \) , there are only two possibilities: either there exist surgeries in finite distance around the time \( {t}_{\infty } \) or the curvature of the limiting solution becomes unbounded as \( t \searrow  {t}_{\infty } \) .

Let \( c > 0 \) be a positive constant much smaller than \( \frac{1}{100}{\eta }^{-1} \) . Note again that the infimum of the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time. Then we can find some point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and some time \( t = {t}_{\infty } + \theta \) with \( 0 < \theta  < \frac{c}{3} \) such that \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty } + \theta }\right)  \leq  2 \) .

Consider the (unrescaled) scalar curvature \( R \) of \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at the point \( \bar{x} \) over the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . Since the scalar curvature \( {R}_{\infty } \) of the limit on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{3},0}\right\rbrack \) is uniformly bounded by some positive constant \( C \) , we have the curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {\bar{x}, t}\right)  \leq  {2C}\bar{Q}
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) and all sufficiently large \( m \) . For each fixed \( m \) and \( {\alpha }_{m} \) , we may require the chosen \( {\beta }_{m} \) to satisfy

\[
{\left( {\bar{\delta }}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\right) }^{-2}{\left( \widetilde{r}\left( \frac{{t}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}}}{2}\right) \right) }^{-2} \geq  m\widetilde{r}{\left( {t}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}}\right) }^{-2} \geq  m\bar{Q}.
\]

When \( m \) is large enough, we observe again that Lemma 3.4.1 (ii) is applicable for \( {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},\bar{x}}\right) \) with \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . Then by repeating the argument as in the derivation of (7.2.1),(7.2.2) and (7.2.3), we deduce that for all sufficiently large \( m \) , the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) . \)

Let \( \left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) be a sequence of associated points and times in the (unrescaled) solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) so that after rescaling, the sequence converges to \( \left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty } + \theta }\right) \) in the limit. Clearly \( \frac{\theta }{2} \leq  {\theta }_{m} \leq  {2\theta } \) for all sufficiently large \( m \) . Then by the argument as in the derivation of (7.5.13), we know that for all sufficiently large \( m \) , the solution \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at \( {y}_{m} \) is defined on the whole time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m} - }\right. }\right. \; \left. {\left. {\frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies the curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {{y}_{m}, t}\right)  \leq  8\bar{Q}
\]

there; moreover the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) with \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  \geq  4\bar{Q} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) .

We now consider the rescaled sequence \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) with the marked points replaced by \( {y}_{m} \) and the times replaced by \( {s}_{m} \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{4}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{c}{4}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) . As before the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality implies the rescaling limit around \( \left( {{y}_{m},{s}_{m}}\right) \) agrees with the original one. Then the arguments in previous paragraphs imply the limit is well-defined and smooth on a space-time open neighborhood of the maximal time slice \( \left\{  {t = {t}_{\infty }}\right\} \) . Particularly this excludes the possibility of existing surgeries in finite distance around the time \( {t}_{\infty } \) . Moreover, the limit at \( t = {t}_{\infty } \) also has bounded curvature. By using the gradient estimates in the canonical neighborhood assumption on the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) , we see that the second possibility is also impossible. Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Therefore we have proved the canonical neighborhood statement (ii).

(iii) This is analogous to Theorem 7.2.1. We also argue by contradiction. Suppose for some \( A <  + \infty \) and sequences of positive numbers \( {K}_{2}^{\alpha } \rightarrow   + \infty ,{\bar{r}}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) there exists a sequence of times \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \) such that for any sequences \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } > 0 \) with \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \rightarrow  0 \) for fixed \( \alpha \) , we have sequences of solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) to the Ricci flow with surgery and sequences of points \( {x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) , of positive constants \( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  {\bar{r}}^{\alpha }\sqrt{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }} \) which satisfy the assumptions, but for all \( \alpha ,\beta \) there hold

(7.5.16)

\[
R\left( {{x}^{\alpha \beta },{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\right)  > {K}_{2}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2}\text{ , for some }{x}^{\alpha \beta } \in  {B}_{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\left( {{x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }, A{r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }}\right) .
\]

We may assume that \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  {\bar{\delta }}_{4A}\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) \) for all \( \alpha ,\beta \) , where \( {\bar{\delta }}_{4A}\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) \) is chosen so that the statements (i) and (ii) hold on \( {B}_{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\left( {{x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta },{4A}{r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }}\right) \) . Let \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) be the rescaled solutions of \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) around the origins \( {x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) with factor \( {\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2} \) and shift the times \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \) to zero. Then by applying the statement (ii), we know that the regions, where the scalar curvature of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) is at least \( {K}_{1}\left( { = {K}_{1}\left( {4A}\right) }\right) \) , are canonical neighborhood regions. Note that canonical \( \varepsilon \) -neck neighborhoods are strong. Also note that the pinching assumption and the assertion

\[
{t}_{0}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2} \geq  {\left( {\bar{r}}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty ,\text{ as }\alpha  \rightarrow   + \infty ,
\]

imply that any subsequent limit of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) must have nonnegative sectional curvature. Thus by the above argument in the proof of the statement (ii) (or the argument in Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 7.1.1), we conclude that there exist subsequences \( \alpha  = {\alpha }_{m},\beta  = {\beta }_{m} \) such that the curvatures of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) stay uniformly bounded at distances from the origins \( {x}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) not exceeding \( {2A} \) . This contradicts (7.5.16) for \( m \) sufficiently large. This proves the statements (iii).

Clearly for fixed \( A \) , after defining the \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) for each \( {t}_{0} \) , one can adjust the \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) so that it is nonincreasing in \( {t}_{0} \) .

Therefore we have completed the proof of the theorem.

From now on we redefine the function \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) so that it is also less than \( {\bar{\delta }}_{2\left( {t + 1}\right) }\left( {2t}\right) \) and then the above theorem always holds for \( A \in  \left\lbrack  {1,2\left( {{t}_{0} + 1}\right) }\right\rbrack \) . Particularly, we still

have

\[
\widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right)  \leq  \bar{\delta }\left( t\right)  = \min \left\{  {\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}\log \left( {1 + t}\right) },{\delta }_{0}}\right\}  ,
\]

which tends to zero as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) . We may also require that \( \widetilde{r}\left( t\right) \) tends to zero as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) .

We argue by contradiction. Suppose that the assertion is false. Then we can find a sequence of Ricci flows with surgery \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) and a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) in space-time with the following properties:

(i) The flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{j}}\right) \) and has surgery parameters \( \varepsilon ,{\widehat{r}}_{j},{h}_{j},{\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) , where \( {\widehat{r}}_{j} \leq  \frac{1}{j} \) and \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \leq  \min \left\{  {\widetilde{\widetilde{\delta }}\left( {\widehat{r}}_{j}\right) ,\frac{1}{j}}\right\} \) . Here, \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( \cdot \right) \) is the function introduced in Proposition 10.9.

(ii) \( {Q}_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 2{\widehat{r}}_{j}\right) }^{-2} \) .

(iii) The point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) does not satisfy the conclusion of Theorem 10.10.

Condition (iii) means that at least one of the following statements is true:

- There does not exist a neighborhood \( B \) of \( {x}_{j} \) with the property that \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{\left( 2{C}_{1}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},2{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) and \( {\left( 2{C}_{2}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \leq  \operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{j}}\right)  \leq  2{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) for all \( x \in  B \) , and such that \( B \) is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck (in the sense of [35]) with center at \( {x}_{j} \) or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap.

- \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  > {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) .

- \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  > {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) .

We will proceed in several steps:

Step 1: By Definition 10.1, we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq \; {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) for each point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  4{Q}_{j} \) . Moreover, by Proposition 10.9, the flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales less than \( \varepsilon \) for some uniform constant \( \kappa \) that may depend on the initial data, but it is independent of \( j \) .

Step 2: Suppose that \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) is a point in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \; + {Q}_{j} \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . The pointwise curvature derivative estimate implies that scal \( \leq \; 8{r}_{0}^{-2} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{{r}_{0}}{100\eta }, - \frac{{r}_{0}^{2}}{100\eta }}\right) \) . Using Proposition 10.4, we conclude that \( \left| {{D}^{m}R}\right|  \leq  C\left( {n, m,\eta }\right) {r}_{0}^{-m - 2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Moreover, Proposition 10.9 implies \( {\operatorname{vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}_{0}^{n} \) for some uniform constant \( \kappa \) that is independent of \( j \) .

Step 3: We next prove a long-range curvature estimate. Given any \( \rho  > 0 \) , we put

\[
\mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{j}}\right) .
\]

The pointwise curvature derivative estimate implies that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  \leq  {16} \) for \( 0 < \; \rho  < \frac{1}{100\eta }. \)

We claim that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \) for all \( \rho  > 0 \) . Suppose this is false. Let

\[
{\rho }^{ * } = \sup \{ \rho  \geq  0 : \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \}  < \infty .
\]

By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , we have an upper bound for the curvature in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . Using the results in Step 2, we obtain bounds for all the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . Moreover, the noncollapsing estimate in Step 2 gives a lower bound for the volume. We rescale around \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) and pass to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) . In the limit, we obtain an incomplete manifold \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) that is weakly PIC2 (cf. [31, Th. 5.6]).

By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , there exists a sequence of points \( {y}_{j} \) such that

\[
{\rho }_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {Q}_{j}^{\frac{1}{2}}{d}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{y}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }^{ * }\;\text{ and }\;{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty .
\]

Let \( {\gamma }_{j} : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) be a unit-speed geodesic such that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( 0\right)  = {x}_{j} \) and \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  = {y}_{j} \) , and let \( {\gamma }_{\infty } : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }^{ * }}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) denote the limit of \( {\gamma }_{j} \) . \[
{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( s\right) }\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {s{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 2\eta \left( {\rho }^{ * } - s\right) \right) }^{-2} \geq  {100}.
\]

Let us consider a real number \( \bar{s} \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) such that \( {64}{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s} \) .
