Indeed, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption implies that the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap. Furthermore, the Canonical Neighborhood is contained in a geodesic ball around \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) of radius \( 8{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , and the scalar curvature is at most \( 8{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) at each point in the Canonical Neighborhood. Since \( \mathbb{M}\left( \bar{s}\right)  < \infty \) , we obtain \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  = \infty \) ; consequently, \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {16}{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {y}_{j} \) . We next observe that \( {32}{C}_{1}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}{\left( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  {64}{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s} \) . This implies \( {16}{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {x}_{j} \) . If the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap, then the geodesic \( {\gamma }_{j} \) must enter and exit this \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap, but this is impossible since \( {\gamma }_{j} \) minimizes length. To summarize, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck. In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) . \)

Passing to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) , we conclude that \( \left| {D{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) . Integrating this estimate along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) gives \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) }\right)  \geq \; {\left( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \left( {\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-2} \) . Moreover, since \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies at the center of a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck for \( j \) sufficiently large, the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) must lie on a strong \( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) .

As in \( \left\lbrack  {{33},§{12.1}}\right\rbrack \) , there is a sequence of rescalings that converges to a piece of a nonflat metric cone in the limit. Let us fix a point on this metric cone. In view of the preceding discussion, this point must lie on a strong \( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \) -neck. This gives a locally defined solution to the Ricci flow that is weakly PIC2 and that, at the final time, is a piece of nonflat metric cone. This contradicts Proposition 6.5.

Step 4: We now dilate the manifold \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) around the point \( {x}_{j} \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) . By Step 3, we have uniform bounds for the curvature at bounded distance. Using the results in Step 2, we obtain bounds for all the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor at bounded distance. Using these estimates together with the noncollapsing estimate in Step 2, we conclude that the rescaled manifolds converge in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a complete limit manifold \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) . Since \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) has \( \left( {f,\theta }\right) \) -pinched curvature, the curvature tensor of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is weakly PIC2 and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC. Using the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption, we conclude that every point in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with scalar curvature greater than 4 has a neighborhood that is either a strong \( {8\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {8\varepsilon } \) -cap.

We claim that \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature. Indeed, if there is a sequence of points in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with curvature going to infinity, then \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) contains a sequence of necks with radii converging to 0 , contradicting Proposition 6.9. This shows that \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature.

Step 5: We now extend the limit \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time. By Step 4, the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is bounded from above by a constant \( \Lambda  > 4 \) . We claim that, given any \( A > 1 \) , the parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right)
\]

is free of surgeries if \( j \) is sufficiently large. To prove this, fix \( A > 1 \) and suppose that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) contains points modified by surgery. Let \( {s}_{j} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }}\right\rbrack \) be the largest number such that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries. The pointwise curvature derivative estimate gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\left. P\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\right) \right) }\operatorname{scal} \leq  {2\Lambda }{Q}_{j}
\]

if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Since the scalar curvature is greater than \( \frac{1}{2}{h}_{j}^{-2} \) at each point modified by surgery, we deduce that \( \frac{1}{2}{h}_{j}^{-2} \leq  {2\Lambda }{Q}_{j} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. In particular, \( {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1} \leq  \frac{1}{10\eta }{h}_{j}^{2} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Since \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) ,

Proposition 10.5 implies that the parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right)
\]

is, after dilating by the factor \( {h}_{j} \) , arbitrarily close to a piece of the standard solution when \( j \) is sufficiently large. Using Corollary 9.3, we conclude that \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap when \( j \) is sufficiently large. If \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on an \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, then this neck is actually a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, since we are assuming that each \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) -neck on which we perform surgery has a large backward parabolic neighborhood that is free of surgeries (cf. Definition 10.1). Moreover, Corollary 9.3 implies that \( \left| {D\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . Therefore, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10, and this contradicts statement (iii). Thus, given any \( A > 1 \) , the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries if \( j \) is sufficiently large.

Let \( {\tau }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }}  - \frac{1}{200\eta \Lambda } \) . In view of the preceding discussion, we may extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  {2\Lambda } \) .

We now repeat this process. Suppose that we can extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack \) , and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{m} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } < \infty \) . Let \( {\tau }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{200\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} \) . We claim that we can extend the solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) backward to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and \( {\Lambda }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m} \) .

Indeed, if this is not possible, then there exists a number \( A > 1 \) with the property that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) contains points modified by surgery for \( j \) sufficiently large. Let \( {s}_{j} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}}}\right\rbrack \) be the largest number such that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries. The pointwise curvature derivative estimate gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\left. P\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}\right) \right) }\operatorname{scal} \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m}{Q}_{j}
\]

if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Let us choose \( {\alpha }_{m} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{n - 1}{2}}\right) \) so that \( \frac{{\alpha }_{m}}{{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) } \geq \; 8{\Lambda }_{m}\left( {\frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) \) . If \( \left( {{s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1} \geq  {\alpha }_{m}{h}_{j}^{2} \) for \( j \) sufficiently large, then Proposition 10.5 together with the lower bound for the scalar curvature on the standard solution (cf. Theorem 9.1) gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal} \geq  \frac{1}{2{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) }{h}_{j}^{-2}
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{{\alpha }_{m}}{2{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) }{\left( {s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}\right) }^{-1}{Q}_{j}
\]

\[
\geq  4{\Lambda }_{m}{Q}_{j}
\]

for \( j \) sufficiently large, which is impossible. Consequently, \( \left( {{s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1} \leq  {\alpha }_{m}{h}_{j}^{2} \) for \( j \) sufficiently large. Since \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) , Proposition 10.5 implies that the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is, after dilating by the factor \( {h}_{j} \) , arbitrarily close to a piece of the standard solution when \( j \) is sufficiently large. Using Corollary 9.3, we conclude that \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap when \( j \) is sufficiently large. If \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on an \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, then this neck is actually a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, since we are assuming that each \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) -neck on which we perform surgery has a large backward parabolic neighborhood that is free of surgeries (cf. Definition 10.1). Moreover, Corollary 9.3 implies that \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . Therefore, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10, and this contradicts statement (iii). Thus, we may extend the flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) backward to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack \) , where \( {\tau }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{200\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} \) , and we have \( {\Lambda }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m}. \)

Let \( {\tau }^{ * } = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\tau }_{m} \leq   - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda } \) . Using a standard diagonal sequence argument, we obtain a complete, smooth limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined on the interval \( \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) and that has bounded curvature for each \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Step 6: We next show that \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) . Indeed, if \( {\tau }^{ * } >  - \infty \) , it follows that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {\tau }_{m + 1}}\right)  = 0 \) , hence \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) . Arguing as in Step 6 in the proof of Theorem 7.2, we can show that the limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) has bounded curvature. This contradicts the fact that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) . Thus, \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) . Hence, if we dilate the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) around the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) , then (after passing to a subsequence) the rescaled flows converge to an ancient solution that is complete, has bounded curvature, is weakly PIC2, and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC. By Proposition 10.9, the limiting ancient solution is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed for some \( \kappa  > 0 \) that depends only on the initial data. By Corollary 6.22, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck with center at \( {x}_{j} \) ; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap; or a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) ; or a quotient neck. Recall that we have discarded all connected components that are diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) (see Definition 10.1). Hence, the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) cannot be a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) . If the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a quotient neck, then Theorem A. 1 in [6] implies that the underlying manifold contains a nontrivial incompressible \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional space form, contrary to our assumption. Consequently, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck with center at \( {x}_{j} \) or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap. Finally, Corollary 6.20 implies that \( \left| {D\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\mathrm{{scal}}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . In summary, we have shown that the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10. This contradicts statement (iii). This completes the proof of Theorem 10.10.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given any \( 0 < \varepsilon  \leq  {\bar{\varepsilon }}_{0} \) (for some sufficiently small universal constant \( {\bar{\varepsilon }}_{0} \) ), suppose we have constructed the sequences satisfying the proposition for \( 1 \leq  j \leq  m \) (for some positive integer \( m \) ). Then there exists \( \kappa  > 0 \) , such that for any \( r,0 < r < \varepsilon \) , one can find \( \widetilde{\delta } = \widetilde{\delta }\left( {r,\varepsilon }\right) ,0 < \widetilde{\delta } < {\varepsilon }^{2} \) , which may also depend on the already constructed sequences, with the following property. Suppose we have a solution with a compact orientable normalized three-manifold as initial data, to the Ricci flow with finite number of surgeries on a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{T}}\right\rbrack \) with \( m{\varepsilon }^{2} \leq  \bar{T} < \left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2} \) , satisfying the assumptions and the conclusions of Proposition 7.4.1 on \( \left\lbrack  {0, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) , and the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r \) on \( \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\bar{T}}\right\rbrack \) , as well as \( 0 < \delta \left( t\right)  \leq  \min \{ \widetilde{\delta },\bar{\delta }\left( t\right) \} \) for any \( \delta \) -cutoff surgery with \( \delta  = \delta \left( t\right) \) at a time \( t \in \; \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2},\bar{T}}\right\rbrack \) . Then the solution is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on \( \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{T}}\right\rbrack \) for all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Consider a parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}, - {r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  \triangleq  \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  x \in  {B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\}
\]

with \( m{\varepsilon }^{2} \leq  {t}_{0} \leq  \bar{T} \) and \( 0 < {r}_{0} < \varepsilon \) , where the solution satisfies \( \left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , whenever it is defined. We will use an argument analogous to the proof of Theorem 3.3.2 (no local collapsing theorem I) to prove

(7.4.1)

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}_{0}^{3}\text{ . }
\]

Let \( \eta \) be the universal positive constant in the definition of the canonical neighborhood assumption. Without loss of generality, we always assume \( \eta  \geq  {10} \) . Firstly, we want to show that one may assume \( {r}_{0} \geq  \frac{1}{2\eta }r \) .

Obviously, the curvature satisfies the estimate

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {20}{r}_{0}^{-2},
\]

for those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{1}{2\eta }{r}_{0}, - \frac{1}{8\eta }{r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  = \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  x \in  {B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{2\eta }{r}_{0}}\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - \frac{1}{8\eta }{r}_{0}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the solution is defined. When \( {r}_{0} < \frac{1}{2\eta }r \) , we can enlarge \( {r}_{0} \) to some \( {r}_{0}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{r}_{0}, r}\right\rbrack \) so that

\[
\left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  {20}{r}_{0}^{\prime  - 2}
\]

on \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{1}{2\eta }{r}_{0}^{\prime }, - \frac{1}{8\eta }{r}_{0}^{\prime 2}}\right) \) (whenever it is defined), and either the equality holds somewhere in \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{1}{2\eta }{r}_{0}^{\prime }, - \left( {\frac{1}{8\eta }{r}_{0}^{\prime 2} + {\epsilon }^{\prime }}\right) }\right) \) for any arbitrarily small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) or \( {r}_{0}^{\prime } = r \) .

In the case that the equality holds somewhere, it follows from the pinching assumption that we have

\[
R > {10}{r}_{0}^{\prime  - 2}
\]

somewhere in \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{1}{2\eta }{r}_{0}^{\prime }, - \left( {\frac{1}{8\eta }{r}_{0}^{\prime }{}^{2} + {\epsilon }^{\prime }}\right) }\right) \) for any arbitrarily small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) . Here, without loss of generality, we have assumed \( r \) is suitably small. Then by the gradient estimates in the definition of the canonical neighborhood assumption, we know

\[
R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  > {r}_{0}^{\prime  - 2} \geq  {r}^{-2}.
\]

Hence the desired noncollapsing estimate (7.4.1) in this case follows directly from the canonical neighborhood assumption. (Recall that we have excluded every compact component which has positive sectional curvature in the surgery procedure and then we have excluded them from the list of canonical neighborhoods. Here we also used the standard volume comparison when the canonical neighborhood is an \( \varepsilon \) -cap.)

While in the case that \( {r}_{0}^{\prime } = r \) , we have the curvature bound

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {\left( \frac{1}{2\eta }r\right) }^{-2},
\]

for those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{1}{2\eta }r, - {\left( \frac{1}{2\eta }r\right) }^{2}}\right)  = \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right) \left| {\;x \in  {B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{2\eta }r}\right) }\right. , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - }\right. }\right. \; \left. \left. {{\left( \frac{1}{2\eta }r\right) }^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  \right\} \) , for which the solution is defined. It follows from the standard volume comparison that we only need to verify the noncollapsing estimate (7.4.1) for \( {r}_{0} = \frac{1}{2\eta }r \) . Thus we have reduced the proof to the case \( {r}_{0} \geq  \frac{1}{2\eta }r \) .

Recall from Theorem 3.3.2 that if a solution is smooth everywhere, we can get a lower bound for the volume of the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) as follows: define \( \tau \left( t\right)  = {t}_{0} - t \) and consider Perelman's reduced volume function and the Li-Yau-Perelman distance associated to the point \( {x}_{0} \) ; take a point \( \bar{x} \) at the time \( t = {\varepsilon }^{2} \) so that the Li-Yau-Perelman distance \( l \) attains its minimum \( {l}_{\min }\left( \tau \right)  = l\left( {\bar{x},\tau }\right)  \leq  \frac{3}{2} \) for \( \tau  = {t}_{0} - {\varepsilon }^{2} \) ; use it to obtain an upper bound for the Li-Yau-Perelman distance from \( {x}_{0} \) to each point of \( {B}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},1}\right) \) , thus getting a lower bound for Perelman’s reduced volume at \( \tau  = {t}_{0} \) ; apply the monotonicity of Perelman's reduced volume to deduce a lower bound for Perelman’s reduced volume at \( \tau \) near 0, and then get the desired estimate for the volume of the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) . Now since our solution has undergone surgeries, we need to localize this argument to the region which is unaffected by surgery.

We call a space-time curve in the solution track admissible if it stays in the spacetime region unaffected by surgery, and we call a space-time curve in the solution track a barely admissible curve if it is on the boundary of the set of admissible curves.

First of all, we want to estimate the \( \mathcal{L} \) -length of a barely admissible curve.

CLAIM. For any \( L < \infty \) one can find \( \bar{\delta } = \bar{\delta }\left( {L, r,{\widetilde{r}}_{m},\varepsilon }\right)  > 0 \) with the following property. Suppose that we have a curve \( \gamma \) , parametrized by \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{T}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  ,\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2} \leq \; {T}_{0} < {t}_{0} \) , such that \( \gamma \left( {t}_{0}\right)  = {x}_{0},{T}_{0} \) is a surgery time, and \( \gamma \left( {T}_{0}\right) \) lies in the gluing cap. Suppose also each \( \delta \) -cutoff surgery at a time in \( \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2},\bar{T}}\right\rbrack \) has \( \delta  \leq  \bar{\delta } \) . Then we have an estimate

(7.4.2)

\[
{\int }_{{T}_{0}}^{{t}_{0}}\sqrt{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {{R}_{ + }\left( {\gamma \left( t\right) , t}\right)  + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\left( t\right) \right| }^{2}}\right) {dt} \geq  L
\]

where \( {R}_{ + } = \max \{ R,0\} \) .

Since \( {r}_{0} \geq  \frac{1}{2\eta }r \) and \( \left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) on \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}, - {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) \) (whenever it is defined), we can require \( \bar{\delta } > 0 \) , depending on \( r \) and \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m} \) , to be so small that \( \gamma \left( {T}_{0}\right) \) does not lie in the region \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}, - {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) \) . Let \( {\Delta t} \) be the maximal number such that \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  {t}_{0} - \Delta t,{t}_{0}\right\rbrack  } \subset \; P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}, - {\Delta t}}\right) \) (i.e., \( {t}_{0} - {\Delta t} \) is the first time when \( \gamma \) escapes the parabolic region \( \left. {P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}, - {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) }\right) \) . Obviously we only need to consider the case:

\[
{\int }_{{t}_{0} - {\Delta t}}^{{t}_{0}}\sqrt{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {{R}_{ + }\left( {\gamma \left( t\right) , t}\right)  + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\left( t\right) \right| }^{2}}\right) {dt} < L.
\]

We observe that \( {\Delta t} \) can be bounded from below in terms of \( L \) and \( {r}_{0} \) . Indeed, if \( {\Delta t} \geq  {r}_{0}^{2} \) , there is nothing to prove. Thus we may assume \( {\Delta t} < {r}_{0}^{2} \) . By the curvature bound \( \left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) on \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}, - {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) \) and the Ricci flow equation we see

\[
{\int }_{{t}_{0} - {\Delta t}}^{{t}_{0}}\left| {\dot{\gamma }\left( t\right) }\right| {dt} \geq  c{r}_{0}
\]

for some universal positive constant \( c \) . On the other hand, by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we have

\[
{\int }_{{t}_{0} - {\Delta t}}^{{t}_{0}}\left| {\dot{\gamma }\left( t\right) }\right| {dt} \leq  {\left( {\int }_{{t}_{0} - {\Delta t}}^{{t}_{0}}\sqrt{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {R}_{ + } + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}\right) dt\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \cdot  {\left( {\int }_{{t}_{0} - {\Delta t}}^{{t}_{0}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}_{0} - t}}dt\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}
\]

\[
\leq  {\left( 2L\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}{\left( \Delta t\right) }^{\frac{1}{4}}
\]

which implies

(7.4.3)

\[
{\left( \Delta t\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \geq  \frac{{c}^{2}{r}_{0}^{2}}{2L}.
\]

Thus

\[
{\int }_{{T}_{0}}^{{t}_{0}}\sqrt{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {{R}_{ + } + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}}\right) {dt} \geq  {\int }_{{T}_{0}}^{{t}_{0} - {\Delta t}}\sqrt{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {{R}_{ + } + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}}\right) {dt}
\]

\[
\geq  {\left( \Delta t\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}{\int }_{{T}_{0}}^{{t}_{0} - {\Delta t}}\left( {{R}_{ + } + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}}\right) {dt}
\]

\[
\left. { \geq  \left( {\min \left\{  {\frac{{c}^{2}{r}_{0}^{2}}{2L},{r}_{0}}\right\}  }\right) {\int }_{{T}_{0}}^{{t}_{0} - {\Delta t}}\left( {{R}_{ + } + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}}\right) {dt}}\right)
\]

while by Corollary 7.3.7, we can find \( \bar{\delta } = \bar{\delta }\left( {L, r,{\widetilde{r}}_{m},\varepsilon }\right)  > 0 \) so small that

\[
{\int }_{{T}_{0}}^{{t}_{0} - {\Delta t}}\left( {{R}_{ + } + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}}\right) {dt} \geq  L{\left( \min \left\{  \frac{{c}^{2}{r}_{0}^{2}}{2L},{r}_{0}\right\}  \right) }^{-1}.
\]

Then we have proved the desired assertion (7.4.2).

Recall that for a curve \( \gamma \) , parametrized by \( \tau  = {t}_{0} - t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{\tau }}\right\rbrack \) , with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = {x}_{0} \) and \( \bar{\tau } \leq  {t}_{0} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2} \) , we have \( L\left( \gamma \right)  = {\int }_{0}^{\bar{\tau }}\sqrt{\tau }\left( {R + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}}\right) {d\tau } \) . We can also define \( {L}_{ + }\left( \gamma \right) \) by replacing \( R \) with \( {R}_{ + } \) in the previous formula. Recall that \( R \geq   - 1 \) at the initial time \( t = 0 \) for the normalized initial manifold. Recall that the surgeries occur at the parts where the scalar curvatures are very large. Thus we can apply the maximum principle to conclude that the solution with surgery still satisfies \( R \geq   - 1 \) everywhere in space-time. This implies

(7.4.4)

\[
{L}_{ + }\left( \gamma \right)  \leq  L\left( \gamma \right)  + {\left( 2{\varepsilon }^{2}\right) }^{\frac{3}{2}}.
\]

By applying the assertion (7.4.2), we now choose \( \widetilde{\delta } > 0 \) (depending on \( r,\varepsilon \) and \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m} \) ) such that as each \( \delta \) -cutoff surgery at the time interval \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, T}\right\rbrack \) has \( \delta  \leq  \widetilde{\delta } \) , every barely admissible curve \( \gamma \) from \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) to a point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) (with \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2},{t}_{0}}\right) \) ) has

\[
{L}_{ + }\left( \gamma \right)  \geq  {22}\sqrt{2}.
\]

Thus if the Li-Yau-Perelman distance from \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) to a point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) (with \( t \in  \lbrack (m - \; 1){\varepsilon }^{2},{t}_{0})) \) is achieved by a space-time curve which is not admissible, then its Li-Yau-Perelman distance has

(7.4.5)

\[
l \geq  \frac{{L}_{ + } - {\left( 2{\varepsilon }^{2}\right) }^{\frac{3}{2}}}{2\sqrt{2}\varepsilon } > {10}{\varepsilon }^{-1}.
\]

We also observe that the absolute value of \( l\left( {{x}_{0},\tau }\right) \) is very small as \( \tau \) closes to zere. Thus the maximum principle argument in Corollary 3.2.6 still works for our solutions with surgery because barely admissible curves do not attain the minimum. So we conclude that

\[
{l}_{\min }\left( \bar{\tau }\right)  = \min \{ l\left( {x,\bar{\tau }}\right)  \mid  x\text{ lies in the solution manifold at }{t}_{0} - \bar{\tau }\}  \leq  \frac{3}{2}
\]

for \( \bar{\tau } \in  \left( {0,{t}_{0} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) . In particular, there exists a minimizing curve \( \gamma \) of \( {l}_{\min }\left( {{t}_{0} - }\right. \; \left. {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) , defined on \( \tau  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = {x}_{0} \) , such that

(7.4.6)

\[
{L}_{ + }\left( \gamma \right)  \leq  \frac{3}{2} \cdot  2\sqrt{2}\varepsilon  + 2\sqrt{2}{\varepsilon }^{3}
\]

\[
\leq  {5\varepsilon }
\]

since \( 0 < \varepsilon  \leq  {\bar{\varepsilon }}_{0} \) with \( {\bar{\varepsilon }}_{0} \) sufficiently small (to be further determined). Consequently, there exists a point \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) on the minimizing curve \( \gamma \) with \( \bar{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2} + \frac{1}{4}{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m - }\right. }\right. \) 1) \( {\varepsilon }^{2} + \frac{3}{4}{\varepsilon }^{2}\rbrack \) (i.e., \( \tau  \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2} - \frac{3}{4}{\varepsilon }^{2},{t}_{0} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2} - \frac{1}{4}{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) ) such that

(7.4.7)

\[
R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  \leq  {25}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{-2}.
\]

Otherwise, we have

\[
{L}_{ + }\left( \gamma \right)  \geq  {\int }_{{t}_{0} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2} - \frac{1}{4}{\varepsilon }^{2}}^{{t}_{0} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2} - \frac{1}{4}{\varepsilon }^{2}}\sqrt{\tau }R\left( {\gamma \left( \tau \right) ,{t}_{0} - \tau }\right) {d\tau }
\]

\[
> {25}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{-2}\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}{\varepsilon }^{2}}\left( {\frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right)
\]

\[
> {5\varepsilon }
\]

since \( 0 < {\widetilde{r}}_{m} < \varepsilon \) . This contradicts (7.4.6).

Next we want to get a lower bound for Perelman's reduced volume of a ball around \( \bar{x} \) of radius about \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m} \) at some time slightly before \( \bar{t} \) .

Denote by \( {\theta }_{1} = \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1} \) and \( {\theta }_{2} = \frac{1}{64}{\eta }^{-1} \) , where \( \eta \) is the universal positive constant in the gradient estimates (7.3.4). Since the solution satisfies the canonical neighborhood assumption on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) , it follows from the gradient estimates (7.3.4) that

(7.4.8)

\[
R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {400}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{-2}
\]

for those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}, - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\right)  \triangleq  \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {B}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the solution is defined. And since the scalar curvature at the points where the \( \delta \) -cutoff surgeries occur in the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) is at least \( {\left( \widetilde{\delta }\right) }^{-2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{-2} \) , the solution is well-defined on the whole parabolic region \( P\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}, - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\right) \) (i.e., this parabolic region is unaffected by surgery). Thus by combining (7.4.6) and (7.4.8), we know that the Li-Yau-Perelman distance from \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) to each point of the ball \( {B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) \) is uniformly bounded by some universal constant. Let us define Perelman’s reduced volume of the ball \( {B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) \) , by

\[
{\widetilde{V}}_{{t}_{0} - \bar{t} + {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {{B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= {\int }_{{B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) }{\left( 4\pi \left( {t}_{0} - \bar{t} + {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}
\]

\[
\cdot  \exp \left( {-l\left( {q,{t}_{0} - \bar{t} + {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\right) }\right) d{V}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( q\right) ,
\]

where \( l\left( {q,\tau }\right) \) is the Li-Yau-Perelman distance from \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Hence by the \( {\kappa }_{{m}^{ - }} \) noncollapsing assumption on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) , we conclude that Perelman’s reduced volume of the ball \( {B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) \) is bounded from below by a positive constant depending only on \( {\kappa }_{m} \) and \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m} \) .

Finally we want to apply a local version of the monotonicity of Perelman's reduced volume to get a lower bound estimate for the volume of the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) .

We have seen that the Li-Yau-Perelman distance from \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) to each point of the ball \( {B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) \) is uniformly bounded by some universal constant. Now we can choose a sufficiently small (universal) positive constant \( {\bar{\varepsilon }}_{0} \) such that when \( 0 < \varepsilon  \leq  {\bar{\varepsilon }}_{0} \) , by (7.4.5), all the points in the ball \( {B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) \) can be connected to \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) by shortest \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesics, and all of these \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesics are admissible (i.e., they stay in the region unaffected by surgery). The union of all shortest \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesics from \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) to the ball \( {B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) \) defined by \( C{B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right)  = \{ \left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  \left( {x, t}\right) \) lies in a shortest \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic from \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) to a point in \( \left. {{B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) }\right\} \) , forms a conelike subset in space-time with the vertex \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Denote \( B\left( t\right) \) by the intersection of the cone-like subset \( C{B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) \) with the time-slice at \( t \) . Perelman’s reduced volume of the subset \( B\left( t\right) \) is given by

\[
{\widetilde{V}}_{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {B\left( t\right) }\right)  = {\int }_{B\left( t\right) }{\left( 4\pi \left( {t}_{0} - t\right) \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,{t}_{0} - t}\right) }\right) d{V}_{t}\left( q\right) .
\]

Since the cone-like subset \( C{B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) \) lies entirely in the region unaffected by surgery, we can apply Perelman's Jacobian comparison theorem (Theorem 3.2.7) to conclude that

(7.4.9)

\[
{\widetilde{V}}_{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {B\left( t\right) }\right)  \geq  {\widetilde{V}}_{{t}_{0} - \bar{t} + {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {{B}_{\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2}}\left( {\bar{x},{\theta }_{1}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\geq  c\left( {{\kappa }_{m},{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right)
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} - {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , where \( c\left( {{\kappa }_{m},{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) \) is some positive constant depending only on \( {\kappa }_{m} \) and \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m} \) .

Set \( \xi  = {r}_{0}^{-1}{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}{\left( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x}_{0},{r}_{0}\right) \right) }^{\frac{1}{3}} \) . Our purpose is to give a positive lower bound for \( \xi \) . Without loss of generality, we may assume \( \xi  < \frac{1}{4} \) , thus \( 0 < \xi {r}_{0}^{2} < {t}_{0} - \bar{t} + {\theta }_{2}{\widetilde{r}}_{m}^{2} \) . Denote by \( \widetilde{B}\left( {{t}_{0} - \xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) \) the subset of the time-slice \( \left\{  {t = {t}_{0} - \xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right\} \) of which every point can be connected to \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) by an admissible shortest \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic. Clearly, \( B\left( {{t}_{0} - \xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  \subset  \widetilde{B}\left( {{t}_{0} - \xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) \) . We now argue as in the proof of Theorem 3.3.2 to bound Perelman’s reduced volume of \( \widetilde{B}\left( {{t}_{0} - \xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) \) from above.

Since \( {r}_{0} \geq  \frac{1}{2\eta }r \) and \( \widetilde{\delta } = \widetilde{\delta }\left( {r,\varepsilon ,{\widetilde{r}}_{m}}\right) \) sufficiently small, the whole region \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right. \) , \( \left. {-{r}_{0}^{2}}\right) \) is unaffected by surgery. Then by exactly the same argument as in deriving (3.3.5), we see that there exists a universal positive constant \( {\xi }_{0} \) such that when \( 0 < \; \xi  \leq  {\xi }_{0} \) , there holds

(7.4.10)

\[
\mathcal{L}{\exp }_{\left\{  \left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right\}  }\left( {\xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  \subset  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) .
\]

Perelman’s reduced volume of \( \widetilde{B}\left( {{t}_{0} - \xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) \) is given by

\[
\text{ (7.4.11) }{\widetilde{V}}_{\xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {\widetilde{B}\left( {{t}_{0} - \xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= {\int }_{\overrightarrow{B}\left( {{t}_{0} - \xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) }{\left( 4\pi \xi {r}_{0}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,\xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - \xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( q\right)
\]

\[
= {\int }_{\widetilde{B}\left( {{t}_{0} - \xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  \cap  \mathcal{L}\exp \left\{  {\left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\}  }{\left( 4\pi \xi {r}_{0}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,\xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - \xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( q\right)
\]

\[
+ {\int }_{\widetilde{B}\left( {{t}_{0} - \xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  \smallsetminus  \mathcal{L}\exp \left\{  {\left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\}  }{\left( 4\pi \xi {r}_{0}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,\xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - \xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( q\right) .
\]

The first term on the RHS of (7.4.11) can be estimated by

(7.4.12)

\[
{\int }_{\bar{B}\left( {{t}_{0} - \xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  \cap  \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{\{ \left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\} }\left( {\xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) }{\left( 4\pi \xi {r}_{0}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,\xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - \xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( q\right)
\]

\[
\leq  {e}^{C\xi }{\left( 4\pi \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}} \cdot  {\xi }^{\frac{3}{2}}
\]

for some universal constant \( C \) , as in deriving (3.3.7). While as in deriving (3.3.8), the second term on the RHS of (7.4.11) can be estimated by

(7.4.13)

\[
{\int }_{\widetilde{B}\left( {{t}_{0} - \xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  \smallsetminus  \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{\{ \left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\} }\left( {\xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) }{\left( 4\pi \xi {r}_{0}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,\xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - \xi {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( q\right)
\]

\[
\leq  {\int }_{\left\{  \left| v\right|  > \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right\}  }{\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}{\left. \exp \left( -l\left( \tau \right) \right) \mathcal{J}\left( \tau \right) \right| }_{\tau  = 0}{dv}
\]

\[
= {\left( 4\pi \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}{\int }_{\left\{  \left| v\right|  > \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right\}  }\exp \left( {-{\left| v\right| }^{2}}\right) {dv},
\]

where we have used Perelman's Jacobian comparison theorem (Theorem 3.2.7) in the first inequality. Hence the combination of (7.4.9), (7.4.11), (7.4.12) and (7.4.13) bounds \( \xi \) from below by a positive constant depending only on \( {\kappa }_{m} \) and \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m} \) . Therefore we have completed the proof of the lemma.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
By supposition, for each \( b \) there is a point \( x \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) at which the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption fails for the parameter \( {r}_{a} \) . We call points at which this condition fails counterexample points. Of course, since \( {r}_{a} \leq  {r}_{i} \) and since the restriction of \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) },{g}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) to \( {\mathbf{t}}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{i}}\right) \right) \) satisfies the hypothesis of the proposition, we see that any counterexample point \( x \) has \( \mathbf{t}\left( x\right)  \geq  {T}_{i} \) . Take a sequence \( {x}_{n} = {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) of counterexample points with \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n + 1}\right)  \leq  \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right) \) for all \( n \) that minimizes \( \mathbf{t} \) among all counterexample points in the sense that for any \( \xi  > 0 \) and for any counterexample point \( x \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) eventually \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right)  < \mathbf{t}\left( x\right)  + \xi \) . Let \( {t}^{\prime } = {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right) \) . Clearly, \( {t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{T}_{i},{T}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) , and by construction the restriction of \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) },{G}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) to \( {\mathbf{t}}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {0,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \right) \) satisfies the \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {r}_{a} \) . Since the surgery times are discrete, there is \( {t}^{\prime \prime } = {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime \prime } \) with \( {t}^{\prime } < {t}^{\prime \prime } \leq  {T}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) and a diffeomorphism \( \psi  = {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) } : {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right)  \rightarrow  {\mathbf{t}}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \right) \) compatible with time and the vector field. We view \( {\psi }^{ * }{G}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) as a one-parameter family of metrics \( g\left( t\right)  = {g}_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( t\right) \) on \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \) . By passing to a subsequence we can arrange that \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right)  \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \) for all \( n \) . Thus, for each \( n \) there are \( {y}_{n} = {y}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \in  {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) and \( {t}_{n} \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \) with \( \psi \left( {{y}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right)  = {x}_{n} \) . Since \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is a compact 3-manifold, by passing to a further subsequence we can assume that \( {y}_{n} \rightarrow  {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . Of course, \( {t}_{n} \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}{x}_{n} = {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b,\right) } \) .

We claim that, for all \( b \) sufficiently large, the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {r}_{a} \) fails at \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . Notice that since \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is the limit of a sequence where the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -neighborhood assumption fails, the points in the sequence converging to \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) have scalar curvature at least \( {r}_{a}^{-2} \) . It follows that \( R\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right)  \geq  {r}_{a}^{-2} \) . Suppose that \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) satisfies the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {r}_{a} \) . This means that there is a neighborhood \( U = {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) of \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) which is a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood of \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . According to Definition 9.78 there are four possibilities. The first two we consider are that \( \left( {U, g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) }\right) \) is an \( \epsilon \) -round component or a \( C \) -component. In either of these cases, since the defining inequalities given in Definition 9.76 and 9.75 are strong inequalities, all metrics on \( U \) sufficiently close to \( g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) - topology satisfy these same inequalities. But as \( n \) tends to \( \infty \) , the metrics \( {\left. g\left( {t}_{n}\right) \right| }_{U} \) converge in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to \( {\left. g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \right| }_{U} \) . Thus, in these two cases, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the metrics \( g\left( {t}_{n}\right) \) on \( U \) are \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood metrics of the same type as \( {\left. g\left( {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }\right) \right| }_{U} \) . Hence, in either of these cases, for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood of the same type as \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) , contrary to our assumption about the sequence \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) .

Now suppose that there is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . This is to say that \( \left( {U, g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) }\right) \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . By Proposition 9.79, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( \left( {U, g\left( {t}_{n}\right) }\right) \) is also a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap with the same core. This core contains \( {y}_{n} \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, showing that \( {x}_{n} \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap for all \( n \) sufficiently large.

Now let us consider the remaining case when \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. In this case we have an embedding

\[
{\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} : {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \times  \left( {{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - {R}^{-1}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) ,{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) }
\]

compatible with time and the vector field and a diffeomorphism \( {f}_{\left( a, b\right) } : {S}^{2} \times \; \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)  \rightarrow  {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) such that

\[
{\left( {f}_{\left( a, b\right) } \times  \mathrm{{Id}}\right) }^{ * }{\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }}^{ * }\left( {R\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) {G}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right)
\]

is \( \epsilon \) -close in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology to the evolving product metric

\[
{h}_{0}\left( t\right)  \times  d{s}^{2}, - 1 < t \leq  0,
\]

where \( {h}_{0}\left( t\right) \) is a round metric of scalar curvature \( 1/\left( {1 - t}\right) \) on \( {S}^{2} \) and \( d{s}^{2} \) is the Euclidean metric on the interval. Here, there are two subcases to consider.

(i) \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) extends backward past \( {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - {R}^{-1}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) .

(ii) There is a flow line through a point \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) that is defined on the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - {R}^{-1}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) ,{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) but with the value of the flow line at \( {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - {R}^{-1}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) an exposed point.

Let us consider the first subcase. The embedding \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) extends forward in time because of the diffeomorphism \( {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) } : {M}_{{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime },{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime \prime }}\right)  \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) and, by assumption, \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) extends backward in time some amount. Thus, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, we can use these extensions of \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) to define an embedding \( {\psi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } : {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \times  \left( {\mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }\right)  - {R}^{-1}\left( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }\right) ,\mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }\right) \rbrack  \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right. \) compatible with time and the vector field. Furthermore, since the \( {\psi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) converge in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) as \( n \) tends to infinity, the Riemannian metrics \( {\left( {f}_{\left( a, b\right) } \times  \mathrm{{Id}}\right) }^{ * }{\psi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }^{ * }\left( {R\left( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }\right) {G}_{a, b}}\right) \) converge in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to the pullback \( {\left( {f}_{\left( a, b\right) } \times  \mathrm{{Id}}\right) }^{ * }{\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }}^{ * }\left( {R\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) {G}_{a, b}}\right) \) . Clearly then, for fixed \( \left( {a, b}\right) \) and for all \( n \) sufficiently large the pullbacks of the rescalings of these metrics by \( R\left( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }\right) \) are within \( \epsilon \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology of the standard evolving flow \( {h}_{0}\left( t\right)  \times  d{s}^{2}, - 1 < t \leq  0 \) , on the product of \( {S}^{2} \) with the interval. Under these identifications the points \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) correspond to points

\[
\left( {{p}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) },{s}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }}\right)  \in  {S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)
\]

where \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}{s}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } = 0 \) . The last thing we do is to choose diffeomorphisms \( {\varphi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } : \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) that are the identity near both ends, such that \( {\varphi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) carries 0 to \( {s}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) and such that the \( {\varphi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) converge to the identity in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology for fixed \( \left( {a, b}\right) \) as \( n \) tends to infinity. Then, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the composition

\[
{S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \overset{\operatorname{Id} \times  {\varphi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }}{ \rightarrow  }{S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \overset{{f}_{\left( a, b\right) }}{ \rightarrow  }U\overset{{\psi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }}{ \rightarrow  }{\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) }
\]

is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) . This shows that for any \( b \) for which the first subcase holds, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, there is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) .

Now suppose that the second subcase holds for all \( b \) . Here, unlike all previous cases, we shall have to let \( b \) vary and we shall prove the result only for \( b \) sufficiently large. We shall show that for all \( b \) sufficiently large, \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. This will establish the result by contradiction, for as we showed in the previous case, if \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap, then the same is true for the \( {x}_{n} \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, contrary to our assumption.

For the moment fix \( b \) . Set \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } = {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - {R}_{{G}_{\left( a, b\right) }}{\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) }^{-1} \) . Since, by supposition the embedding \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) does not extend backwards past \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) , it must be the case that \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is a surgery time and furthermore that there is a surgery cap \( {\mathcal{C}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) at this time with the property that there is a point \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) such that \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\left( {{y}_{\left( a, b\right) }, t}\right) \) converges to a point \( {z}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {\mathcal{C}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) as \( t \) tends to \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) from above. (See FIG. 1.) We denote by \( {p}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) the tip of \( {\mathcal{C}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) , and we denote by \( {\bar{h}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) the scale of the surgery at time \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) .

Since the statement that \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap is a scale invariant statement, we are free to replace \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) },{G}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) with \( \left( {{\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{\left( a, b\right) },{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) , which has been rescaled to make \( {\bar{h}}_{\left( a, b\right) } = 1 \) and shifted in time so that \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } = 0 \) . We denote the new time function by \( \widetilde{\mathbf{t}} \) . (Notice that this rescaling and time-shifting is different from what we usually do. Normally, when we have a base point like \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) we rescale to make its scalar curvature 1 and we shift time to make it be at time 0 . Here we have rescaled based on the scale of the surgery cap rather than \( R\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) .) We set \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } = \; {R}_{{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) and we set \( {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } = \widetilde{\mathbf{t}}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) . Since the initial time of the strong \( \epsilon \) -neck is zero, \( {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } = {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1} \) . We denote the flow line backward in time from \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) by \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( \widetilde{t}\right) ,0 \leq  \widetilde{t} \leq  {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } \) , so that \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }\right)  = {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . Since \( {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck, by our choice of \( \epsilon \) , it follows from Lemma A. 2 and rescaling that \( R\left( {\psi \left( {{y}_{\left( a, b\right) },\widetilde{t}}\right) }\right) \) is within \( \left( {0.01}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) of \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }/\left( {1 + {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - \widetilde{t}}\right) }\right) \) for all \( t \in  \left( {0,{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) . By taking limits as \( t \) approaches 0, we see that \( {R}_{{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\left( {z}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) is within \( \left( {0.01}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) of \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }/2 \) . Let \( D \) be the universal constant given in Lemma 12.3, so that the scalar curvature at any point of the standard initial metric is at least \( {D}^{-1} \) and at most \( D \) . It follows from the third item in Theorem 13.2 that, since we have rescaled to make the surgery scale 1, for all \( b \) sufficiently large the scalar curvature on the surgery \( {\mathcal{C}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is at least \( {\left( 2D\right) }^{-1} \) and at most \( {2D} \) . In particular, for all \( b \) sufficiently large

\[
{\left( 2D\right) }^{-1} \leq  {R}_{\widetilde{G}\left( {a, b}\right) }\left( {z}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right)  \leq  {2D}.
\]

Together with the above estimate relating \( {R}_{{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\left( {z}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) and \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) , this gives

(17.1)

\[
{\left( 5D\right) }^{-1} \leq  {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \leq  {5D}.
\]

Since the flow line from \( {z}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) to \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) lies in the closure of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck of scale \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1/2} \) , the scalar curvature is less than \( {6D} \) at every point of this flow line. According to Proposition 12.31 there is \( {\theta }_{1} < 1 \) (depending only on \( D \) ) such that \( R\left( {q, t}\right)  \geq  {8D} \) for all \( \left( {q, t}\right) \) in the standard solution with \( t \geq  {\theta }_{1} \) .

![019eafdb-e076-77f6-81c2-3ca4f7500935_41_452_584_887_382_0.jpg](images/019eafdb-e076-77f6-81c2-3ca4f7500935_41_452_584_887_382_0.jpg)

Figure 1. A strong neck with initial time in a surgery cap.

By the fifth property of Theorem 12.5 there is \( {A}^{\prime }\left( {\theta }_{1}\right)  < \infty \) such that in the standard flow, \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right) \) contains \( B\left( {{p}_{0},{\theta }_{1}, A/2}\right) \) for every \( A \geq  {A}^{\prime }\left( {\theta }_{1}\right) \) . We set \( A \) equal to the maximum of \( {A}^{\prime }\left( {\theta }_{1}\right) \) and

\[
3\left( {\left( {1.2}\right) \sqrt{5D}{\epsilon }^{-1} + \left( {1.1}\right) \left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right)  + C\sqrt{5D}}\right) .
\]

Now for any \( \bar{\delta } > 0 \) for all \( b \) sufficiently large, we have \( {\delta }_{\left( a, b\right) } \leq  {\delta }^{\prime \prime }\left( {A,{\theta }_{1},\bar{\delta }}\right) \) , where \( {\delta }^{\prime \prime }\left( {A,{\theta }_{1},\bar{\delta }}\right) \) is the constant given in Proposition 16.13.

CLAIM 17.3. Suppose \( b \) is sufficiently large so that \( {\delta }_{\left( a, b\right) } \leq  {\delta }^{\prime \prime }\left( {A,{\theta }_{1},{\bar{\delta }}_{0}}\right) \) , where \( {\bar{\delta }}_{0} \) is the constant given in Definition 16.12. Then \( {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } \leq  {\theta }_{1} \) .

Proof. In this proof we shall fix \( \left( {a, b}\right) \) , so we drop these indices from the notation. Consider \( s \leq  {\theta }_{1} \) maximal so that there is an embedding

\[
\psi  = {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) } : B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right)  \times  \lbrack 0, s) \rightarrow  {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{\left( a, b\right) }
\]

compatible with time and the vector field. First suppose that \( s < {\theta }_{1} \) . Then according to Proposition 16.5 either the entire ball \( B\left( {p,0, A}\right) \) disappears at time \( s \) or \( s \) is the final time of the time interval of definition for the flow \( \left( {{\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{\left( a, b\right) },{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) . Since we have the flow line from \( z \in  B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right) \) extending to time \( {\widetilde{t}}^{\prime } = {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } \) , in either case this implies that \( {\widetilde{t}}^{\prime } < s \) , proving that \( {t}^{\prime } < {\theta }_{1} \) in this case.

Now suppose that \( s = {\theta }_{1} \) . By the choice of \( {\theta }_{1} \) , for the standard solution the scalar curvature at every \( \left( {q,{\theta }_{1}}\right) \) is at least \( {8D} \) . Since \( {\delta }_{\left( a, b\right) } \leq  {\delta }^{\prime \prime }\left( {A,{\theta }_{1},{\bar{\delta }}_{0}}\right) \) , by the definition of \( {\bar{\delta }}_{0} \) given in Definition 16.12 and by Proposition 16.5 the scalar curvature of the pullback of the metric under \( \psi \) is within a factor of 2 of the scalar curvature of the rescaled standard solution. Hence, the scalar curvature along the flow line \( \left( {z, t}\right) \) through \( z \) limits to at least \( {8D} \) as \( t \) tends to \( {\theta }_{1} \) . Since the scalar curvature on \( \left( {z, t}\right) \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{\widetilde{t}}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) is bounded above by \( {6D} \) , it follows that \( {\widetilde{t}}^{\prime } < {\theta }_{1} \) in this case as well. This completes the proof of the claim.

Thus, we have maps

\[
{\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) } : B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{\left( a, b\right) }
\]

compatible with time and the vector field, with the property that for each \( \delta  > 0 \) , for all \( b \) sufficiently large the pullback under this map of \( {\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is within \( \delta \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\delta \right\rbrack  } \) -topology of the restriction of the standard solution. Let \( {w}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) be the result of flowing \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) backward to time 0 .

CLAIM 17.4. For all \( b \) sufficiently large, \( {w}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right) \times \{ 0\} }\right) \) .

Proof. First notice that, by our choice of \( \epsilon \) , every point in the 0 time-slice of the closure of the strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is within distance (1.1) \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1}{\epsilon }^{-1} \) of \( {w}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . In particular,

\[
{d}_{{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\left( {{w}_{\left( a, b\right) },{y}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right)  < \left( {1.1}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1}.
\]

Since \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is contained in the surgery cap and the scale of the surgery at this time is \( 1,{y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is within distance \( {A}_{0} + 5 \) of \( {p}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . Hence, by the triangle inequality and Inequality (17.1), we have

\[
{d}_{{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\left( {{w}_{\left( a, b\right) },{p}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right)  < \left( {1.1}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1} + \left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right)
\]

\[
< \left( {1.1}\right) \sqrt{5D}{\epsilon }^{-1} + \left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) \text{ . }
\]

For \( b \) sufficiently large, the image \( {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right) }\right) \) contains the ball of radius \( \left( {0.95}\right) A \) centered at \( {p}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . Since by our choice of \( A \) we have \( \left( {0.95}\right) A > \) (1.1) \( \sqrt{5D}{\epsilon }^{-1} + \left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) \) , the claim follows.

We define \( {q}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right) \) so that \( {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {{q}_{\left( a, b\right) },0}\right)  = {w}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . Of course,

\[
{\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {{q}_{\left( a, b\right) },{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right)  = {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }.
\]

If follows from the above computation that for all \( b \) sufficiently large we have

\[
{d}_{0}\left( {{q}_{\left( a, b\right) },{p}_{0}}\right)  < \left( {1.15}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1} + \left( {1.05}\right) \left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) .
\]

Since the standard flow has non-negative curvature, it is a distance nonincreasing flow. Therefore,

\[
{d}_{{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\left( {{q}_{\left( a, b\right) },{p}_{0}}\right)  < \left( {1.15}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1} + \left( {1.05}\right) \left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) .
\]

Suppose that a point \( \left( {q,{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) in the standard solution were the center of a \( {\beta \epsilon }/3 \) -neck, where \( \beta \) is the constant from Proposition 15.2. Of course, for all \( b \) sufficiently large, \( R\left( {q,{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right)  > \left( {0.99}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . Since \( \beta  < 1/2 \) and \( \epsilon  < \sqrt{5D}\left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) /2 \) and \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \leq  {5D} \) , it follows from the above distance estimate that this neck would contain \( \left( {{p}_{0},{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) . But this is impossible: since \( \left( {{p}_{0},{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) is an isolated fixed point of an isometric \( {SO}\left( 3\right) \) -action on the standard flow, all the sectional curvatures at \( \left( {{p}_{0},{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) are equal, and this is in contradiction with estimates on the sectional curvatures at any point of an \( \epsilon \) -neck given in Lemma A.2. We can then conclude from Theorem 12.32 that for all \( b \) sufficiently large, the point \( \left( {{p}_{0},{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C\left( {{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right) ,{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right) \) -cap \( {Y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) in the \( {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } \) time-slice of the standard solution. Now note that for all \( b \) sufficiently large, the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{q}_{\left( a, b\right) },{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) is at least \( \left( {0.99}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) , since the scalar curvature of \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is equal to \( {Q}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . This implies that the diameter of \( {Y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is at most

\[
\text{ (1.01) }{\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1/2}C\left( {{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right)  < \left( {1.1}\right) \sqrt{5D}C\left( {{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right) \text{ . }
\]

Since \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right) \) contains \( B\left( {{p}_{0},{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }, A/2}\right) \) , and since \( C > C\left( {{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right) \) , it follows from the definition of \( A \) , the above distance estimate, and the triangle inequality that for all \( b \) sufficiently large \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right)  \times  \left\{  {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }\right\} \) contains \( {Y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) .

Since \( C > C\left( {{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right)  + 1 \) and since for \( b \) sufficiently large \( {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) }^{ * }{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is arbitrarily close to the restriction of the standard solution metric, it follows from Theorem 12.32 and Proposition 9.79 that for all \( b \) sufficiently large, the image \( {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {Y}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . As we have already remarked, this contradicts the assumption that no \( {x}_{n} \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood.

This completes the proof in the last case and establishes Lemma 17.2.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given any \( 0 < \varepsilon  \leq  {\bar{\varepsilon }}_{0} \) (for some sufficiently small universal constant \( {\bar{\varepsilon }}_{0} \) ), suppose we have constructed the sequences satisfying the proposition for \( 1 \leq  j \leq  m \) (for some positive integer \( m \) ). Then there exists \( \kappa  > 0 \) , such that for any \( r,0 < r < \varepsilon \) , one can find \( \widetilde{\delta } = \widetilde{\delta }\left( {r,\varepsilon }\right) ,0 < \widetilde{\delta } < {\varepsilon }^{2} \) , which may also depend on the already constructed sequences, with the following property. Suppose we have a solution with a compact orientable normalized three-manifold as initial data, to the Ricci flow with finite number of surgeries on a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{T}}\right\rbrack \) with \( m{\varepsilon }^{2} \leq  \bar{T} < \left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2} \) , satisfying the assumptions and the conclusions of Proposition 7.4.1 on \( \left\lbrack  {0, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) , and the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r \) on \( \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\bar{T}}\right\rbrack \) , as well as \( 0 < \delta \left( t\right)  \leq  \min \{ \widetilde{\delta },\bar{\delta }\left( t\right) \} \) for any \( \delta \) -cutoff surgery with \( \delta  = \delta \left( t\right) \) at a time \( t \in \; \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2},\bar{T}}\right\rbrack \) . Then the solution is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on \( \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{T}}\right\rbrack \) for all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) .
